stem:
A 6-week-old, ex-39-week, formula-fed, vaccinated-to-age boy is brought to ED by his mother after a measured rectal temperature of 38.4 deg C at home this morning. He has fed slightly less than usual for 6 hours but has had wet nappies, no vomiting, no diarrhoea, no rash and no cough. Maternal GBS negative at 36 weeks, membranes ruptured 4 hours, discharged day 2 without antibiotics.

He was previously well. On arrival he is alert, settles to feed, central capillary refill 2 seconds, no focus on examination (clear chest, soft abdomen, flat fontanelle, clean umbilicus). Recorded temperature in ED is 38.2 deg C. Initial bloods: WCC 9.8, neutrophils 5.2, lymphocytes 3.6, CRP 8. Catheter urinalysis: nitrites negative, leukocytes negative. T 38.2, HR 148, RR 42, SpO2 99 percent. The ED registrar is deciding whether lumbar puncture is required.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 degC, HR 148 bpm, RR 42, SpO2 99% RA, cap refill 2 s.
data_table.Examination: Alert, feeds well. No rash. Fontanelle flat. Chest clear. Abdomen soft. Umbilicus clean.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.8, neutrophils 5.2, lymphocytes 3.6, CRP 8 mg/L. Urine dip negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and open 24-hour GP review
Blood and urine cultures (catheter), lumbar puncture, then commence IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin plus cefotaxime; admit
Blood and urine cultures only and observe without antibiotics pending results
Oral amoxicillin and ED review at 24 hours
Chest x-ray and 4 hours observation without further investigation

subtopic_detail: Febrile young infant - septic workup criteria

stem:
A 3-year-old girl, weight 14 kg, presents to a regional ED at 02:30 with 18 hours of fever to 39.4 degC, reduced oral intake and increasing lethargy. She had a coryzal illness in the family last week. Past history includes mild eczema only and her vaccinations are up to date. On triage she is sleepy but rousable to voice, with mottled peripheries to the knees and elbows, cool hands and feet, a central capillary refill of 4 seconds, and a non-blanching petechial rash spreading on the trunk.

She has not passed urine since the previous evening. Temperature is 39.1 degC, heart rate 178 bpm, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 96% on room air, and non-invasive BP is 92/58 mmHg. She does not localise to pain on abdominal examination. The nurse has activated a Paediatric Early Warning Score escalation and IV access has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 degC, HR 178 bpm, RR 44, SpO2 96% RA, BP 92/58, cap refill 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Sleepy, rousable. Mottled to elbows/knees. Non-blanching petechial rash trunk. No neck stiffness elicited.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.28, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 4.1 mmol/L, BE -7.

lead_in: Which set of interventions best meets the paediatric sepsis 1-hour bundle?

options.text: IV adrenaline infusion as first intervention
Oral amoxicillin, 10 mL/kg saline bolus, then urgent CT head
Blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone, 20 mL/kg saline bolus, lactate, then reassess
Paracetamol PO and observation pending senior review
Lumbar puncture first, then IV antibiotics, then fluid bolus over 15 minutes

stem:
An 18-month-old boy weighing 11 kg (clinic weight 2 weeks ago 11.5 kg) presents with 36 hours of profuse non-bloody diarrhoea and three episodes of vomiting today. His older sibling had similar symptoms last week. He has been drinking some water but refuses solids. On examination he is irritable but consolable, with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, mildly delayed skin recoil, central capillary refill 2-3 seconds, warm peripheries and tears with crying.

Triage nappy was dry; the last wet nappy was 6 hours ago. HR 142, RR 28, T 37.4 deg C, BP 96/60. There is no abdominal mass and no peritonism.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 degC, HR 142 bpm, RR 28, BP 96/60, cap refill 2-3 s.
data_table.Examination: Irritable. Sunken eyes, dry mucosae. Tears present. Skin recoil mildly delayed. Warm peripheries.
data_table.Investigations: Weight 11 kg (4% below recent baseline 11.5 kg). Urine output reduced.

lead_in: Which combination of dehydration assessment and immediate rehydration plan is most appropriate?

options.text: No clinically detectable dehydration (under 3 percent); oral fluids ad lib at home without need for any structured rehydration regimen today
Mild to moderate dehydration ~4-6% (3-5 Gorelick signs, preserved consciousness/tears/BP, weight deficit 0.5/11.5 kg = ~4.3%); commence NGT or ORS at 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus losses
Severe dehydration (at least 10%) with compensated shock; resuscitate with 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline boluses repeated as needed in the resuscitation bay
Decompensated hypovolaemic shock from severe dehydration; intubate and resuscitate with rapid sequence induction and large-volume isotonic boluses now
Euvolaemic viral illness; reassure and discharge on oral fluids ad libitum with GP review in 24 hours and no structured rehydration regimen today

stem:
A 2-year-old girl, weight 12 kg, presents with 48 hours of viral gastroenteritis (vomiting and watery diarrhoea, no blood). She is assessed in ED as approximately 5-6% dehydrated: dry mucosae, sunken eyes, capillary refill 2 s, reduced urine output. She is alert and accepts sips of water but vomits a 30 mL bolus after 5 minutes. She has no ileus, no abdominal distension and no surgical concerns.

Electrolytes are not yet available. She has no significant comorbidity, no allergies and weighs near her plotted growth centile. The ED is busy and IV cannulation has been attempted unsuccessfully once. Her parents are willing to assist with whatever route is recommended. She has been in family day care this week where two other children have had similar symptoms. Her mother reports approximately 6-8 large watery stools per day and increasing thirst, and she has been refusing the Gastrolyte sachets the GP recommended yesterday because of taste. She has no underlying renal, cardiac or metabolic disease and was born at term with no neonatal complications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 degC, HR 138, RR 28, BP 98/62, cap refill 2 s.
data_table.Examination: Alert, irritable. Dry mucosae. Soft abdomen, no distension, no peritonism. Bowel sounds active.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L. No electrolytes yet.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate rehydration approach?

options.text: IV 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus then deficit IV over 24 hours
IV 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose at maintenance rate only, no bolus
Water and dilute apple juice ad libitum with GP review in 24 hours
Nasogastric oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours then reassess
Single ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg IV then discharge without any rehydration

stem:
A 5-year-old boy weighing 20 kg is brought to a school sick bay 10 minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich. He had a mild rash to peanut at age 2. Staff describe him as flushed with widespread urticaria, persistent coughing with audible wheeze, hoarse voice and reported throat tightness. He is anxious but responsive, sitting forward. He has no past history of asthma.

HR 138, RR 38, SpO2 94 percent on room air. There is no stridor at rest. His EpiPen Jr 150 microgram is in the school office and an ambulance has been called. He has not received any treatment yet.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 degC, HR 138 bpm, RR 38, SpO2 94% RA.
data_table.Examination: Flushed, widespread urticaria. Hoarse voice, throat tightness, audible wheeze. Sitting forward. No stridor at rest.
data_table.Investigations: None available in sick bay.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate action, including correct adrenaline dose for his weight?

options.text: Lay supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; IM adrenaline 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr) anterolateral mid-thigh - he weighs 20 kg, inside the 7.5-20 kg band
Salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer first as the primary bronchodilator and observe for response before considering any intramuscular adrenaline dose
Oral cetirizine and prednisolone with 1-hour observation in the surgery, deferring intramuscular adrenaline pending the antihistamine response
IM adrenaline 300 microgram (EpiPen) immediately without weight-checking, accepting the overdose risk in order to avoid any further delay
Withhold adrenaline as he is talking and responsive; await paramedic arrival before any intramuscular pharmacological intervention is given

stem:
A 10-year-old boy, weight 32 kg, presents to ED 25 minutes after a wasp sting with urticaria, lip swelling, stridor, expiratory wheeze and persistent hypotension. Paramedics gave IM adrenaline 300 microg en route. On arrival to ED 10 minutes later he remained tachypnoeic with stridor, wheeze and BP 78/40, so a second IM adrenaline 300 microg was given into the anterolateral thigh and an IV 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus was commenced.

Now 5 minutes after the second IM dose he remains drowsy with BP 82/44, HR 156, RR 40, SpO2 92% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather, with audible stridor and wheeze. Both IM doses were confirmed delivered correctly. The ED consultant is at the bedside, anaesthetics has been called for airway support, and a second IV line has been sited.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 82/44, HR 156, RR 40, SpO2 92% on 15 L NRB.
data_table.Examination: Drowsy. Stridor and expiratory wheeze. Lip and tongue swelling. Mottled peripheries.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.30, lactate 3.4 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Bolus IV adrenaline 1 mg (1:10,000) over 1 minute
Give IV hydrocortisone and IV promethazine
Commence IV adrenaline infusion, titrated to response
Continue IM adrenaline every 5 minutes only and avoid IV adrenaline
Commence IV glucagon as first-line, no further adrenaline

subtopic_detail: Refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses

stem:
A 4-year-old girl, weight 16 kg, is brought into ED by ambulance with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that began at home 12 minutes ago. Paramedics gave buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg 8 minutes after onset, but the seizure has continued. On arrival she is convulsing, with intact airway, no cyanosis, SpO2 96% on 8 L Hudson mask, HR 168, BP 110/70, T 38.1 degC.

Bedside glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. She has no known epilepsy, no medications, and no significant past medical history. IV access has just been obtained. There is no preceding head trauma, no toxin exposure and no recent vaccination. She has no congenital heart disease, no metabolic disorder and no family history of epilepsy. Her mother reports a 2-day febrile coryzal illness with mild diarrhoea, treated with paracetamol only.

On arrival a nurse-led airway manoeuvre maintains a patent airway with oropharyngeal suction of secretions, the ED consultant is at the bedside and PIPER retrieval has been alerted to assist with potential PICU transfer.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.1 degC, HR 168, RR breaths irregular, SpO2 96% on 8 L Hudson, BP 110/70.
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic activity ongoing. Airway patent with jaw thrust. No focal lateralising features evident.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L. No bloods yet.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next medication?

options.text: Repeat buccal midazolam now
IV phenytoin load over 20 min
IV phenobarbital load now
Rapid sequence intubation with thiopentone, rocuronium
IV midazolam bolus now

stem:
A previously well 5-year-old boy, weight 19 kg, is brought to ED after a witnessed event at home in which he became suddenly unresponsive, stiffened, then had rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for about 90 seconds, followed by 10 minutes of confusion and sleepiness. He has now fully recovered. He has had no fever, no head injury, and no family history of epilepsy.

Birth and developmental history are normal and he is fully immunised. On examination he is alert, neurologically intact with no focal deficit, no rash, normal fundi, and a normal cardiovascular exam. Bedside glucose is 4.9 mmol/L. Sodium, calcium and magnesium are normal. He has no further seizures during 4 hours of ED observation. His mother reports no preceding head injury, no toxic ingestion, and no recent travel. He attends mainstream kindergarten where he is meeting expected milestones, and there is no family history of epilepsy or sudden cardiac death.

data_table.Examination: GCS 15. Normal cranial nerves, tone, power, reflexes, coordination, gait. No rash. No meningism.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 4.9, Na 139, K 4.1, Ca 2.35, Mg 0.85, FBC normal, CRP <5.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient EEG in 1-2 weeks, safety advice, no anti-epileptic medication
Admit and commence sodium valproate daily, refer neurology
Urgent inpatient CT head and lumbar puncture now before any discharge
Discharge with buccal midazolam rescue kit, no follow-up unless seizures recur
Discharge with same-day MRI brain and start levetiracetam if MRI abnormal

subtopic_detail: First non-febrile seizure - investigations and counselling

stem:
A previously well 18-month-old boy weighing 11 kg presents to ED after a single 3-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. He had been febrile to 39.0 deg C with coryzal symptoms for 24 hours. He recovered fully within 20 minutes. On examination he is alert and playful with a clear viral URTI and no other source of infection. There is no rash, no meningism and no focal neurology.

He has no past seizure history; his father had two febrile seizures as a toddler. He is fully immunised, has not received sedating medication and has no known allergies. Bedside glucose 5.2. T 38.7, HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 degC, HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful. Coryza. No rash, no meningism, no focal signs. Anterior fontanelle closed.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L. No further investigations performed.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Admit overnight for inpatient EEG and brain MRI to investigate the seizure aetiology before considering any discharge from the emergency department
Lumbar puncture before discharge given the age under 2 years, as part of routine post-febrile-seizure workup at this age
Regular alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen at home to prevent further febrile seizure recurrence over the next 24-48 hours of this illness
Reassurance, treat the febrile focus per eTG, discharge with written safety-net advice; advise recurrence risk is around 30% and epilepsy risk 1-2%
Prescribe maintenance sodium valproate at discharge to prevent further febrile seizures, with paediatric neurology follow-up arranged in 4 weeks

stem:
A 4-year-old boy, weight 18 kg, presents with 3 days of high fever and a 1-day history of vomiting and reduced intake. He has no chronic illness. On examination he is irritable but rousable to voice, tachycardic, with mottled knees, cool hands and feet, central capillary refill of 4 seconds, peripheral pulses present but thready, and a non-tender abdomen with no rash.

His HR is 168, RR 36, T 39.4 degC, SpO2 97% on room air, and his non-invasive BP is 96/64 mmHg. He has not voided in 8 hours. Bedside glucose is 4.4 mmol/L, venous lactate 3.6 mmol/L. IV access is being established. He has not received antibiotics in the last 3 months and his vaccinations including pneumococcal and meningococcal B are up to date. The senior nurse has activated the local sepsis pathway and broad-spectrum antibiotics are being drawn up while access is established.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 degC, HR 168, RR 36, BP 96/64, SpO2 97% RA, cap refill 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Irritable, rousable. Mottled, cool peripheries. Thready pulses. Soft abdomen. No rash.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 4.4, venous lactate 3.6 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which best describes his haemodynamic state and the immediate management?

options.text: Cardiogenic shock; restrict fluid and commence IV dobutamine infusion
Decompensated shock; commence adrenaline infusion immediately before any fluid
No shock; give maintenance fluid only and observe
Warm vasodilatory shock; give noradrenaline infusion as first-line
Compensated cold shock; give 10-20 mL/kg saline bolus

stem:
A 6-year-old girl, weight 22 kg, was brought in shocked with presumed septic source (community-acquired pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion on bedside lung ultrasound). She received empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg early in the resuscitation. Over the last 40 minutes she has received three 20 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% saline (total 60 mL/kg) and remains tachycardic at 156, with central capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool mottled peripheries, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 94% on 8 L Hudson mask.

She has not voided since arrival. The hepatic edge is now palpable 1 cm below the costal margin and there are bibasal crackles. Lactate has fallen from 5.4 to 3.8 mmol/L. The retrieval service is on the phone and the paediatric registrar is preparing for central access. Her mother reports a 3-day febrile illness with cough and lethargy treated by the GP with oral amoxicillin 48 hours ago without improvement. The bedside echocardiogram clip the registrar has just performed shows a hyperdynamic but underfilled left ventricle with no pericardial effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, BP 78/40, RR 38, SpO2 94% on 8 L, cap refill 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Cool mottled peripheries, narrow pulse pressure. Hepatomegaly 1 cm. Bibasal crackles. Anuric.
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.8 mmol/L (was 5.4). VBG pH 7.28. CXR: right lower lobe consolidation with small effusion.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence peripheral adrenaline infusion and prepare for intubation
Give a fourth 20 mL/kg saline bolus before any vasoactive medication
Start noradrenaline as first-line inotrope peripherally
Commence dopamine infusion peripherally as first-line
Give IV hydrocortisone as next step, no inotrope

stem:
A 4-month-old, ex-term, breastfed boy is brought to ED by his mother because of unsettled crying for the last 12 hours. She mentions that she noticed two bruises on his cheek and a bruise on his left ear earlier in the day, which she attributes to him knocking himself on a toy in the cot. He has not yet rolled or crawled and is not pulling himself up.

There is no preceding illness and no fever. He is fully immunised and has had routine well-child checks with no concerns. Examination reveals a well-grown alert infant with a 2 cm bruise to the right cheek, a 1 cm bruise to the left pinna and a 1.5 cm bruise on the left frontal scalp, no other external injuries, a normal anterior fontanelle, no focal neurology, no retinal haemorrhages on examination by the registrar, normal tone, and a normal abdomen with no organomegaly. Coagulation screen, FBC and LFTs are normal. The mother is alone and tearful when asked about who else cares for the baby.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 degC, HR 142, RR 36, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Three bruises (cheek, ear, frontal scalp). Otherwise unremarkable. Pre-mobile.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, coags, LFTs normal. No CT or skeletal survey yet.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send for outpatient coagulation studies only and review in 2 weeks
Reassure the mother and discharge with GP follow-up in 1 week
Admit for skeletal survey, CT head, ophthalmology review, child protection consult and mandatory report
Order a skeletal survey only, without notifying child protection, pending the imaging result
Confront the mother directly about possible abuse before doing any investigations

stem:
A 4-year-old girl, weight 16 kg, was pulled from a backyard pool by her father approximately 6 minutes ago after an unwitnessed submersion estimated at 3-5 minutes. She was apnoeic and unresponsive at poolside. Her father began chest compressions immediately and bystander CPR continued until paramedics arrived 4 minutes ago. Paramedics found her in asystole, established a supraglottic airway, ventilated with 100% oxygen and continued compressions; ROSC was achieved after 3 minutes of resuscitation.

She arrives in ED still intubated (now endotracheal), with HR 132, BP 86/52, SpO2 92% on 100% FiO2, T 33.4 degC tympanic, GCS 3 with no sedation, pupils 4 mm sluggish bilaterally. Bedside lung ultrasound shows bilateral B-lines and the CXR is in progress. An indwelling urinary catheter has drained 20 mL of clear urine since insertion 15 minutes ago, and the PICU retrieval team has been activated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 86/52, SpO2 92% on FiO2 1.0, T 33.4 degC, GCS 3.
data_table.Examination: Intubated and ventilated. Bilateral crackles. Cool peripheries. Pupils 4 mm, sluggish.
data_table.Investigations: Lung US: bilateral B-lines. VBG pending. Bedside glucose 7.1 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which best reflects current ANZCOR-aligned management priorities for this child?

options.text: Withdraw care now given asystole at scene; outcome is uniformly poor
Hyperventilate to PaCO2 25 mmHg and target SpO2 100% on FiO2 1.0
Aggressive rapid rewarming to 38 degC plus prophylactic broad-spectrum IV ceftriaxone now
Early extubation because the lungs are clear on auscultation and CXR is unremarkable
Lung-protective ventilation with PEEP, controlled rewarming to 36 degC, post-arrest care, discuss ECMO retrieval

stem:
A 3-year-old girl, weight 15 kg, sustained a scald injury 90 minutes ago when she pulled a pot of hot water onto herself. On assessment in ED, she has partial-thickness burns to the anterior chest, anterior abdomen and the front of both thighs, with sparing of the face, hands, perineum and circumferential injuries. Using a Lund-Browder chart for her age, the total burn surface area (TBSA) is calculated at 18%.

She is alert, in pain (Faces score 8/10), HR 148, BP 96/60, RR 32, SpO2 99% on room air, T 36.4 degC. IV access has been obtained and tetanus status is up to date. She last ate 4 hours ago and has no known allergies. She has no underlying skin condition, no chronic illnessies. The burn was cooled with running tap water for 20 minutes at the scene by an attending neighbour who is a nurse, and the wounds have been covered with cling film during transport.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 96/60, RR 32, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.4 degC.
data_table.Examination: Partial-thickness burns anterior chest, abdomen, anterior thighs. 18% TBSA. Mucosae moist. Peripheral perfusion adequate.
data_table.Investigations: VBG pending. No carboxyhaemoglobin elevation (no inhalation injury suspected).

lead_in: Which fluid prescription?

options.text: 5% albumin 20 mL/kg bolus immediately then 1 mL/kg/%TBSA over the next 24 hours
Parkland: 4 mL/kg/%TBSA 0.9% saline = 1080 mL over 24 hours INSTEAD OF maintenance
Hypertonic 3% saline at 3 mL/kg/hour for 24 hours, no maintenance separately
Hartmann's 3 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 hours (half in first 8 hours) plus separate maintenance
Maintenance fluid only (60 mL/h of 0.9% saline plus dextrose) with no resuscitation fluid

stem:
A 15-year-old girl, weight 60 kg, is brought to ED by her mother 5 hours after ingesting an unknown number of paracetamol 500 mg tablets in an acute single ingestion. She is now tearful but cooperative, denies co-ingestion, has no abdominal pain, no jaundice, and a soft non-tender abdomen. She has no chronic liver disease and is not on enzyme-inducing medications.

Vital signs are normal. Bloods drawn 4 hours and 30 minutes post-ingestion show paracetamol concentration 165 mg/L, ALT 28 U/L, INR 1.0, creatinine 58 micromol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, and a negative beta-hCG. The empty packet retrieved at home suggests she may have taken approximately 14 g (around 230 mg/kg) but the ingestion history is uncertain.

data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful. No jaundice. Soft non-tender abdomen.
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol 165 mg/L at 4.5 h. ALT 28. INR 1.0. Creatinine 58. Bicarbonate 24. Lactate 1.4. Glucose 5.0. beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat paracetamol level at 8 hours and only commence NAC if above 75 mg/L
IV N-acetylcysteine two-bag regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h) and admit
Give oral activated charcoal 1 g/kg now and reassess level at 12 hours
Discharge with mental health follow-up only; level is below treatment line and dose under 200 mg/kg
Commence oral methionine and arrange urgent liver transplant assessment at tertiary centre now

stem:
A 3-month-old ex-term breastfed boy is brought to the GP for intermittent noisy breathing since 4 weeks of age that has slowly become more prominent. The noise is a soft inspiratory stridor that is worse when feeding, crying or lying supine, and almost resolves when held upright or in prone. He is thriving on the 50th centile, has had no fevers, no coryza, no preceding URTI, and feeds well with no choking or coughing.

On examination he is alert, T 36.8 deg C, RR 36, HR 130, SpO2 98% on room air, with no recession at rest. Auscultation is clear. There is no barking cough and no hoarse cry. Examination of the oropharynx is normal, the cry is normal in pitch, and there is no haemangioma over the beard distribution. He has not had any feeding-related choking episodes and there is no history suggestive of an inhaled foreign body.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, RR 36, HR 130, SpO2 98% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Soft inspiratory stridor when supine, resolves prone or upright. No recession. Clear auscultation. Thriving on 50th centile.
data_table.Investigations: No fever, no preceding URTI. No cough, no choking with feeds.

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and need for further investigation is correct?

options.text: Laryngomalacia; no investigation required while thriving without red flags (no cyanotic spells, feeding failure or failure to thrive); paediatric ENT referral only if red flags emerge
Subglottic haemangioma; arrange urgent MRI airway given biphasic stridor that worsens supine, with propranolol commenced after confirmation of diagnosis
Viral croup; commence oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single stat dose and observe for 4 hours before considering discharge home
Inhaled foreign body; arrange urgent rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in theatre with combined ENT and paediatric anaesthetics involvement
Vascular ring (double aortic arch or pulmonary sling); arrange CT angiography of the chest given the positional stridor pattern described in this infant

stem:
A 6-year-old boy with a 2-year diagnosis of asthma on PRN salbutamol presents in winter with worsening wheeze over 6 hours despite three sets of 6 puffs of salbutamol via spacer at home. He has had two ED presentations in the last year and no ICU admissions. On arrival he is too breathless to speak in full sentences, RR 44, HR 142, SpO2 90 percent on room air.

There is marked accessory muscle use with tracheal tug and intercostal recession, widespread polyphonic wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase and only moderate air entry bilaterally. He is alert but anxious. PEFR cannot be obtained. He has had no recent oral steroid courses, no fever, and no focal chest signs. Chest examination shows no asymmetry to suggest foreign body or pneumothorax.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 44, HR 142, SpO2 90% room air, T 37.0 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Speaks in phrases. Marked accessory muscle use. Widespread wheeze, moderate air entry. Alert.
data_table.Investigations: PEFR unobtainable. No focal signs. No fever.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate first-line therapy package?

options.text: Continuous nebulised salbutamol 5 mg, ipratropium 250 microgram added to each of the first three nebs, oral prednisolone (maximum 50 mg) as soon as possible, controlled supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 over 94 percent
Salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for one hour; withhold steroids until registrar review
IV magnesium sulfate over 20 minutes and IV hydrocortisone, with no inhaled therapy
Oral amoxicillin, oral prednisolone, nebulised salbutamol every 4 hours as required
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg, oral dexamethasone, observe for 4 hours

stem:
An 8-year-old with mild persistent asthma attends a routine GP review. His mother reports symptoms remain uncontrolled despite using salbutamol via MDI with a mouthpiece spacer for 12 months. Adherence is good. On observed technique he shakes the canister, attaches it to the spacer, places the mouthpiece in his mouth, fires four puffs into the spacer in rapid succession, then takes two quick breaths without sealing his lips around the mouthpiece between actuations.

He has no oromotor or developmental concerns and is growing on the 50th centile. He is asymptomatic with normal spirometry (FEV1 92 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84) at review.

data_table.Vital signs: Asymptomatic at review. T 36.7 deg C, RR 18, HR 92, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Normal chest examination. No wheeze.
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry FEV1 92% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84 (within normal limits).

lead_in: Which is the single most important correction to make to his spacer technique?

options.text: Switch from a mouthpiece spacer to a face-mask spacer to maximise drug delivery for his age
Wash the spacer with hot soapy water before each use and dry it with a clean towel
Hold the breath for 30 seconds after each inhalation to maximise small-airway deposition
Fire one puff at a time, take 4 tidal breaths (or one slow deep breath with 5-second breath-hold) per puff, and maintain a lip seal on the mouthpiece throughout
Replace the MDI-spacer with a dry-powder inhaler now that he is old enough to follow staged instructions

stem:
A 5-week-old ex-34-week infant is brought to the resuscitation bay at a tertiary paediatric ED with day 4 of an RSV-positive bronchiolitis. Over the last hour she has had two witnessed apnoeic pauses of 20 seconds each with bradycardia to 80 and desaturation to 78% requiring tactile stimulation to recover. On arrival she has RR 70, HR 184, SpO2 89% on 2 L/min nasal prong oxygen, T 37.3 deg C.

She has marked subcostal and intercostal recession with head bobbing, nasal flaring and grunting. Air entry is fair bilaterally with widespread fine crackles and wheeze. She is mottled and her capillary refill is 3 seconds peripherally. She is lethargic but rousable. A venous gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 65 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L. NG feeds were started 12 hours ago and have been tolerated at 50% volume. The PICU registrar is at the bedside. She is fully immunised and weighs 3.6 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 70, HR 184, SpO2 89% on 2 L O2, T 37.3 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Marked recession, head bobbing, grunting. Mottled, CRT 3 sec. Lethargic but rousable.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.28, pCO2 65 mmHg, HCO3 24, lactate 2.1. RSV PCR positive. Two apnoeas with bradycardia in last hour.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase nasal prong O2 to 4 L/min and continue NG feeds
Commence nebulised hypertonic saline 3% 4 mL six-hourly with nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg
Start high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min, titrate FiO2 to SpO2 92-96%
Intubate immediately with rapid sequence induction and start mechanical ventilation now
Administer IV dexamethasone and a single dose of IV ceftriaxone

stem:
A 7-year-old girl with known asthma has been in the paediatric ED for 90 minutes with a severe exacerbation. She has received continuous nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 microg added to the first three nebs, plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg administered at arrival. Despite this she continues to speak only in single words, RR 42, HR 154, SpO2 90% on 6 L Hudson mask, with marked accessory muscle use and a prolonged expiratory phase.

There has been no improvement in her wheeze, work of breathing or air entry over the last 30 minutes. She has had two previous PICU admissions for asthma but has never been intubated. She remains alert and oriented. She has a patent IV cannula. Her venous gas shows pH 7.34, pCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 19 mmol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L (attributed to high-dose salbutamol). PICU has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 42, HR 154, SpO2 90% on 6 L Hudson mask, T 36.9 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Single-word speech. Marked accessory use. Prolonged expiration. Air entry reduced. Alert.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.34, pCO2 38, HCO3 19, lactate 4.8. CXR: hyperinflation, no focal consolidation, no pneumothorax.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IV aminophylline loading dose over 60 minutes followed by infusion
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg every 20 minutes for three doses, no IV therapy
IV salbutamol bolus over 10 minutes followed by an infusion
IV hydrocortisone in addition to the oral prednisolone already given at arrival
IV magnesium sulfate (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes now

stem:
A 5-year-old boy presents to the GP after his mother noticed 4 days of cough, fever to 39.0 deg C, and lethargy. He is fully immunised. His older brother has a coryzal illness with low-grade fever. On examination he is flushed, T 38.7 deg C, RR 36, HR 128, SpO2 96% on room air. Auscultation reveals focal bronchial breathing and end-inspiratory crackles at the left upper zone with normal findings elsewhere.

He is mildly tachypnoeic but has no recession. CXR (obtained earlier at the request of an after-hours GP) shows a dense lobar consolidation of the left upper lobe with air bronchograms and no effusion. CRP is 124 mg/L, white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, and procalcitonin is 2.4 microg/L. He is feeding adequately and the GP needs to decide whether the picture supports bacterial or viral aetiology before prescribing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 deg C, RR 36, HR 128, SpO2 96% room air.
data_table.Examination: Focal LUZ bronchial breathing and crackles. No recession. Otherwise normal.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: dense LUL lobar consolidation with air bronchograms. CRP 124 mg/L. WCC 18.2 with neutrophilia. Procalcitonin 2.4 microg/L.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly favours a bacterial (typically pneumococcal) aetiology over a viral cause?

options.text: Respiratory rate persistently around 36 breaths per minute today
Dense lobar consolidation with air bronchograms on a focal CXR
An isolated CRP of 124 mg/L without any other supporting features
Procalcitonin of 2.4 microg/L with neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis on the FBC
Symptom duration of 4 days, sibling with coryzal illness at home

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to ED by his grandmother 3 hours after a sudden coughing and choking episode while eating peanuts on the lounge floor. He had a few minutes of distress and gagging that settled, but since then he has had an intermittent dry cough and noisy breathing. He is alert and playful in the ED, T 36.9 deg C, RR 32, HR 124, SpO2 97% on room air.

He has no respiratory distress at rest and no stridor. Auscultation reveals reduced breath sounds and a focal monophonic wheeze over the right side, with normal air entry on the left. There is no recession at rest. He has no history of recurrent wheeze and has never been diagnosed with asthma. There is no fever, drooling, or systemic illness. An inspiratory CXR appears unremarkable with symmetrical lung volumes and no focal opacity.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, RR 32, HR 124, SpO2 97% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful. Reduced breath sounds and focal monophonic wheeze on the right. No stridor. No recession.
data_table.Investigations: Inspiratory CXR unremarkable, symmetrical lung volumes.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with safety-netting given the normal CXR and absence of acute distress
Trial salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and review in 1 hour for response
IV ceftriaxone and oral prednisolone for post-aspiration pneumonitis empirically
Chest CT to confirm presence and location of foreign body before intervention
Inspiratory and expiratory chest radiographs and refer for urgent rigid bronchoscopy now

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is reviewed at the GP after his third episode of viral-triggered wheeze in 12 months. Each episode has lasted around 3 to 5 days, has been associated with a clear upper respiratory tract infection and has responded to salbutamol via spacer with mask within 24 to 48 hours. None of the episodes have required oral steroids, ED presentation or hospital admission.

He has been completely asymptomatic between episodes, with no nocturnal cough, no exercise-induced wheeze and no daytime symptoms when he is not unwell with a virus. There is no personal history of eczema or food allergy. Family history is significant for an older sibling with allergic rhinitis but no asthma. His parents ask whether he should be on a daily inhaled corticosteroid because his older cousin is on one. On examination he is well, has a normal chest examination, height and weight on the 60th centile, and is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Asymptomatic at review. T 36.8 deg C, RR 22, HR 100, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Well child. Normal chest examination.
data_table.Investigations: Symptom-free between three viral-triggered episodes in last 12 months. No interval symptoms. No atopy.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone propionate 50 microg twice daily) via spacer with mask
Commence a daily oral leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast 4 mg) as maintenance
Continue PRN salbutamol via spacer for episodes and provide a written action plan
Commence pre-emptive high-dose inhaled corticosteroid at the onset of each upper respiratory tract infection
Refer to a paediatric respiratory specialist for assessment and formal lung function testing

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents at 2030 on Friday with 24 hours of a barking cough and hoarse cry that has worsened over the evening. She has had a 2-day coryzal illness. Her father reports increasing work of breathing in the last hour and audible noise on breathing in. In the resuscitation cubicle she is sitting upright on her father's lap, anxious, and refusing to drink.

She has continuous inspiratory stridor at rest with marked sternal recession and tracheal tug. There is no drooling, she is afebrile at 37.7 deg C, SpO2 95 percent on room air, RR 36, HR 142. Her cry is hoarse but she can speak in short phrases. She is fully immunised including Hib, with no atopy and no history suggestive of foreign body aspiration.

Air entry is symmetrical without focal crackles or wheeze. She has had no previous croup admissions or recurrent stridor between viral illnesses. Weight 13 kg. The clinician calculates a Westley score of 6.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.7 deg C, RR 36, HR 142, SpO2 95% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Continuous stridor at rest. Marked sternal recession and tracheal tug. No drooling. Hoarse but phonating.
data_table.Investigations: Westley score 6 (moderate). No CXR. Weight 13 kg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combination of immediate management and minimum observation?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone alone, discharge after 1-hour observation if stable
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus oral dexamethasone (or prednisolone if no oral access), observe 3 hours (RCH minimum) after the last adrenaline dose before considering discharge
IV ceftriaxone and urgent ENT for suspected epiglottitis
Heliox via face mask and humidified oxygen; defer dexamethasone pending ENT review
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg, ipratropium 250 microgram and oral prednisolone

stem:
A 10-year-old girl with asthma has been reviewed in the GP clinic with her mother for a routine 3-monthly follow-up. She has been on fluticasone propionate 100 microg twice daily (low-dose ICS) for 8 months. Over the last 3 months she has had daytime wheeze or cough on most days, has woken at night with cough at least once a week, and has needed her salbutamol on average 4 to 5 days per week including before sport.

There have been no oral steroid courses in this period and no hospital presentations. The GP has watched her use her MDI and spacer (mouthpiece) in clinic and the technique is excellent. Adherence on Webster pack review is 90% and the parents confirm she takes it morning and night. There are no environmental triggers identified - no smoking in the household, no pets, and no recent changes in housing. Spirometry today shows FEV1 78% predicted and FEV1/FVC 0.74 with significant bronchodilator reversibility of 14%.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, RR 18, HR 92, SpO2 99% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Well, normal chest examination. Growth on 50th centile.
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FEV1 78% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.74, bronchodilator reversibility 14%. Adherence 90%, technique correct.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in her controller therapy?

options.text: Continue current low-dose ICS and add daily oral montelukast 5 mg as maintenance add-on
Step up to combination ICS plus LABA (fluticasone-salmeterol 100/50 microg twice daily)
Stop the regular ICS and commence as-needed budesonide-formoterol via MDI plus spacer
Refer to a paediatric respiratory specialist for assessment for omalizumab or biologic therapy
Add a daily long-acting muscarinic antagonist such as tiotropium via Respimat inhaler

stem:
A 7-week-old previously well boy is brought to ED by his mother after 10 days of a worsening cough. The cough started as a non-specific coryzal illness with mild rhinorrhoea but over the last 5 days has become severely paroxysmal, with episodes of coughing lasting 30 to 60 seconds followed by vomiting and a sharp inspiratory sound. Between paroxysms he is settled and appears well.

He has had two witnessed brief apnoeic episodes at home, each lasting less than 15 seconds, with no colour change. He is bottle-fed and taking only about 80% of his usual volume. He is not yet immunised because his mother declined the antenatal pertussis booster and the 6-week vaccines were missed. His mother has had a 3-week non-productive cough that she has attributed to a viral illness.

On examination he is afebrile at 36.9 deg C, RR 42, HR 158, SpO2 97% on room air, with mild intercostal recession and unremarkable auscultation between paroxysms. FBC shows white cell count 28 x10^9/L with a marked lymphocytosis. CXR shows perihilar peribronchial thickening with no focal consolidation. A nasopharyngeal pertussis PCR has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, RR 42, HR 158, SpO2 97% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Settled between paroxysms. Mild recession. Auscultation clear between coughs.
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 28 x10^9/L, marked lymphocytosis. CXR: perihilar peribronchial thickening. Pertussis PCR sent.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combination of management steps?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin every 8 hours for 5 days, discharge home with safety-netting
Oral azithromycin daily for 5 days plus salbutamol nebs, no public health action
Admit for monitoring, oral azithromycin for 5 days, notify public health, household chemoprophylaxis
Oral erythromycin in 4 doses for 14 days, no admission required
IV ceftriaxone with oral prednisolone, defer notification until pertussis PCR confirms

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is reviewed in the GP clinic 2 weeks after a moderate asthma exacerbation that required oral prednisolone in ED but no admission. She is on fluticasone-salmeterol 100/50 microgram twice daily and PRN salbutamol via MDI plus spacer. Technique is excellent and adherence is good. Over the past year she has had three exacerbations, each beginning with several days of increased salbutamol use and mild nocturnal cough; on two occasions her mother gave a single dose of salbutamol and waited overnight before review, and the girl ended up needing oral prednisolone.

The clinician is now writing a National Asthma Council action plan and wants the family to act earlier. The school has the previous plan but it is 18 months old. The family lives 15 minutes from the nearest ED.

data_table.Vital signs: Asymptomatic at review. T 36.6 deg C, RR 16, HR 84, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Well. Normal chest examination.
data_table.Investigations: Three exacerbations in 12 months, two required oral prednisolone. Technique and adherence good.

lead_in: Which yellow-zone instruction set is most appropriate to write into her plan?

options.text: Continue preventer at current dose; salbutamol 2 puffs every 4 hours; no other change
Self-initiate a 3-day course of oral prednisolone at home at first sign of worsening before any clinician contact
Stop the preventer and rely on salbutamol alone until the worsening symptoms resolve

Salbutamol 4-6 puffs via spacer every 4 hours; temporarily increase preventer (e.g. quadruple ICS or as specified in her plan); GP review within 24-48 hours; clear red-flag escalation criteria (no relief from salbutamol, severe breathlessness, blue lips, inability to speak in sentences) prompting call-000 or ED
Present immediately to ED for any increase in salbutamol use regardless of severity

stem:
A 12-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis (homozygous F508del) is admitted with a 7-day history of worsening productive cough, increased sputum volume that has become darker green and more tenacious than her usual baseline, reduced exercise tolerance with breathlessness climbing one flight of stairs at school, anorexia and 1.5 kg of weight loss over the previous 2 weeks despite her usual enzyme dosing. Her baseline FEV1 is 78% predicted; today it has fallen to 61% predicted on bedside spirometry, the largest single-visit drop she has had since starting her current modulator.

She is fully adherent to her usual regimen of nebulised hypertonic saline 6%, dornase alfa, pancreatic enzyme replacement and twice-daily airway clearance physiotherapy with a positive expiratory pressure device. She is on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor and has been stable for the last 18 months. Her last sputum culture 6 weeks ago grew mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa sensitive to tobramycin, ceftazidime, piperacillin-tazobactam, and meropenem, and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin.

She has no penicillin allergy and her baseline serum creatinine 6 weeks ago was 55 micromol/L. On examination she is alert, T 37.8 deg C, RR 26, HR 110, SpO2 93% on room air. Auscultation reveals coarse crackles at both upper lobes and the right middle lobe with widespread expiratory wheeze. CXR shows bilateral upper-lobe bronchiectasis with new patchy consolidation at the right middle lobe compared to her baseline. A sputum culture has been sent on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 deg C, RR 26, HR 110, SpO2 93% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Alert. Coarse crackles both upper lobes + RML. Widespread expiratory wheeze. Cachectic appearance.
data_table.Investigations: FEV1 61% (baseline 78%). Last sputum: mucoid Pseudomonas (sensitive to tobramycin, ceftazidime, pip-taz, meropenem); MSSA. New CXR consolidation at RML.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate empirical IV antibiotic regimen pending fresh sputum culture results?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 20 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days as outpatient antipseudomonal monotherapy with home physiotherapy
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily plus oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 14 days
IV flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours plus oral rifampicin as targeted antistaphylococcal combination therapy
IV meropenem 40 mg/kg every 8 hours as broad-spectrum antipseudomonal monotherapy for 14 days
IV ceftazidime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours plus IV tobramycin 10 mg/kg once daily, alongside intensified airway clearance physiotherapy

stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a metropolitan general practice for a sports clearance before joining a school netball squad. She arrives with her mother, who fills out the registration form and remains in the consulting room while the patient gives a brief history of an ankle sprain six weeks ago that has fully resolved. The patient is fully immunised, takes no regular medications, and her growth chart sits along the 50th centile for height and weight.

The general practitioner has 20 minutes booked and intends to perform a HEEADSSS psychosocial screen as part of the routine adolescent encounter. The mother is keen to stay and mentions in passing that the patient has been 'a bit moody' but she is sure it is just school stress. The patient looks at the floor when this is said and gives short answers.

There is no history of self-harm, no current school refusal, and the academic report card last term was unchanged. The practice has private rooms available and a chaperone is offered. Pre-consult observations are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 14 /min, T 36.7 deg C, BMI 21.3 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Healed ankle, full range of movement, no joint laxity, mood guarded
data_table.Social context: Year 10 student, lives with mother and younger sister, parents separated 2 years ago
data_table.History: Fully immunised, no previous mental health contact

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate way to begin the HEEADSSS assessment?

options.text: Ask the mother to leave, then explain confidentiality and its mandatory reporting limits clearly before any HEEADSSS questions
Proceed with the mother in the room and start with Home and Education questions as a way to build rapport gradually
Open with the Sexuality and Suicide domains immediately while the rapport built from the joint history is still warm
Defer the HEEADSSS assessment to a follow-up visit and only address the sports clearance ankle today since rapport is limited
Give the patient a paper HEEADSSS self report questionnaire to complete alone in the waiting room before the consultation

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to a youth health clinic alone after school for a contraception and STI check before a planned first sexual encounter with a same-age girlfriend. He is articulate, knows about condoms, denies coercion, and reports no drug use. The nurse practitioner introduces herself, offers a chaperone, and prepares to start a HEEADSSS screen. The patient interrupts to ask whether anything he says today will be told to his mother, his school, or the police.

He specifically wants to know what would trigger the clinician to break confidentiality before he answers any further questions. He has no previous mental health contact, has not self-harmed, and there is no current disclosure of abuse. He has read on a youth website that 'doctors keep everything secret under 16' and wants to know if this is correct. He is fully immunised, in Year 9, lives with both biological parents, and there is no Child Protection history known to the practice.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14 /min, T 36.6 deg C
data_table.Examination: Well appearing, age-appropriate Tanner staging, no signs of injury
data_table.Social context: Year 9, lives with parents, no Child Protection involvement
data_table.History: No prior mental health contact, no self-harm history

lead_in: Which framing of confidentiality limits is the single most appropriate response?

options.text: Promise full unconditional confidentiality for today's entire consultation because he is plainly competent and the topic raised today is only contraception advice
Explain that conversation is private unless he discloses serious risk to himself, risk to others, or abuse, in which case agencies are informed
Explain that everything will be shared with both of his parents today because he is currently aged under 16 years
Tell him that only the disclosure of sexual activity will trigger a notification today and that drug use questions are entirely private under all circumstances
Defer the entire conversation today until one of his parents or a legal guardian can attend to consent to confidentiality

stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a community general practice in NSW alone, requesting the etonogestrel subdermal implant for contraception. She has been in a relationship with a 16-year-old boyfriend for six months and they have used condoms consistently. She explains that she does not want to involve her mother because of cultural concerns but agrees that talking to a parent could be helpful in principle.

She knows the implant works for three years, can give the side effect profile including irregular bleeding and possible weight change, and demonstrates that she has thought about what she would do if condom use lapses. She denies coercion, denies pressure to be sexually active, and there is no power imbalance in the relationship. She has no medical conditions that would alter the contraceptive choice and is not at risk of pregnancy today.

Her HEEADSSS screen is otherwise reassuring, with no self-harm, no substance use beyond occasional alcohol, and good school engagement. There is no Child Protection history and the relationship is not subject to mandatory reporting.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg, BMI 23 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Well, no contraindication to LARC identified
data_table.Social context: Year 10, no power imbalance, no coercion, consensual relationship
data_table.History: Regular cycles, no VTE history, non-smoker

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Decline to prescribe any hormonal contraception today because formal parental consent is required for every patient under the age of 16
Make a mandatory report to NSW Child Protection today on the basis that the patient is sexually active under the age of 16
Assess and document Gillick competence today, encourage but do not require parental involvement, and proceed with the implant
Prescribe condoms alone today and review her in 12 months once she has turned 16 to revisit longer acting reversible options
Insist that she bring her mother to the next appointment before any form of contraception can be prescribed for her

stem:
A 15-year-old girl presents to a Victorian general practice with her 18-year-old sister. She has confirmed pregnancy at 7 weeks by dating ultrasound today and is requesting termination of pregnancy. The biological father is her 16-year-old boyfriend and the relationship is described by both as consensual and non-coercive. The patient does not want to tell either parent at present and asks specifically about confidentiality.

She can describe both medical (mifepristone with misoprostol) and surgical termination options, explains the risks of each in age-appropriate language, and articulates that continuing the pregnancy is not what she wants. Her HEEADSSS screen reveals no self-harm, no substance use, and her mood is appropriately anxious but not depressed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peritonism, no PV bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 22,000 IU/L, dating scan 7+0 weeks intrauterine, blood group O Rh positive, Hb 128 g/L
data_table.Social context: Year 10, stable home, sister supporting, no coercion
data_table.History: G1P0, no medical conditions, no medications

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer the case to the Victorian Children's Court for authorisation because termination decisions for under 16s require judicial sanction
Mandatorily report the pregnancy to Victorian Child Protection today because the patient is under 16 and currently pregnant
Require written parental consent from at least one parent before any termination referral because Gillick does not apply to termination decisions
Document Gillick competence today, maintain confidentiality, encourage parental involvement, and refer for the patient's chosen termination pathway
Defer the decision by two weeks of additional counselling because the patient is too young to consent in the first trimester

stem:
A general practitioner working in a community practice in NSW reviews a 6-year-old boy brought in by his maternal grandmother for assessment of recurrent settled cough. The history reveals that the child has been living with the grandmother for two months because the mother is in a methamphetamine-related relapse and the maternal home is unsafe. The boy is fully immunised, has met all developmental milestones, and his growth chart sits at the 25th centile.

The grandmother reports that the mother has been violent toward the child's stepfather during intoxication episodes, but the child has not directly witnessed this in the past month while staying with her. The grandmother has informal care, has been in contact with the maternal aunt and a school welfare officer, and is aware the mother is engaged with an alcohol and other drugs service.

The child shows no signs of physical injury, no behavioural regression, and his school attendance has improved since moving in with the grandmother. No prior Child Protection report has been made. The cough is from a settled URTI and not the concern of the consultation. The GP is considering whether the history meets the NSW mandatory reporting threshold.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, RR 22 /min, T 37.0 deg C
data_table.Examination: Well child, no bruising, no injury, growth 25th centile
data_table.Social context: Informal care with grandmother, mother in relapse, AOD engaged, no current direct witness of violence
data_table.History: Fully immunised, attending school, no developmental regression

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step regarding mandatory reporting?

options.text: Make an immediate report to the NSW Child Protection Helpline today because the mother is in current relapse with active methamphetamine use disorder
Refer the mother to a parenting program and document the family concerns clearly without taking any further statutory action today
Take no further action today because the child is now in informal kinship care with the maternal grandmother and is well
Notify NSW Police directly today because of the disclosed domestic violence between the mother and the stepfather in the past month
Use the NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide decision tool to determine whether the Risk of Significant Harm threshold is met before reporting or referring

stem:
A paediatric registrar at a metropolitan Victorian public hospital is asked to review an 11-year-old boy admitted after an episode of self-harm at boarding school. During the admission the boy discloses that a residential care worker employed by the boarding school, who is not a teacher, has been entering his bedroom at night for the past three weeks and tickling and wrestling with him in a way that has made him uncomfortable.

There has been no disclosed penetrative contact and no injury, but the boy describes the contact as making him anxious and not wanting to return to the school. The boy's parents live overseas and the school is the legal guardian during term. The registrar discusses the case with the consultant paediatrician on call. The hospital has both Child Protection and Police pathways available, and the consultant raises the additional question of whether the conduct falls under the Victorian Reportable Conduct Scheme administered by the Commission for Children and Young People.

data_table.Examination: Well, no acute injury, multiple superficial linear forearm abrasions, age-appropriate Tanner stage
data_table.Mental state: Anxious, congruent affect, no current SI, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Social context: Boarding school in loco parentis, parents overseas, identified worker is residential care staff
data_table.History: First admission, no prior DHHS / Department of Families involvement, fully immunised

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate combination of statutory pathways for this disclosure?

options.text: Report to Victoria Police and Child Protection only and skip the Reportable Conduct Scheme today because it only covers schoolteachers and not residential care workers
Make a Child Protection report alone because the boy is currently admitted to hospital and is safe under medical supervision
Notify the Department of Families and Victoria Police of possible offending, and have the school notify the Commission under the Reportable Conduct Scheme
Notify the school principal alone and ask the principal to manage the staff member and any subsequent reports internally
Defer all statutory reporting until the boy has completed a forensic interview with the Victorian Forensic Paediatric Medical Service later this week

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric ED by his father for assessment of a single bruise noted that morning while changing the nappy. The bruise is on the left buttock, measures 2 cm by 3 cm, and is yellow-green in colour. The father is unsure how the bruise occurred but suggests the baby may have rolled against a cot rail.

The infant is not yet pulling to stand and only cruises with support. He was born at term with a normal newborn check, is fully immunised, growing along the 50th centile, and has met all developmental milestones to date. He is otherwise well, feeding normally, and there is no history of bleeding disorder, no family history of coagulopathy, and no other current bruising visible.

Examination is otherwise unremarkable with no torn frenulum, no posterior rib tenderness, and no facial findings. The triage nurse asks the ED registrar to apply the TEN-4-FACESp clinical decision rule to determine whether further child protection assessment is warranted. The father is co-operative and the mother is at home with siblings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124 bpm, RR 28 /min, T 36.9 deg C, weight 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Single 2 x 3 cm yellow-green bruise left buttock, no other bruising, no torn frenulum, no rib tenderness
data_table.Development: Cruises with support, not yet pulling to stand, no rolling onto furniture
data_table.History: Fully immunised, no medications, no FH bleeding disorder

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge the infant home today with parental reassurance because a single small bruise is within normal infant variation
Refer for routine outpatient haematology review to exclude an inherited bleeding disorder before any safeguarding concerns are raised
Order a plain X-ray of the affected limb today and review the infant in 48 hours if any new symptoms develop
Admit for formal non-accidental injury workup with senior paediatric review, social work, skeletal survey, and mandatory child protection notification
Photograph and document the bruise today, then arrange a routine general practitioner review for the following week

stem:
A 5-week-old girl is referred to a tertiary paediatric ED by her general practitioner with a 1 cm torn upper labial frenulum that the mother attributes to a recent bottle feed. The baby was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery, vitamin K was given, and she has been feeding adequately with appropriate weight gain. She has no other visible injuries and no current bleeding.

The parents live together, both are employed, and there has been no previous contact with Child Protection. The infant is fully immunised to age and there is no family history of bleeding disorder, osteogenesis imperfecta, or sudden infant death. On examination there is the torn frenulum, an otherwise normal mouth, no posterior rib tenderness, normal anterior fontanelle, no head circumference change from birth percentile, and a normal neurological exam. Bedside coagulation screen and FBC are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142 bpm, RR 42 /min, T 36.8 deg C, weight tracking 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Torn upper labial frenulum 1 cm, no other injury, normal fontanelle, normal eyes externally, no rib tenderness
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, INR 1.1, APTT normal, fibrinogen normal
data_table.History: Fully immunised, vitamin K given at birth, no FH bleeding

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate complete sentinel injury workup for this infant?

options.text: Skeletal survey now and at 11 to 14 days, neuroimaging, dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy, coagulation and bone studies, and forensic paediatric involvement
Skeletal survey performed once at admission only today, with no follow-up skeletal imaging and no dilated formal eye examination
MRI brain only today, with no skeletal imaging and no formal eye examination given the absence of bruising elsewhere on the body
Bedside eye examination by the paediatric registrar without pupil dilation today, with no skeletal imaging and no brain imaging arranged
Coagulation screen alone and a routine outpatient paediatric follow-up arranged because the injury appears small and isolated today

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is referred to a paediatric developmental clinic for behavioural and learning difficulties. He was placed in long-term foster care at 3 months. His birth mother is documented to have consumed alcohol at hazardous levels throughout pregnancy. School reports document impulsivity, poor adaptive functioning, and specific maths and language deficits despite intensive support. Cognitive testing (educational psychologist) shows FSIQ 78 with significant scatter and severe impairment in three neurodevelopmental domains (executive function, adaptive behaviour, language).

Physical growth tracks the 25th centile. On focused facial examination: smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, and short palpebral fissures (below 3rd centile for age) - all three sentinel features present. There is no head injury, no seizure disorder and no other syndromic features. The foster carer is engaged with an Aboriginal community-controlled health service.

data_table.Growth: Height and weight 25th centile, OFC 25th centile
data_table.Facial features: Smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, short palpebral fissures (<3rd centile)
data_table.Cognitive: FSIQ 78, severe impairment in executive function, adaptive behaviour, and language domains
data_table.Prenatal: Confirmed hazardous prenatal alcohol exposure throughout pregnancy
data_table.History: Foster care from 3 months, fully immunised, no other syndromic features

lead_in: Which Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD category best applies?

options.text: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder without confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure, attributing facial features and impairment to teratogenic effect
ADHD combined presentation alone; the sentinel facial features are attributed to familial resemblance rather than prenatal alcohol teratogenicity
FASD with less than three sentinel facial features but with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure
Static encephalopathy of unknown cause because the measured IQ is above 70, with neurology follow-up for symptomatic management
FASD with three sentinel facial features (smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion, short palpebral fissures), severe impairment in at least three domains, plus confirmed exposure

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to a tertiary ED by her mother for review after losing 12 kg over five months. She has been progressively restricting her intake, exercising compulsively, and has missed three menstrual periods. She is medically naive and on no medications. On arrival she is alert and oriented, denies suicidal ideation, but is cold to touch and describes near-syncope on standing this morning.

Her current weight is 38 kg and her premorbid weight was 50 kg. Body mass index is 14.8 kg/m2 (well below the 3rd centile for age). Her supine heart rate is 38 beats per minute with a postural drop to systolic blood pressure of 78 mmHg standing. Core temperature is 35.4 deg C. Bedside ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 470 ms. Bloods reveal potassium 3.0 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, magnesium 0.65 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, and liver enzymes mildly raised with ALT 78 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 bpm supine, BP 96/60 supine to 78/52 standing, T 35.4 deg C, RR 14 /min
data_table.Anthropometrics: Weight 38 kg, BMI 14.8 kg/m2 (<3rd centile), 24% weight loss over 5 months
data_table.ECG: Sinus bradycardia, QTc 470 ms, no arrhythmia
data_table.Investigations: K 3.0 mmol/L, PO4 0.7 mmol/L, Mg 0.65 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, ALT 78 U/L
data_table.Mental state: Cognitively intact, no SI, mildly depressed mood, motivated to recover

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home today with twice-weekly community eating disorder team review and oral potassium and phosphate replacement at home
Admit to the paediatric ward under medical care with cardiac monitoring, cautious refeeding starting at 20 kcal/kg/day, electrolyte replacement, and ED team involvement
Admit directly to a child and adolescent mental health inpatient unit today with full caloric refeeding at 50 kcal/kg/day starting from day one
Transfer her today to a peripheral hospital for rapid IV crystalloid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg boluses and overnight monitoring
Refer her today for outpatient review in an eating disorder day program with weekly bloods, ECG monitoring and a six week follow up plan

stem:
A 17-year-old girl presents to her general practitioner for dental review following her dentist's discovery of bilateral enamel erosion on the lingual surfaces of her upper incisors. On gentle questioning she discloses six months of binge eating once or twice weekly followed by self-induced vomiting, with intermittent use of laxatives. She maintains a body mass index of 22 kg/m2 with stable weight.

She describes a marked sense of loss of control during binges, intense subsequent shame, and persistent overvaluation of body shape and weight. Her menstrual cycle remains regular and she is not currently using any contraception. She denies suicidal ideation but has felt low in mood and isolated from friends. Examination is unremarkable apart from mild parotid swelling and Russell's sign on the dorsum of one hand.

Bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc of 410 ms. Bloods show potassium 3.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, with normal phosphate, magnesium, and glucose. She lives at home with both parents and is in Year 12 studying for the HSC. She has not previously sought help.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral parotid swelling, Russell's sign, dental erosion, no postural hypotension
data_table.Investigations: K 3.4 mmol/L, HCO3 30 mmol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, ECG QTc 410 ms
data_table.Mental state: Low mood, shame, no suicidal ideation, body image overvaluation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer her today for inpatient medical admission to a paediatric ward for refeeding under the MARSIPAN-AU protocol
Reassure her today and advise dietary balance with no specialist referral because weight is normal and physical risk is low
Prescribe high dose fluoxetine 60 mg daily today as first line monotherapy without any structured psychological therapy
Commence outpatient enhanced cognitive behaviour therapy for eating disorders with GP medical monitoring and dental follow up
Prescribe oral potassium chloride supplementation today and review her in three months with no psychological intervention

stem:
A 16-year-old boy is seen in general practice with a 6-month history of being unable to fall asleep until 0200 to 0300 despite being in bed from 2200, severely impaired wake on school mornings at 0630, and missing first period most days. On weekends and during recent school holidays he sleeps from approximately 0300 to 1200 and wakes refreshed and functioning well.

He uses his phone in bed, denies caffeine after midday, denies illicit substance use, denies snoring or witnessed apnoeas, and a HEEADSSS screen is otherwise reassuring with no self-harm or pervasive low mood. His mother brought him today after two unsuccessful attempts at simply enforcing an earlier bedtime over the past month. He is otherwise well, on no medications, and his examination is unremarkable.

A sleep diary over the past 14 days confirms a stable late sleep onset with normal total sleep duration when free running. You diagnose delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and discuss management with him and his mother.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Sleep diary: School nights: sleep onset 0200-0300, wake 0630; weekends: sleep onset 0300, wake 1200
data_table.Examination: Mallampati 1, no tonsillar hypertrophy, no obesity, alert in clinic
data_table.History: No medications, no substance use, occasional phone use in bed, no snoring

lead_in: Which initial management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Sleep hygiene counselling alone, with planned review in 6 weeks before considering any pharmacological or light-based measure
Low-dose melatonin 0.5 mg taken 5 to 7 hours before current sleep onset, with morning bright light and gradual schedule advance
Melatonin 3 mg at the desired bedtime of 2200 with screen reduction advice and review in 4 weeks
Trial of temazepam at 2200 for 2 weeks to entrain an earlier sleep onset, then taper while consolidating sleep hygiene
Referral for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the sole initial intervention before any light or melatonin trial

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to a general practice by his parents with a six month history of nightly loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing followed by gasping arousals. He sleeps in unusual positions with neck extended and his parents describe loud restless sleep, occasional bed wetting, and morning headaches. His behaviour at preschool has changed with increased hyperactivity, poor concentration, and emerging difficulty with letter recognition.

He is not overweight, with growth tracking the 50th centile, and is fully immunised. He has had three episodes of acute otitis media in the past year and a current persistent mouth breathing pattern. On examination he has Brodsky grade 3 tonsillar hypertrophy that meets in the midline, an enlarged adenoid pad inferred from chronic mouth breathing, no Mallampati view assessable due to tonsillar size, and an otherwise normal cardiovascular examination with no parasternal heave.

There is no craniofacial syndrome, no neuromuscular disorder, and no family history of sudden cardiac death. He has no Indigenous status documented and lives in metropolitan Sydney with both parents and a younger sister.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 22 /min, BMI 16.0 kg/m2 (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Brodsky grade 3 tonsils, chronic mouth breathing, no parasternal heave, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Behaviour: Hyperactivity, poor concentration, declining letter recognition
data_table.History: Witnessed apnoeas, gasping arousals, morning headaches, secondary enuresis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of intranasal corticosteroid spray for 12 weeks with a parental sleep diary and clinical review at end of trial
Commence stimulant methylphenidate based on the school report of hyperactivity and inattention noted in class
Trial of CPAP at home overnight pending review without prior ENT review or sleep service involvement arranged
Reassure the family that loud snoring is developmentally normal in a 5-year-old and arrange routine review in 12 months
Refer to ENT for adenotonsillectomy assessment with paediatric sleep service involvement and consideration of polysomnography

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is referred by her general practitioner to a community paediatric service for assessment of probable attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. School and parent Conners 3 rating scales show clinically elevated inattention and hyperactive impulsive symptoms present since early primary school across home and school. Her mother reports persistent difficulty falling asleep, low mood since the start of the year with tearfulness on most school days, episodes of refusing to attend school, and a recent disclosure of being bullied for two years.

She avoids social activities, has lost two close friendships, and her academic performance has dropped sharply this year. She is otherwise well, growing along the 50th centile, takes no regular medications and has no medical comorbidity. Her hearing and vision screens at school have been normal in the past 12 months. There is no history of trauma, no head injury, and no Child Protection involvement.

The paediatrician is preparing to confirm a diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria and is considering whether and how to assess for comorbid conditions before any pharmacological treatment is considered.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg, growth 50th centile
data_table.Rating scales: Conners 3 inattention T-score 78, hyperactive-impulsive T-score 72 (both parent and teacher)
data_table.Social context: Two year bullying history, two friendship losses, school refusal episodes
data_table.Mental state: Tearful, low mood, sleep onset difficulty, no SI elicited but not formally screened

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step before starting medication?

options.text: Start immediate release methylphenidate today at low dose and titrate the dose while planning ongoing structured review
Refer her today for full neuropsychological testing battery before any other clinical intervention or medication is considered
Perform structured assessment for common ADHD comorbidities with validated screens and address them in parallel with the ADHD treatment plan
Refer her back to the school to manage bullying alone and review again in 6 months before any further clinical intervention
Prescribe melatonin alone tonight for sleep without further ADHD-specific intervention or any structured comorbidity assessment

stem:
A 13-year-old girl in Year 7 has missed 18 of the last 30 school days. She presents on school mornings with abdominal pain, nausea, and tearfulness and is unable to leave the house once school is mentioned. She reports being terrified of going to school but cannot name a specific bully, teacher, or academic concern. She is happy to spend time with friends on weekends, attends netball training without difficulty, and goes to her grandmother's house overnight without distress.

She sleeps in her own room without separation distress. At a recent paediatric review the school counsellor noted that her academic performance was previously above average and a transition from primary to secondary school in February has been associated with the new symptoms. There is no history of trauma, no bullying disclosed. She is fully immunised, growing along the 50th centile, takes no medications, and has no medical disorder identified. On HEEADSSS the only significant finding is the school distress. Her parents are supportive and engaged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, BMI 21 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peritonism, well outside school context
data_table.Mental state: Anxious on school mornings, euthymic at weekends, no SI, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.History: Year 7 transition February, no bullying disclosed, peer relationships intact
