lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Separation anxiety disorder with persistent excessive distress on separation from her primary attachment figures during the day
Conduct disorder with truancy and aggressive antisocial behaviour directed toward both peers and classroom teachers across multiple settings and contexts
School refusal driven by anxiety in the context of a recent school transition with no co-occurring conduct disorder features
Functional abdominal pain alone with no underlying comorbid mental health driver and full resolution outside the school environment
Major depressive disorder with pervasive social withdrawal and anhedonia present across both school and non-school contexts

stem:
A 13-year-old boy is seen at a community child and adolescent mental health service after 18 months of escalating behaviour: repeated school fights, theft from a local shop, deliberate fire-setting in a school rubbish bin, cruelty to the family cat on multiple occasions, breaking into a neighbour's shed and damaging tools, lying, breaking curfew, and overnight absconding. He shows little remorse.

He has had episodes of defiance and rule-refusal since age 6, but the present behaviours represent a clear escalation. There is no documented substance use disorder, no psychotic features, no manic features, and no significant trauma history disclosed. He has no intellectual disability and attends mainstream Year 8 inconsistently. He is up to date with immunisations and his physical examination is normal.

He meets DSM-5 criteria for adolescent-onset conduct disorder. His parents are exhausted, his school principal has indicated that one more incident will result in expulsion, and he and his parents have agreed to engage with treatment.

data_table.History: Fights, theft, fire-setting, animal cruelty, breaking and entering, lying, curfew breaking, low remorse
data_table.Duration: 18 months of escalating behaviour, defiant features from age 6
data_table.Mental state: No psychotic features, no manic features, no substance use disorder
data_table.Examination: Well, normal cardio-respiratory, no neurological deficit

lead_in: Which first-line evidence-based intervention is most appropriate to recommend?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily to target aggression and impulsivity, with monitoring of weight and metabolic parameters
Refer for structured family-based behavioural intervention (parent management training or multisystemic therapy); screen and treat comorbid ADHD, mood, substance use
Recommend a boot-camp style residential discipline program to interrupt the current escalating behavioural pattern in a structured environment
Individual psychodynamic psychotherapy weekly for 12 months as the sole intervention without parent or systemic involvement
Mandatory notification to police and child protection only, deferring any mental-health intervention until the legal pathway concludes fully

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is reviewed by a child and adolescent psychiatrist after 8 weeks of structured cognitive behaviour therapy delivered weekly by a psychologist for a moderate to severe major depressive episode without psychotic features. She continues to have pervasive anhedonia, weight loss, early morning awakening, hopelessness, and passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. There is no substance use, no mania history, and she lives with both parents who are engaged in her care.

She has no medical comorbidity, no QT prolonging medicationsion intolerance, and her ECG is unremarkable with QTc 410 ms. Her clinician is now considering adding antidepressant pharmacotherapy. The family is concerned about the Therapeutic Goods Administration boxed warning regarding antidepressants and suicidal thinking in young people and wants to understand both the choice of medication and the monitoring required if treatment is started. The patient is open to medication trial with appropriate safety planning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, T 36.6 deg C
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, QTc 410 ms, no arrhythmia
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH all normal; urine pregnancy negative
data_table.Mental state: Pervasive anhedonia, early morning awakening, hopelessness, passive SI without plan
data_table.Medications: Nil regular, no QT prolonging agents

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate pharmacological choice with associated monitoring plan?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 10 mg daily with weekly clinical review in the first 4 weeks for emergent suicidality, alongside ongoing CBT
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg extended release daily with monthly clinical review and no additional suicidal thinking monitoring planned
Commence paroxetine 20 mg daily with monthly clinical review and no formal safety planning arranged for the next four weeks
Commence amitriptyline 25 mg at night and titrate to therapeutic dose, with regular ECG monitoring planned over the coming months
Stop the current psychological therapy today and commence sertraline 50 mg daily as monotherapy without further structured psychological therapy

stem:
A 14-year-old presents to a tertiary gender service for assessment having identified as a transgender boy for the past four years. He was assigned female at birth, has been consistently insistent and persistent regarding gender identity, has socially transitioned two years ago with family support including legal name change at school, and reports persistent and increasing distress related to ongoing pubertal development.

Menarche occurred at age 12 and he reports menstrual periods as a major and worsening source of dysphoria over the past 18 months. He is at Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development with regular menstrual cycles every 28 days. He has been supported by an experienced child and adolescent psychiatrist for the past 18 months with no current major mental health condition; previous mild depressive symptoms have improved substantially with social transition and ongoing family acceptance.

data_table.Pubertal staging: Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair, menarche at 12, regular cycles
data_table.Mental health: 18 months psychiatric care, prior mild depression improved with social transition
data_table.Bone health: Bone age normal, no prior fractures, vitamin D 78 nmol/L, DEXA scheduled
data_table.Investigations: LH and FSH baseline normal, oestradiol mid follicular, normal pelvic ultrasound
data_table.Family + MDT: Both parents supportive, MDT includes endocrinology, psychiatry, gynaecology, fertility counselling

lead_in: According to current Australian standards of care, what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence gender affirming testosterone immediately because the patient is past Tanner stage 2 and has already menstruated for some years
Commence GnRH analogue puberty suppression following multidisciplinary review, with planned monitoring during therapy
Refer to the Family Court for authorisation of stage 1 puberty suppression as the required pathway under current Australian law
Decline any medical intervention today until the patient reaches the age of 18 and continue with psychological support alone in the interim
Perform irreversible chest reconstruction surgery now to relieve dysphoria before any further pubertal progression continues to develop

stem:
A previously well 5-year-old girl is brought to a Melbourne general practice with a 4-day history of crusted sores around the nose and right cheek that began after a minor scratch in the playground. She is systemically well and attending school. She has no drug allergies, no eczema and no household members with skin disease. She is afebrile with normal vital signs.

On examination there are three discrete lesions less than 3 cm in total area with classic honey-coloured crust, no surrounding cellulitis, no bullae, no lymphangitis and palpable but non-tender submandibular nodes under 1 cm. There is no mucosal involvement and no other skin lesions. She lives in a non-remote setting; the family does not identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. There has been no recent overseas travel and there is no local MRSA outbreak.

data_table.Examination: Three honey-crusted lesions <3 cm total area on face, no cellulitis, no bullae, no mucosal involvement
data_table.Social: Non-remote setting, attends school, no household skin disease

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Topical mupirocin 2% ointment to lesions three times daily for 5 days, with lesions kept covered or to remain home until lesions are dry; no oral antibiotics
Oral cefalexin up to 500 mg twice daily for 7 days plus daily chlorhexidine washes for the household
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole twice daily for 5 days as empirical community-acquired MRSA cover
IV flucloxacillin up to 2 g six-hourly with admission for paediatric observation
Reassurance and observation only with return at 7 days if not resolved

subtopic_detail: Non-bullous impetigo first-line therapy in primary care

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents to a GP clinic with one day of low-grade fever (38.1 deg C), reduced oral intake and new tender oral and skin lesions. Her older brother attended childcare with a known outbreak of hand foot and mouth disease last week. She is fully immunised and previously well. On examination she has several shallow oral ulcers on the soft palate and buccal mucosa and small grey-roofed vesicles surrounded by an erythematous halo on the palms, soles and around the buttocks.

There is no rash on the trunk or scalp, no lymphadenopathy, no conjunctivitis and no genital or perianal blistering. Vitals are otherwise normal. Her mother is 30 weeks pregnant and asks specifically when the child can return to childcare.

data_table.Examination: Shallow oral ulcers; grey-roofed vesicles on palms, soles, buttocks; no truncal rash

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnosis-and-exclusion advice per current Australian guidance?

options.text: Hand foot and mouth disease; no formal exclusion is required under NHMRC Staying Healthy provided the child feels well enough to participate; advise good hand hygiene and cover any weeping lesions
Hand foot and mouth disease; exclude until all blisters have completely dried, regardless of how well the child is
Primary herpes simplex gingivostomatitis; exclude until afebrile and lesions crusted
Varicella; exclude for at least 5 days from rash onset and until all lesions have crusted
Erythema multiforme minor; no exclusion required as the condition is non-infectious

subtopic_detail: Hand foot and mouth disease recognition and exclusion advice

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is seen with a 24-hour history of bilateral facial rash following a mild flu-like illness last week. She has had no fever, is eating normally and is attending school. On examination she has a confluent red rash on both cheeks with circumoral sparing and a faint lacy, reticular rash on the extensor surfaces of both forearms. She is afebrile with normal vital signs.

Her mother is 22 weeks pregnant and her younger brother has known sickle cell disease (HbSS) with a baseline haemoglobin of 78 g/L. The school has reported recent cases of slapped cheek disease. There is no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 90, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Confluent erythematous rash both cheeks with circumoral sparing; lacy reticular rash on extensor forearms
data_table.Household: Mother 22/40 pregnant; brother has sickle cell disease (Hb baseline 78 g/L)

lead_in: Which household contact warrants the most urgent specific action, and what is the appropriate first investigation for that contact?

options.text: All family members: reassure that the index case is no longer infectious now that the rash has appeared; no further action required

Brother with sickle cell disease: clinical review and urgent FBC plus reticulocyte count; arrange admission for transfusion if Hb is markedly below baseline with reticulocytopenia (transient aplastic crisis)
Mother: immediate empirical IVIG to prevent fetal hydrops irrespective of her immunity status
Mother: termination counselling because of high fetal loss risk in the second trimester
Index patient: exclude from school for a further 5 days because she is now most infectious

subtopic_detail: Erythema infectiosum and household risk stratification

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is reviewed in a community allergy clinic after two reactions to egg: hives and lip swelling, and a separate episode of vomiting plus audible wheeze within 20 minutes of ingestion. One reaction received adrenaline in the ED. There has been no hypotension or collapse. Skin prick test today shows an 8 mm wheal to egg white and specific IgE to egg white is 22 kU/L.

He has mild persistent asthma well controlled on a low-dose ICS. He weighs 17 kg. He has no other allergies. The family has not previously been prescribed an adrenaline autoinjector. Both parents have completed asthma first aid training and the childcare requires a written ASCIA plan.

data_table.Investigations: SPT egg white wheal 8 mm; sIgE egg white 22 kU/L
data_table.History: Two reactions to egg with wheeze and one ED adrenaline; mild persistent asthma on low-dose ICS

lead_in: Which combination of ASCIA action plan and autoinjector strength is correct?

options.text: ASCIA Action Plan for Allergic Reactions (non-anaphylaxis plan), no autoinjector, oral cetirizine PRN
ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis with a 150 microgram adrenaline autoinjector (EpiPen Jr) given his current weight of 17 kg
ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis with a 300 microgram autoinjector (EpiPen)
Refer for supervised oral food challenge to egg with no action plan until the challenge result is known
Discharge with an ASCIA Asthma First Aid Plan only, treating the wheeze as asthma-driven

subtopic_detail: ASCIA Action Plan selection in IgE-mediated food allergy

stem:
A 2-year-old boy with established atopic dermatitis returns to the GP for review after 6 weeks on hydrocortisone 1% applied sparingly once daily to active flares and intermittent moisturiser use. His mother reports nightly scratching, broken sleep for the whole family, and frequent flares despite avoiding soap and using cotton clothing. There is no honey-coloured crust, no clustered vesiclesitic spread.

He is otherwise well, fully immunised, has no food allergies and has a normal growth trajectory. Examination shows extensive erythema, lichenification and excoriation in the antecubital and popliteal fossae and on the cheeks, covering approximately 25 percent of the body surface area, with no overt secondary infection and no peri-orbital involvement. The mother is hesitant about stronger topical steroids because of online concerns about skin thinning, growth suppression and steroid-induced adrenal failure.

She has been using a single 50 g tube of bland moisturiser per week, applied only when the skin looks visibly dry. She has not been shown the fingertip-unit technique.

data_table.Examination: Erythema, lichenification, excoriation in flexures and cheeks; BSA ~25%; no honey crust, no vesicles
data_table.Current therapy: Hydrocortisone 1% sparingly once daily; moisturiser intermittently (50 g/week)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue hydrocortisone 1% ointment once daily to active eczema and add sedating oral cetirizine 5 mg nightly for pruritus with written instruction to limit moisturiser to dry areas
Step up to methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment daily to active eczema with at least 250 g per week of bland moisturiser and written fingertip-unit instructions
Commence oral prednisolone daily for 7 days to break the flare cycle followed by tapering wean over a further week, continuing hydrocortisone 1% once daily
Start topical tacrolimus 0.03% ointment twice daily to all active areas and stop topical corticosteroids entirely while continuing intermittent emollient as the sole adjunct
Refer urgently to paediatric dermatology this week for systemic immunomodulation with methotrexate or ciclosporin without further trial of stepped-up topical corticosteroid therapy

subtopic_detail: Eczema severity step-up using fingertip units and topical potency

stem:
A first-time mother brings her 5-month-old breastfed infant to the GP for advice. The infant has moderate atopic dermatitis well-controlled on regular emollient and intermittent methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% under paediatric dermatology supervision. There is no history of immediate reactions to any food and no breast-milk-related symptoms. The mother and father both have hay fever and the mother has mild asthma.

The paternal grandfather has confirmed peanut allergy. The infant is starting to show developmental signs of readiness for solids - good head control, interest in food, loss of tongue thrust. She has read conflicting online advice about delaying highly allergenic foods, especially peanut, until age 1 to 'wait until the gut is more mature'. She asks specifically how and when peanut should be introduced.

She is not vegan and there is no cultural restriction. She specifically asks whether peanut should be deferred until 12 months because of the family history, and whether referral for skin prick testing should occur before any home introduction. The family wants a clear, written, ASCIA-aligned plan to give the childcare centre.

data_table.Background: 5-month-old, moderate eczema controlled on emollient + moderate TCS
data_table.Family history: Both parents atopic; paternal grandfather peanut allergic

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice regarding allergenic solid introduction?

options.text: Introduce smooth peanut butter or peanut paste from around 6 months while continuing breastfeeding and continue including it regularly in the diet
Delay peanut introduction until 12 months of age given the strong family history of peanut allergy and continue exclusive breastfeeding with avoidance of all tree nuts
Refer for skin prick testing to peanut and other common allergens before any home introduction is attempted, and defer introduction pending the result
Introduce peanut only in the supervised setting of the GP clinic given moderate eczema and parental atopy, with observation for 2 hours after the first dose
Replace breastfeeding with extensively hydrolysed formula from now to prevent food allergy and delay solid introduction until at least 9 months of age

subtopic_detail: Atopic march counselling and early peanut introduction

stem:
A 3-year-old girl with previously confirmed IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy attends a paediatric allergy day-stay for a supervised oral food challenge. Her most recent reaction was 15 months ago with urticaria but no respiratory symptoms. She has well-controlled mild eczema and no asthma. Skin prick test today shows a wheal of 4 mm to cow's milk extract (negative control 0 mm, histamine 6 mm).

Specific IgE to cow's milk is 1.2 kU/L. She remains on a milk-free diet with calcium-fortified soy. After incremental doses up to a cumulative 200 mL of full-fat cow's milk over 3 hours she develops two small urticarial wheals on the trunk, no peri-oral swelling, no wheeze, and remains haemodynamically stable. Repeat observation at 90 minutes shows no progression and the wheals resolve with oral cetirizine.

The family asks whether milk can now be reintroduced freely at home or whether further specialist input is required before any dietary change. They request a written plan for childcare and for grandparents.

data_table.Pre-challenge: SPT cow's milk 4 mm; sIgE 1.2 kU/L; no asthma; last reaction 15 months ago (urticaria only)
data_table.Challenge response: Two urticarial wheals at 200 mL; no respiratory, GI, mucosal or cardiovascular features; resolved with cetirizine

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate interpretation and ongoing plan?

options.text: Failed challenge - continue strict milk avoidance and re-challenge in 12-18 months with an ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis and EpiPen Jr
Passed challenge - introduce cow's milk fully into the diet from tomorrow with no further action and discontinue calcium-fortified soy entirely without ongoing specialist follow-up
Equivocal challenge - commence the baked milk ladder at home over the next 6 weeks without further specialist input and reintroduce fresh milk if no symptoms arise
Passed challenge - replace soy with cow's milk over 7 days, reduce calcium supplementation and discharge from allergy follow-up with no autoinjector required
Indeterminate challenge - administer same-day intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg and admit for 24 hours of cardiorespiratory observation before any further dietary advice

subtopic_detail: Oral food challenge interpretation for resolving cow's milk allergy

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric ED by his parents 2 hours after the sudden onset of widespread itchy wheals on the trunk, limbs and face, plus puffiness of the lips and right eyelid. He took ibuprofen 3 hours ago for a viral upper respiratory tract infection that started 4 days ago. He has no food triggers, no insect exposure and no recent new medications other than ibuprofen and a 2-day course of amoxicillin started yesterday for presumed otitis media.

He has no asthma. On arrival his temperature is 37.4 deg C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 99% in room air and BP 105/68. He is settled, talking in sentences, with no stridor, no wheezeice. Lung auscultation is clear and he has brisk capillary refill. There is no abdominal pain, no vomiting and no hypotension.

data_table.Examination: Widespread wheals, lip and right eyelid swelling; no stridor, no wheeze, no tongue swelling, normal voice
data_table.Exposures: Ibuprofen 3 hours ago; amoxicillin day 2 for OM; viral URTI day 4

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 0.3 mg into the mid anterolateral thigh, IV fluid bolus normal saline and admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring overnight
Oral non-sedating antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine), withhold the ibuprofen and amoxicillin, observe for 4 hours and discharge with action plan if stable
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus oral promethazine as a sedating antihistamine, with discharge if asymptomatic at 2 hours after a single dose
Continue both amoxicillin and ibuprofen at current doses, add an oral non-sedating antihistamine for symptom control, and counsel that viral exanthem is the most likely cause
Refer for outpatient intramuscular omalizumab as first-line acute therapy for urticaria with angioedema and discharge after a single dose of oral antihistamine

subtopic_detail: Acute urticaria with angioedema in the ED

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is reviewed in general practice with a 6-week history of itchy, sharply demarcated dermatitis confined to a thin horizontal band across the upper abdomen and to both earlobes. The rash started 3 weeks after she received costume jewellery and a new metallic belt buckle for her birthday. There is no involvement of the rest of the trunk, no involvement of the hands or wrists, no joint pain, no oral lesionsrsonal or family history.

She is otherwise well, fully immunised, on no medications and has no history of eczema. Examination shows pink, scaly, lichenified plaques in the exact distribution of the buckle and earring posts with crisp angular borders and no spread to surrounding skin. Hand washing is performed with standard soap several times a day with no rash. Application of bland moisturiser has not helped.

data_table.Examination: Sharply demarcated, scaly, lichenified plaques confined to belt-buckle line on abdomen and to both earlobes; no spread, no mucosal involvement
data_table.History: New costume jewellery and metallic belt buckle 3 weeks before onset
data_table.Other: No atopy, no eczema, no systemic symptoms

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Allergic contact dermatitis to nickel with confirmatory referral for standard-series patch testing
Irritant contact dermatitis from soap with skin scraping for fungal microscopy
Atopic dermatitis in flexural distribution with referral for serum total IgE
Tinea corporis with Wood's lamp examination at the bedside today
Discoid nummular eczema with direct immunofluorescence biopsy for confirmation

subtopic_detail: Allergic versus irritant contact dermatitis discrimination in a child

stem:
A 4-year-old Aboriginal boy is referred from a remote community clinic to a regional paediatric service with a 6-week history of widespread itch, worse at night, and skin changes. He lives in a household with seven other people, three of whom also have itch. He has had two courses of topical hydrocortisone with no improvement. On examination he is well-grown, afebrile and systemically well.

There is hyperkeratotic, fissured scale on the palms, soles and elbows, multiple excoriated papules and a few burrows in finger web spaces and on the wrists. There is no facial or scalp involvement. He has no immune deficiency, no significant past medical history and is fully immunised. Skin scraping under microscopy shows mites and eggs. There is no secondary impetigo. The community has been advised by environmental health that there has been a recent cluster of scabies cases.

data_table.Examination: Hyperkeratotic palms/soles/elbows; burrows in finger webs and wrists; widespread excoriations; no facial or scalp involvement
data_table.Household: 8 people, 3 with itch; remote community with current scabies cluster
data_table.Microscopy: Mites and eggs visualised on scraping

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Permethrin 5% cream applied to the index patient only once now and repeated at 7 days, with continued hydrocortisone 1% for residual itch, no contact treatment and no environmental laundry measures

Permethrin 5% cream to the entire body of the patient and all household and close contacts simultaneously, repeat at 7-14 days, plus environmental measures (hot wash of bedding/clothing) and consider oral ivermectin given crusted features
Oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg as monotherapy on day 0 and day 7 with no topical scabicide for the index patient or contacts, no environmental decontamination and no school exclusion
Benzyl benzoate 25% emulsion applied head to toe to the patient and all family members on 7 consecutive nights without repeat dosing, environmental laundry measures or specialist follow-up
Defer all treatment pending dermatology incisional biopsy for definitive histological confirmation, with no interim scabicide therapy or household contact tracing today

subtopic_detail: Crusted scabies and household management in a paediatric setting

stem:
A 6-year-old boy presents to a general practice with a 4-week history of a progressively enlarging, tender, boggy scalp lesion with overlying pustules and patchy hair loss in the affected area. His older sister recently completed treatment for scalp ringworm at the same school. He has no fever, no headache and no neck stiffness. On examination he has a 4 cm boggy inflammatory plaque on the vertex with several superficial pustules, surrounding scale, broken hairs and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

There is no fluctuant abscess, no facial swelling and no cellulitic spread. Skin scraping and hair pluck for fungal microscopy and culture have been sent. He has no other dermatological disease and no allergies. His mother is worried about scarring alopecia and has read online about needing oral antibiotics for the pustules. The mother specifically asks whether incision and drainage of the boggy lesion is required and whether oral antibiotics for the pustules should be commenced today.

data_table.Examination: 4 cm boggy inflammatory scalp plaque with pustules and broken hairs; tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; no fluctuant abscess
data_table.Investigations: Fungal microscopy and culture sent
data_table.Contacts: Sister recently treated for scalp ringworm

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?

options.text: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for at least 4-8 weeks plus a topical antifungal shampoo, with topical/oral antibiotics only if bacterial superinfection is proven
Topical ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly and topical terbinafine 1% cream applied to the scalp lesion daily for 4 weeks with no systemic antifungal therapy
Incision and drainage of the boggy kerion under procedural sedation followed by oral flucloxacillin six-hourly for 7 days with no antifungal cover
Oral prednisolone once daily for 7 days as monotherapy to reduce scalp inflammation, with no antifungal therapy commenced until fungal culture returns
Watchful waiting for 4 weeks pending the fungal culture result with no antifungal therapy in the interim and review only if the lesion enlarges

subtopic_detail: Tinea capitis with kerion and systemic antifungal selection

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to general practice with a 6-week history of a slowly progressive linear band of small, slightly hypopigmented, mildly itchy papules along the side of her right leg. The band starts on the lateral thigh, follows a curving line down to the lateral ankle, does not cross the midline, and has no associated swelling, ulceration or pustules.

She is otherwise well, fully immunised, with no relevant past history. There has been no trauma, no insect bites at the siteo contact with anyone with similar rash. She has no eczema, no asthma and no recognised allergies. Examination shows a 30 cm linear band of pinhead-sized flat-topped papules in the line described, with no scaling, no indurationted lymphadenopathy. The mother is anxious about scarring and is keen to start any available treatment immediately.

data_table.Examination: 30 cm linear band of small flat papules along right leg following lines of Blaschko, no crossing of midline; no scaling, no induration, no nail change
data_table.Symptoms: Mild pruritus only; no systemic features
data_table.History: No trauma, no contact triggers, no atopic history

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Reassurance with bland emollient and a short course of mild topical corticosteroid (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) for pruritus, with expected spontaneous resolution over 1-2 years and warning that post-inflammatory pigment change may persist

Refer urgently to paediatric dermatology for incisional skin biopsy of the band to histologically exclude linear morphoea and other sclerosing dermatoses, with topical clobetasol commenced empirically pending result

Commence methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment twice daily for 6 weeks along the entire band with monthly review for tapering, assessment of skin atrophy and consideration of switching to tacrolimus
Refer for systemic immunosuppression with methotrexate given the linear distribution and 6-week chronicity, with weekly folic acid and monthly bloods for liver and renal function monitoring
Treat with topical clotrimazole 1% antifungal cream applied to the band twice daily for 4 weeks as for cutaneous candidiasis with review at 2 weeks and oral fluconazole if no response

stem:
A 14-year-old girl recently arrived from a country without routine MMR vaccination presents to a community health clinic with a 2-day history of fine pink maculopapular rash that began on the face and is spreading caudally. She has had a mild fever, a sore throat, and tender lumps behind both ears for 24 hours preceding the rash, along with mild joint discomfort in the hands.

She has not had any specific food trigger and there are no medications. She is otherwise well, eating, drinking and ambulant with stable vital signs (T 37.8, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99%). On examination she has discrete tender post-auricular and sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild conjunctival injection, no Koplik spots, mild oropharyngeal redness, and a fading erythematous fine rash now on the trunk. There are no purpura, no oral ulcers and no joint swelling. The clinic has several pregnant women attending today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Fine maculopapular rash spreading from face to trunk; tender post-auricular and sub-occipital lymphadenopathy; mild conjunctival injection; no Koplik spots, no purpura
data_table.History: Unvaccinated; recent arrival from country without routine MMR; pregnant women in waiting room

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate public-health action?

options.text: Isolate the patient immediately, notify the local public health unit on clinical suspicion, and identify and counsel any pregnant contacts about rubella serology
Send rubella IgM and IgG serology and discharge home with no isolation pending the laboratory result before considering notification to the public health unit
Administer MMR vaccination immediately to the patient and to any pregnant contacts in the clinic as urgent post-exposure prophylaxis for rubella
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone empirically pending blood cultures and PCR for meningococcal disease and admit for 24 hours of cardiovascular monitoring
Treat as measles with high-dose oral vitamin A and MMR post-exposure prophylaxis for unvaccinated household contacts within 72 hours of exposure

subtopic_detail: Rubella in an unvaccinated migrant teenager and public-health priorities

stem:
A 12-year-old boy with known peanut allergy and mild persistent asthma is brought to a metropolitan paediatric ED after a school excursion exposure. Witnesses describe sudden generalised urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting, audible wheeze and progression to a brief loss of postural tone within 15 minutes of eating a granola bar. The school nurse administered intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram via an EpiPen at 10 minutes and a second dose was given by paramedics 8 minutes later with sustained improvement.

On arrival to ED 45 minutes after the initial reaction he is alert, with HR 96, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 2 L oxygen, with no audible wheeze, no stridor, mild residual peri-oral oedema and clearing urticaria. He has had no further drop in BP, no recurrence of wheeze, and no further vomiting. The family asks whether he can be discharged after a short observation. His usual asthma is well-controlled with no recent exacerbations.

data_table.Pre-hospital: 2 doses IM adrenaline (school then paramedics, 8 min apart) with sustained improvement
data_table.Vital signs on arrival: HR 96, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 2 L O2
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild residual peri-oral oedema; no wheeze, no stridor; clearing urticaria
data_table.Background: Known peanut allergy; mild persistent asthma on ICS; well-controlled

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate disposition and observation plan?

options.text: Discharge home now with oral cetirizine 10 mg daily, a written ASCIA Action Plan for Allergic Reactions, a single in-date EpiPen and follow-up review in primary care within 48 hours of discharge

Observe in the ED short-stay unit for 4 hours from the last adrenaline dose and discharge if asymptomatic with the standard discharge bundle, adrenaline autoinjector and 2-week allergy clinic follow-up

Admit for at least 6-12 hours of monitored observation given severe features (two adrenaline doses, asthma, transient collapse) and discharge with updated Anaphylaxis Action Plan, two in-date adrenaline autoinjectors, ICS optimisation and immunology referral

Admit to PICU for 24 hours of intubated airway monitoring with a continuous intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to MAP and prophylactic salbutamol nebuliser regardless of current clinical stability
Discharge after 1 hour of observation with a 3-day course of oral prednisolone as routine pharmacological prevention of a biphasic reaction without extended ED observation

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis with biphasic risk - disposition decision

stem:
A 10-year-old girl presents to ED with a third episode in six months of recurrent, non-itchy, non-erythematous swelling of the face, hands and tongue lasting 36-72 hours each time, often preceded by colicky abdominal pain. There is never any urticaria, no hypotension, no respiratory distress and no clear food, medication or insect trigger. Two previous ED visits resulted in administration of intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous hydrocortisone and chlorphenamine with no apparent response and slow spontaneous resolution.

Her father has had similar episodes since childhood and her paternal uncle died from a 'throat swelling' aged 28. On examination today she is comfortable with non-pitting, non-erythematous swelling of the lips and left hand, no airway compromise, soft non-tender abdomen and normal vital signs. She has no known food, drug or environmental allergy and no asthma.

data_table.Examination: Non-pitting, non-erythematous lip and left hand swelling; no airway compromise; no urticaria; soft abdomen
data_table.Family history: Father with recurrent episodes since childhood; paternal uncle died from throat swelling age 28
data_table.Investigations: C4 low

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation and acute management?

options.text: Send serum tryptase during the current attack and commence intravenous adrenaline infusion with hydrocortisone as for refractory anaphylaxis unresponsive to intramuscular adrenaline

Send C1 inhibitor antigenic level and function (and consider SERPING1 testing); treat acute attack with C1 inhibitor concentrate (or icatibant) and arrange immunology follow-up for long-term prophylaxis planning
Send total IgE and a paediatric food-specific IgE panel and commence daily non-sedating antihistamine prophylaxis with up-titration as needed for symptom control
Refer for contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and outpatient gastroenterology workup for the recurrent colicky abdominal pain in isolation without further immunology investigation
Commence daily oral tranexamic acid as immediate definitive long-term prophylaxis without C1 inhibitor testing or specialist immunology input at this presentation

subtopic_detail: Hereditary angioedema versus allergic angioedema in a paediatric patient

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to a tertiary paediatric ED with a 4-day history of progressive fever, malaise, facial swelling and a widespread morbilliform rash that started on the trunk and spread to the limbs and face. He was started on carbamazepine 5 weeks ago for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. There is no preceding URTI, no new foodssect exposure. On arrival temperature is 38.9 deg C, HR 122, RR 24, SpO2 97% RA, BP 110/65.

Examination shows facial oedema, a confluent erythematous morbilliform eruption covering 70 percent of the body surface area without Nikolsky sign or epidermal sloughing, no mucositis, and palpable cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Investigations: WCC 18.0 x10^9/L with 12% eosinophils, ALT 320 U/L, ALP 250 U/L, creatinine 95 micromol/L (baseline 55), CRP 90 mg/L. Blood film shows atypical lymphocytes.

data_table.Examination: Facial oedema; confluent morbilliform rash 70% BSA; no Nikolsky, no mucositis; generalised lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.0 (12% eosinophils), ALT 320, ALP 250, creatinine 95 (baseline 55), CRP 90; atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue carbamazepine at the current dose, treat as a self-limiting viral exanthem with supportive paracetamol and oral cetirizine, and review in clinic in 7 days

Stop carbamazepine immediately, admit for organ-function monitoring, commence systemic corticosteroid (e.g. prednisolone) and consult dermatology and immunology; document the reaction and avoid aromatic anticonvulsants
Diagnose Stevens-Johnson syndrome based on fever and rash and arrange transfer to a tertiary burns unit for crystalloid fluid resuscitation and burns-style dressing care
Diagnose incomplete Kawasaki disease, commence IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin and obtain urgent echocardiography to exclude coronary artery aneurysms
Switch carbamazepine to phenytoin at an equivalent maintenance dose and monitor liver function tests weekly without specific dermatology or immunology referral

subtopic_detail: DRESS syndrome recognition after anticonvulsant exposure

stem:
A 15-year-old girl with a 14-week history of daily widespread itchy wheals appearing without identifiable trigger and lasting less than 24 hours per individual lesion, with occasional lip swelling, is reviewed in a paediatric allergy clinic. She has been taking cetirizine 10 mg daily for 8 weeks with partial benefit but daily lesions continue and sleep is broken. She has no anaphylaxis, no respiratory or cardiovascular features, no joint pain, no fever and no systemic upset.

Investigations show normal FBC, normal CRP, normal ESR, normal LFTs, normal TSH and negative coeliac serology. There is no preceding infection and no new medication. There is no clear physical trigger such as heat, cold, pressure or exercise. Symptoms are interfering with her schoolwork and mood.

data_table.History: 14 weeks daily wheals <24 hours each; occasional lip swelling; no anaphylaxis or systemic features
data_table.Trial: Cetirizine 10 mg daily for 8 weeks - partial response only
data_table.Investigations: FBC, CRP, ESR, LFTs, TSH, coeliac serology all normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue cetirizine 10 mg daily at the standard dose and add a 6-week course of oral prednisolone daily with no taper, then reassess for biologic therapy
Up-titrate the non-sedating H1 antihistamine to up to fourfold the standard dose (e.g. cetirizine 40 mg/day or equivalent) and review at 4 weeks before considering omalizumab
Add a sedating antihistamine such as promethazine at bedtime as the primary add-on therapy for chronic urticaria refractory to standard-dose cetirizine
Start intramuscular adrenaline 0.3 mg twice weekly as suppressive therapy until the wheals subside, with a written ASCIA Anaphylaxis Action Plan for school staff
Commence ciclosporin in divided doses as the preferred next-line agent before any consideration of antihistamine up-titration or biologic omalizumab therapy

stem:
A previously well, immunocompetent 4-year-old boy is brought to ED on day 4 of varicella. The parents report new escalating severe pain in the left thigh disproportionate to skin appearance, a fresh fever spike to 39.6 deg C after defervescence yesterday, and reduced weight-bearing. He has not been on ibuprofen. On examination he is unwell-appearing, HR 160, RR 36, SpO2 97% RA, BP 88/50, capillary refill 3 seconds and cool peripheries.

Over the left antero-medial thigh there is a 6 cm area of dusky violaceous skin around two coalesced varicella lesions, exquisite tenderness extending beyond the visible edge, indurated subcutaneous tissue and no crepitus. There are typical varicella lesions at multiple stages elsewhere. WCC 22 x10^9/L with left shift, CRP 280 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L (baseline 45), Na 132 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6, HR 160, RR 36, SpO2 97% RA, BP 88/50, CRT 3 s
data_table.Examination: 6 cm dusky violaceous patch around varicella lesions on left thigh; tenderness beyond visible edge; indurated subcutaneous tissue; no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 (left shift), CRP 280, lactate 4.2, creatinine 80 (baseline 45), Na 132

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Continue oral aciclovir six-hourly, observe in the short-stay unit for 4 hours and discharge home if the pain settles with simple analgesia and reassurance

Resuscitate with crystalloid, administer empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering Group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus (including clindamycin for toxin suppression) and arrange urgent surgical assessment for source control
Apply topical mupirocin 2% ointment three times daily to the dusky area and commence oral cefalexin six-hourly for presumed impetiginised varicella lesions
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as definitive monotherapy for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome without empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics or surgical input
Obtain urgent MRI of the left thigh with contrast to characterise fascial involvement before commencing intravenous antibiotics, fluid resuscitation or surgical consultation

subtopic_detail: Varicella complication in an immunocompetent child requiring escalation

stem:
An 8-year-old boy presents to a tertiary paediatric ED on day 3 of a febrile illness with progressive painful rash. He was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 9 days ago for recurrent UTI. Over the past 24 hours he has developed conjunctival redness with photophobia, painful oral erosions, dysphagia and dusky atypical targetoid macules on the trunk and face that are becoming confluent.

On examination temperature is 39.0 deg C, HR 140, RR 30, SpO2 96% RA, BP 95/55. There are haemorrhagic crusted lips, fibrinous oral mucosal erosions, conjunctival injection with serous discharge, urethral meatal erosion, and dusky atypical targetoid lesions over approximately 18 percent of body surface area with Nikolsky sign positive in two areas. Investigations show WCC 12 x10^9/L, CRP 70 mg/L, ALT 85 U/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L (baseline 50), Na 134 mmol/L, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. He has no immune deficiency and is otherwise well-grown. The retrieval team and burns unit are en route.

data_table.Examination: Haemorrhagic crusted lips, fibrinous oral erosions, conjunctivitis, urethral erosion; dusky atypical targetoid lesions ~18% BSA; Nikolsky positive
data_table.Investigations: WCC 12, CRP 70, ALT 85, creatinine 90 (baseline 50), Na 134, HCO3 18

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Cease trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole immediately, transfer to a centre with paediatric burns/intensive-care capability with ophthalmology and dermatology input, commence supportive care (fluid resuscitation, temperature control, analgesia, sterile non-adherent dressings, mucosal care), and document drug allergy and consider specialist-directed immunomodulation

Continue trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at half dose, commence oral prednisolone daily with topical chlorhexidine 0.05% to mucosal surfaces twice daily, and admit for 24 hours of fluid balance and pain monitoring before reassessment

Treat as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome with intravenous flucloxacillin six-hourly plus encourage oral hydration with maintenance fluids, paracetamol for fever and observation in the ED short-stay unit for 24 hours before discharge

Diagnose incomplete Kawasaki disease, commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours and high-dose aspirin in four divided doses with echocardiography on day 3 of admission to exclude coronary aneurysms

Perform a 4 mm punch biopsy of involved skin in ED, send for routine histology and direct immunofluorescence, and defer all therapy including culprit drug withdrawal and transfer until the histology result is available

subtopic_detail: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis early management in a child

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to his GP for a pre-kinder health check. He is otherwise well, growing along the 50th centile, fully immunised, with no exercise intolerance, syncope, cyanosis or breathlessness on play. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death or congenital heart disease, no recent sore throats, no joint pains, and no rashes. On examination he is pink and well perfused with normal femoral pulses, no thrill, a quiet S1 and S2 with no fixed splitting, and a soft musical murmur best heard at the lower left sternal edge while supine.

The murmur has a distinctly vibratory or twangy quality, occupies early to mid-systole, is grade 2/6 in intensity, softens considerably on sitting up, and almost disappears with the Valsalva manoeuvre. There is no diastolic component and no radiation to the neck or axilla.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 95/58 mmHg right arm
data_table.Examination: Pink, no clubbing or cyanosis, femoral pulses equal to brachials, apex non-displaced, no thrill, no diastolic component, no radiation to neck or axilla
data_table.Growth: Height and weight on 50th centile, head circumference appropriate

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that this is a Still's vibratory innocent murmur and document review at routine health checks; no investigations or paediatric cardiology referral are required
Refer for paediatric cardiology assessment and echocardiogram because innocent murmurs cannot be distinguished from pathological murmurs on examination alone
Arrange ECG and ASOT today and treat as possible acute rheumatic carditis pending results
Arrange exercise stress testing to exclude hypertrophic cardiomyopathy before clearing for kindergarten sport
Document the murmur as a small ventricular septal defect and arrange echocardiogram within one month

stem:
An 8-month-old boy with known unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot presents to a regional ED with his mother. He is awaiting elective surgical repair scheduled in 6 weeks. This morning after a feed he became inconsolable, cried vigorously, and then turned a dusky blue colour with deep, rapid breathing. The episode has been going on for around 10 minutes by the time he reaches the resuscitation cubicle.

He has not vomited, has had no recent fever, and there is no diarrhoea or reduced wet nappies. Baseline SpO2 is usually 88 to 92% per cardiology letters. On arrival he is markedly cyanosed centrally with extremities mottled, breathing deeply at 70 per minute, and the previously loud harsh ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge is now barely audible. He has good IV access from the ambulance. His weight today is 7.8 kg and he has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 188 bpm, RR 70 /min, SpO2 62% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather, BP 78/46 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed, irritable but rousable, deep Kussmaul-like respirations, soft 1/6 ESM ULSE (previously 4/6), CRT 4 seconds peripherally
data_table.Background: Known TOF, awaiting repair, baseline SpO2 88 to 92%, no prior tet spells documented

lead_in: After applying high-flow oxygen, which single next intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous adenosine rapid push at the paediatric SVT dose followed by saline flush
Knee-chest positioning with IV morphine slow push
IV furosemide to offload the right ventricle now
Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion peripherally
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate bolus before any other intervention

stem:
A 10-week-old term male infant is brought to a paediatric clinic by his parents because of poor feeding and slow weight gain. They report that he sweats profusely during breastfeeds, often pauses to catch his breath after a few sucks, and takes more than 40 minutes per feed. He has dropped from the 50th to the 9th weight centile over 6 weeks.

There has been no cyanosis, no syncope, and no fevers. At his newborn baby check a soft murmur had been noted and an echocardiogram at 4 weeks showed a moderately large perimembranous ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunt and mild left atrial and ventricular dilatation. He is now visibly tachypnoeic at rest, with intercostal recession, a hyperdynamic precordium, a 3/6 harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, and a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 170 bpm, RR 64 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 82/48 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tachypnoeic with subcostal and intercostal recession, hyperdynamic precordium, 3/6 PSM LLSE with thrill, hepatomegaly 3 cm, mild bibasal crackles
data_table.Growth: Weight dropped from 50th to 9th centile since birth
data_table.Echo (4 weeks): Moderate perimembranous VSD, left-to-right shunt, mild LA and LV dilatation, normal LV function

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial medical management?

options.text: Reassure parents and review in 3 months expecting spontaneous closure
Commence oral propranolol three times daily and high-energy formula
Commence oral furosemide BD and an ACE inhibitor with high-energy feeds
Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
Commence oxygen therapy at 2 L/min via nasal prongs for resting tachypnoea

stem:
A preterm male infant born at 27 weeks gestation is now day 6 of life on the neonatal intensive care unit. Birthweight was 950 g. He was initially ventilated for surfactant-deficient lung disease and is currently on synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation with FiO2 0.35 and mean airway pressure 9 cm H2O. Over the past 24 hours he has required escalating ventilatory support, has developed widening pulse pressure, bounding femoral pulses, and a continuous murmur at the upper left sternal edge.

He has been passing only 0.8 mL/kg/h of urine despite normal fluid intake. A formal echocardiogram performed this morning confirms a haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus with a 2.4 mm internal diameter, left-to-right shunt, left atrium to aortic root ratio of 1.8, and reversed end-diastolic flow in the post-ductal descending aorta. Renal function and platelet count are within accepted neonatal limits and there is no evidence of necrotising enterocolitis or active intraventricular haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR per vent 50, SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.35, BP 48/22 mmHg (wide pulse pressure), MAP 31 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bounding peripheral pulses, hyperdynamic precordium, continuous machinery murmur ULSE, lungs with diffuse crackles
data_table.Echo: PDA 2.4 mm, LA:Ao 1.8, reversed end-diastolic flow descending aorta, no other structural disease
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 220 x10^9/L, creatinine 55 micromol/L, urine output 0.8 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
Restrict fluids to a conservative ml/kg/day target and continue conservative management
Refer for surgical PDA ligation now as first-line therapy
Course of ibuprofen or indometacin for pharmacological PDA closure
Commence oral paracetamol six-hourly indefinitely as definitive closure agent

stem:
A 6-day-old term male infant is brought to a regional ED by his mother. He was born by uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery at 39+2 weeks with birthweight 3.4 kg, passed all routine newborn checks, and was discharged at 36 hours of life. Over the past 24 hours he has fed poorly, has been increasingly lethargic, and his mother noticed his legs looking mottled and feeling cool while his upper body remained warm.

He has had no fevers and no vomiting. On arrival he is pale, lethargic, and grunting. Brachial pulses are easily palpable bilaterally, but the femoral pulses are absent. Pre-ductal SpO2 on the right hand is 96%, while post-ductal SpO2 on the right foot is 84%. Blood pressure in the right arm is 78/44 mmHg and in the right leg is 42/28 mmHg, giving a clear upper-to-lower limb gradient. The liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin and there is metabolic acidosis on the venous blood gas.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4 deg C, HR 180 bpm, RR 70 /min, BP arm 78/44 / leg 42/28 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Absent femoral pulses, brachial pulses present, mottled cool legs, warm upper body, hepatomegaly 3 cm, single loud S2
data_table.VBG: pH 7.18, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, HCO3 12 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management while awaiting transfer?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide and conservative fluid restriction
Intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and oral feeds withheld pending surgical review
High-flow nasal cannula oxygen titrated to SpO2 above 95%
Intravenous adenosine rapid push to terminate suspected supraventricular tachycardia
Commence prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion via secure IV access

stem:
A 5-month-old previously well girl is brought to a metropolitan ED by ambulance because of poor feeding and pallor for 3 hours. Her mother reports that she felt the baby's chest racing earlier this morning and noticed she was breathing fast and looking sweaty during a feed. There has been no fever, no diarrhoea, and no preceding viral illness over the past week.

On arrival to resus she is pale, mottled, and lethargic but responsive to voice. Femoral and brachial pulses are present but extremely rapid and impossible to count manually. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 285 bpm with no clearly visible P waves and a constant RR interval. There are no delta waves on the resting trace once an experienced cardiologist reviews her baseline ECG from a previous well-child check. She has good peripheral IV access placed by paramedics en route. She is not yet hypotensive and remains alert.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 285 bpm (ECG), RR 60 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 76/48 mmHg
data_table.ECG: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia, rate 285, no visible P waves, constant RR, no QRS widening
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled, responsive, CRT 3 seconds, no hepatomegaly yet, lungs clear

lead_in: After applying continuous cardiac monitoring and defibrillation pads, what is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Crushed ice to the face for 30 seconds
Immediate unsynchronised defibrillation now
Intravenous verapamil by slow IV push
Oral propranolol as a stat dose
Right carotid sinus massage for 10 seconds

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is referred to a paediatric cardiology outpatient clinic after two episodes of exertional syncope. The first occurred while sprinting at school athletics, with a brief loss of consciousness during which her friends say her limbs jerked for around 10 seconds before she came round confused for 30 seconds. The second was while jumping in a pool 6 weeks later.

There is no history of typical post-ictal phase, tongue biting, or incontinence. A maternal uncle died suddenly in his 20s while swimming; the family was told it was drowning. She takes no regular medications and has never used a QT-prolonging drug. Examination is unremarkable with normal heart sounds, no murmur, and normal blood pressure. A resting 12-lead ECG at the clinic is shown to a paediatric electrophysiologist.

Manual measurement and Bazett correction across multiple leads in the same patient give a QTc of 510 ms, with broad-based notched T-waves in the precordial leads.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, BMI 21
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm 72 bpm, QTc 510 ms (Bazett), broad-based notched T waves V2 to V4, no delta wave
data_table.Family history: Maternal uncle sudden death in 20s while swimming, no other known cardiac disease
data_table.Triggers: Both episodes occurred during exertion (sprint, swimming)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance, electrolyte replacement, and follow-up ECG in 12 months
Non-selective beta-blocker propranolol, exercise restriction, cascade ECG screening of relatives
Commence sotalol 80 mg twice daily for QT shortening
Immediate implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) implantation as first-line therapy
Commence levetiracetam after referral to a neurologist for presumed seizures

stem:
A 9-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote community in the Northern Territory is reviewed at a regional hospital after 10 days of migratory polyarthritis affecting her knees, ankles, and wrists in sequence over the preceding week. Each joint has been hot, painful, and swollen for 2 to 3 days before migrating to another joint, with dramatic and rapid resolution. She also had a sore throat 4 weeks ago that resolved without antibiotic treatment, and a throat swab taken at that time was not collected.

She has no prior diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever and no known rheumatic heart disease on previous school-based screening echocardiograms performed at age 7. She has not had a documented fever during her current presentation, though her mother reports a febrile illness during the recent pharyngitis. There is no carditis clinically and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed today shows a structurally normal heart with no valvular regurgitation or pericardial effusion.

ECG demonstrates sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 220 ms (above the age-related upper limit). Anti-streptolysin O titre is 540 IU/mL and anti-DNase B is 380 U/mL, both elevated above the laboratory reference range. C-reactive protein is 60 mg/L, ESR is 65 mm/h, and a full blood count is otherwise unremarkable. The treating team is applying the 2020 RHDAustralia guideline using the criteria for high-risk populations.

data_table.Clinical: Migratory polyarthritis (knees, ankles, wrists), no carditis, no chorea, no subcutaneous nodules, no erythema marginatum, afebrile
data_table.Investigations: ASOT 540 IU/mL, anti-DNase B 380 U/mL, CRP 60 mg/L, ESR 65 mm/h, ECG PR 220 ms (above age threshold), echo normal
data_table.Background: Remote NT community, high-risk population, no prior ARF or RHD, sore throat 4 weeks ago

lead_in: Which single statement most accurately reflects whether this presentation meets the 2020 RHDAustralia Jones criteria for an initial episode of acute rheumatic fever in a high-risk population?

options.text: Does not meet criteria because she is afebrile and fever is mandatory for diagnosis
Does not meet criteria because echocardiogram is normal and subclinical carditis is required
Meets definite initial ARF: polyarthritis (major in high-risk), prolonged PR and elevated APRs (minors), plus recent GAS
Meets criteria only as probable ARF because monoarthritis is required in high-risk populations
Does not meet criteria because anti-DNase B is non-specific and only ASOT counts as GAS evidence

stem:
A 5-month-old male infant is referred to a paediatric ED with 6 days of unexplained fever to 39.5 deg C unresponsive to paracetamol. His mother reports increasing irritability and one day of red, cracked lips. He has had no diarrhoea, no cough, and no contact with sick household members. He has been investigated extensively in the community over 3 days.

Urinalysis is sterile on culture. Blood cultures at 48 hours are negative, and a full septic screen including CSF is unremarkable. He has had no rash and no peripheral changes apart from puffy hands noted today. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection but no lymphadenopathy is palpable. C-reactive protein is 90 mg/L, ESR 70 mm/h, platelets 580 x10^9/L, ALT 65 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, white cell count 17 x10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, and urine microscopy shows 25 white cells per high-power field without organisms.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 175 bpm, RR 42 /min, BP 92/50 mmHg
data_table.Clinical features: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, red cracked lips, puffy hands, no rash, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: CRP 90 mg/L, ESR 70 mm/h, platelets 580 x10^9/L, WCC 17 with neutrophilia, ALT 65, albumin 28, sterile pyuria (25 WBC/hpf, no organisms)
data_table.Cultures: Blood, urine, CSF all negative at 48 h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home on paracetamol and ibuprofen for presumed viral illness, review 48 hours
Commence IV ceftriaxone for occult bacterial sepsis and continue cultures
Request transthoracic echocardiogram to look for coronary artery aneurysms before any further treatment decisions
Treat empirically with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin and arrange echocardiogram
Commence high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone as monotherapy without IVIG

stem:
A 36-hour-old term male newborn is reviewed on the postnatal ward at a metropolitan tertiary hospital. His mother is 39 years old and declined non-invasive prenatal testing and combined first-trimester screening during pregnancy; the antenatal morphology scan at 20 weeks was reported as normal with limited views of the cardiac four-chamber view. Birthweight was 3.1 kg at 39+1 weeks gestation.

On clinical examination the baby has marked generalised hypotonia, brachycephaly with flattened occiput, upslanting palpebral fissures with bilateral epicanthic folds, small low-set ears with overfolded helices, a flat nasal bridge, a protruding tongue, a single palmar crease bilaterally, and a wide gap between the first and second toes. The midwife noted bilious green vomiting after the first three feeds and the abdomen is now distended with absent bowel sounds.

A plain abdominal radiograph performed at 24 hours of life shows a classic double bubble appearance with no distal gas. There is a soft 2/6 systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge with no thrill. Femoral pulses are easily palpable and equal bilaterally. He is not cyanotic and pre/post-ductal saturations are both 96%. Full blood count taken on capillary sample shows a white cell count of 24 x10^9/L with 35% blasts on the film, although the consultant haematologist notes the morphology and clinical context are most consistent with transient abnormal myelopoiesis. The neonatal team needs to prioritise the most urgent investigation in the first 24 hours.

data_table.Dysmorphology: Hypotonia, brachycephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar creases, sandal-gap toes
data_table.GI: Bilious vomiting, double-bubble on AXR, no distal gas
data_table.Cardiac: Soft 2/6 LLSE systolic murmur, femoral pulses present, no cyanosis
data_table.Haematology: WCC 24 x10^9/L, 35% blasts, morphology in keeping with TAM
data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 158, RR 50, SpO2 96% on room air

lead_in: Which single investigation is the highest priority in the newborn screening period for this infant?

options.text: Lumbar puncture and CSF cytology to exclude CNS involvement of leukaemia
MRI brain to characterise dysmorphology and exclude structural CNS malformation
Hip ultrasound to screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip
TSH and free T4 measurement to detect congenital hypothyroidism
Transthoracic echocardiogram to define cardiac anatomy before surgical correction of duodenal atresia

stem:
A 2-day-old term female neonate is reviewed on the postnatal ward after the midwife noted persistent bilateral lower limb swelling and unusual neck skin folds. Birthweight was 2.8 kg at 39 weeks; the pregnancy was complicated by increased nuchal translucency at 12 weeks, but the parents declined further prenatal testing. On examination she has marked pedal and dorsal hand lymphoedema, a webbed posterior neck with redundant skin folds, a broad shield chest with widely spaced nipples, and a low posterior hairline.

Right brachial pulse is normal but both femoral pulses feel weaker than the brachials and there is a 22 mmHg systolic differential between right arm and right leg cuff blood pressures. She is feeding well and not cyanosed. SpO2 pre-ductal is 97% and post-ductal is 95%. A genetic karyotype has been sent and is pending. The team must decide which finding warrants the most urgent investigation now.

data_table.Dysmorphology: Pedal lymphoedema, webbed neck, broad shield chest, widely spaced nipples, low posterior hairline
data_table.Cardiovascular: Right brachial pulse normal, both femoral pulses weaker, right arm BP 78/46 vs right leg 56/30 mmHg (22 mmHg systolic gradient)
data_table.Vitals: T 36.7, HR 148, RR 46, SpO2 97 pre-ductal / 95 post-ductal

lead_in: Which single feature in this newborn most urgently warrants an immediate echocardiogram?

options.text: Weakened femoral pulses with a right arm-leg BP differential suggesting coarctation
Pedal lymphoedema, which suggests a renovascular cause requiring urgent renal artery Doppler
Webbed neck, which mandates urgent cervical spine MRI for atlanto-axial instability
Widely spaced nipples, which require urgent breast ultrasound to exclude congenital absence of breast tissue
Low posterior hairline, which warrants urgent thyroid ultrasound for ectopic thyroid

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is referred to a community paediatrician for short stature and a heart murmur. He was born at term with a birthweight of 3.2 kg. Height has tracked along the 3rd centile and weight on the 10th centile, despite a mid-parental height on the 50th centile. He sat unsupported at 9 months, walked at 18 months and now uses only 2 to 3 word phrases.

He has hypertelorism with downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, a webbed neck with low posterior hairline, and a pectus carinatum superiorly with pectus excavatum inferiorly. There is a 3/6 ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge that is loudest on inspiration, with a soft single S2 and no thrill. Four-limb blood pressures are symmetric and femoral pulses are equal.

Echocardiography shows a thickened, dysplastic pulmonary valve with a peak gradient of 45 mmHg, mild post-stenotic dilatation of the main pulmonary artery, and no left ventricular hypertrophy.

data_table.Dysmorphology: Hypertelorism with downslanting fissures, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, webbed neck, pectus carinatum superior/excavatum inferior
data_table.Growth: Height 3rd centile, weight 10th centile, mid-parental height 50th centile
data_table.Cardiac: 3/6 ESM ULSE louder on inspiration, soft single S2, no thrill, no LVH, symmetric arm BPs
data_table.Echo: Dysplastic pulmonary valve, peak gradient 45 mmHg, no LV hypertrophy
data_table.Development: Walked 18 months, 2 to 3 word phrases, mild delay

lead_in: Which combination of underlying diagnosis and confirmatory genetic test is most appropriate?

options.text: Williams syndrome; request fluorescence in situ hybridisation for the 7q11.23 elastin region
Turner syndrome; request peripheral blood karyotype with 30-cell count for mosaicism
Noonan syndrome; request a multi-gene RASopathy panel (PTPN11, SOS1, RAF1 and related genes)
Marfan syndrome; request FBN1 sequencing
Trisomy 21; request peripheral blood karyotype

stem:
A 14-year-old boy is referred to a paediatric cardiology clinic by his GP because of a tall, thin habitus and a recently identified murmur during a sports pre-participation examination. He has a height on the 99th centile and an arm span 7 cm greater than his height, with a reduced upper-to-lower segment ratio. He has long, slender fingers with positive Steinberg (thumb) and Walker-Murdoch (wrist) signs bilaterally.

There is significant pectus excavatum requiring surgical consideration, a high-arched palate with dental crowding requiring orthodontic intervention, and mild scoliosis with Cobb angle 22 degrees on standing radiograph. An ophthalmology slit-lamp examination performed last month demonstrates bilateral superior ectopia lentis with mild myopia. Echocardiogram performed today shows aortic root dilatation at the sinuses of Valsalva of 4.4 cm, corresponding to a Z-score of 3.8 indexed to body surface area, with mild aortic regurgitation and no evidence of dissection.

The remaining cardiac anatomy is normal. His father died suddenly aged 38 from a presumed dissection of the ascending aorta while playing tennis; no formal post-mortem genetic testing was performed at the time. He currently plays competitive rugby league at school and trains four times per week with intensive resistance work. There is no history of joint dislocation or skin hyperextensibility.

data_table.Skeletal: Height 99th centile, arm span > height by 7 cm, positive thumb (Steinberg) and wrist (Walker-Murdoch) signs, pectus excavatum, scoliosis (Cobb 22 deg), high-arched palate with dental crowding
data_table.Ocular: Bilateral superior ectopia lentis on slit lamp
data_table.Cardiovascular: Aortic root 4.4 cm at sinuses of Valsalva, Z-score 3.8, mild aortic regurgitation
data_table.Family history: Father died at 38 of presumed aortic dissection

lead_in: Which single management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure as athletic build, continue rugby league, and arrange repeat echo in 5 years
Commence sotalol 80 mg twice daily and clear him to play competitive contact sport
Refer for immediate elective ascending aortic root replacement irrespective of Z-score
Atenolol or losartan, restrict competitive sport, annual echo and ophthalmology, FBN1 cascade screening
Treat with ramipril 5 mg daily and clear him for non-contact competitive swimming

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is referred for assessment of moderate intellectual disability (recent WISC FSIQ 58), comorbid attentional difficulties, hand-flapping when excited, poor eye contact, echolalia and tactile defensiveness. He attends mainstream school with full-time aide support. Examination shows a long narrow face with prominent forehead, large protruding ears, a high-arched palate, hyperextensible joints, soft velvety skin, mild pectus excavatum, pes planus, and symmetrically enlarged testes at a Prader orchidometer volume of 6 mL bilaterally for prepubertal age.

There is no microcephaly and no neurocutaneous stigmata. Family history shows a maternal uncle with late-onset intention tremor and gait disorder diagnosed in his 60s, and a maternal grandmother with primary ovarian insufficiency at age 36. Microarray comparative genomic hybridisation at age 4 was normal and a metabolic screen including very long chain fatty acids was normal.

data_table.Cognitive/behaviour: FSIQ 58, global delay, hand-flapping, poor eye contact, echolalia, tactile defensiveness, attentional difficulties
data_table.Examination: Long narrow face, prominent ears, high-arched palate, joint hypermobility, soft velvety skin, mild pectus excavatum, pes planus, prepubertal macroorchidism
data_table.Family history: Maternal uncle late-onset tremor/ataxia diagnosed in 60s; maternal grandmother primary ovarian insufficiency at 36

lead_in: Which diagnosis-and-investigation pair best fits and would have been missed by the prior microarray?

options.text: Klinefelter syndrome; peripheral blood karyotype
Williams syndrome; FISH for 7q11.23 elastin
Prader-Willi syndrome; DNA methylation analysis at 15q11-q13
Tuberous sclerosis complex; TSC1 and TSC2 sequencing
Fragile X syndrome; targeted FMR1 PCR with methylation analysis

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to his GP because of pallor. He was born at 39 weeks (3.4 kg) and was breastfed until 11 months, transitioning to full-cream cow's milk. He drinks about 900 mL of cow's milk per day from a bottle, including overnight, and refuses red meat, eggs and most green vegetables. He passes soft stool daily with no blood, has had no recurrent infections, no bruising and no overseas travel.

He is developmentally appropriate (walked 13 months, about 20 words). Examination: alert, well, height and weight on the 50th centile, conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no organomegaly, no purpura. HR 118, RR 28, T 36.8, SpO2 99 percent on room air. Bloods: Hb 80 g/L, MCV 62, MCH 19, RDW 18 percent, platelets 480, WCC 8.2, ferritin 6, CRP under 5, reticulocytes 1.0 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 bpm, RR 28, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 99% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, soft non-tender abdomen, no organomegaly, no purpura.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 80 g/L, MCV 62 fL, MCH 19 pg, RDW 18%, platelets 480 x10^9/L, WCC 8.2 x10^9/L, ferritin 6 microg/L, CRP <5 mg/L, reticulocytes 1.0%.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day, increase iron-rich foods AND commence oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day; recheck Hb at 4 weeks (expect a rise of at least 10 g/L)
Refer for inpatient packed red cell transfusion now because Hb is under 90 g/L, with type-and-screen and consent for transfusion at the receiving hospital
Order haemoglobin electrophoresis and HbA2 quantification before any treatment to exclude underlying thalassaemia trait or variant disease
Day-stay IV iron polymaltose infusion now, bypassing any trial of oral iron in this otherwise well child with chronic dietary deficiency aetiology
Multivitamin containing 5 mg elemental iron daily and continue current 1.5 L/day milk intake without specific dietary modification or recheck

subtopic_detail: Microcytic anaemia in a toddler with dietary risk factor

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to her GP by her parents for ongoing management of atopic dermatitis diagnosed at 4 months. She has had multiple flares despite the parents using an over-the-counter aqueous cream as a soap substitute and 1% hydrocortisone applied 'when it gets really bad' for two to three days at a time, then stopped. She has dry skin with lichenified plaques in the antecubital and popliteal fossae, mild erythema on the cheeks, and excoriated patches on the dorsum of both hands.

Her sleep is disrupted by scratching most nights. She had cow's milk protein allergy as an infant which has resolved, and her father has hay fever. There is no fever, no weeping or honey-crusting, and her growth and development are normal. The parents are worried about 'steroid damage' and ask whether they can avoid topical steroids altogether.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, HR 110, RR 24.
data_table.Examination: Generalised xerosis. Lichenified flexural plaques. Excoriated dorsa of hands. No pustules, no monomorphic vesicles, no honey-crust. Weight on 60th centile.
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated at this point.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate maintenance regimen?

options.text: Stop topical steroids; use thick paraffin-based emollient three to four times daily as monotherapy
Thick emollient BD, methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment daily then twice weekly, hydrocortisone 1% face
Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% twice daily to face and body until clear, then stop
Refer for systemic ciclosporin given the chronicity of her disease today
Daily bleach baths and oral cefalexin for two weeks as antimicrobial maintenance

stem:
A 3-year-old boy with longstanding moderate atopic dermatitis is brought to ED by his mother with a 36-hour history of a rapidly worsening rash on his face and neck, fever to 38.7 degC, and poor oral intake. He has been using methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment twice weekly proactively and an emollient four times daily, with good control until this week.

There has been no overseas travel and his immunisations are up to date including MMR and varicella. His maternal grandfather had a cold sore on his lip when he kissed the patient three days ago. On examination he is miserable, drinking small sips, with grouped 2-3 mm punched-out monomorphic erosions and umbilicated vesicles in clusters on the left cheek, periorbital region and chin, some now coalescing.

There is no honey-coloured crusting elsewhere, no ocular involvement on fluorescein staining, no neck stiffness, and no focal neurology. His pre-existing flexural eczema is otherwise stable. There are scattered satellite lesions on the right cheek and on his chest. He has had no contact with hand-foot-and-mouth disease at day care, no prior episodes of this kind, and his last wet nappy was 8 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 degC, HR 142, RR 28, SpO2 99% on room air, capillary refill 2 sec.
