data_table.Examination: Clusters of monomorphic umbilicated 2-3 mm vesicles and punched-out erosions on left cheek, periorbital and chin. No corneal fluorescein uptake. No meningism.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside HSV PCR swab from a deroofed vesicle sent. FBC, CRP, U&E pending.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Daily bleach baths and increase topical methylprednisolone aceponate to twice daily on the face
Topical mupirocin 2% three times daily for five days and continue topical corticosteroids as usual
Oral cefalexin four times daily for seven days for impetiginised eczema
Admit, commence IV aciclovir 8-hourly and arrange urgent ophthalmology review
Discharge home on oral valaciclovir with planned review at 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Eczema flare with painful clustered vesicles

stem:
A 7-week-old boy is brought to ED by his parents because he has not opened his bowels for 6 days and has had increasing abdominal distension and two episodes of bilious vomiting overnight. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3.5 kg. The mother reports that he did not pass meconium until day 3 of life and the midwife had needed to perform a rectal stimulation.

He is exclusively formula-fed at 90 mL every 3 hours but has been taking less today. His weight today is 4.2 kg (birth weight 3.5 kg). When the registrar performs a careful digital rectal examination there is an explosive release of foul gas and liquid stool. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. There is no fever. The anus is normally positioned, the sacrum is intact and lower limb neurology is normal.

The plain abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops with a paucity of rectal gas. Antenatal scans were unremarkable and there was no polyhydramnios. The newborn screening heel-prick was reported as normal including immunoreactive trypsinogen. He has no associated dysmorphism, no abnormal facies and no cardiac murmur.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 degC, HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 98%, capillary refill 3 sec.
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, tympanic, ribbon-like rectum on PR, explosive release on PR. Anus normally sited. No sacral dimple. Weight gain inadequate (only 700 g over 7 weeks).
data_table.Investigations: AXR: dilated bowel loops with paucity of rectal gas. FBC, U&E, VBG sent.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Functional constipation; commence oral macrogol disimpaction and discharge with GP review
Anal stenosis; perform serial anal dilatation in the GP clinic
Cow's milk protein allergy; trial hydrolysed formula and review in 2 weeks
Hirschsprung disease; refer for surgical review and arrange suction rectal biopsy
Hypothyroidism; check TSH and free T4 before any further workup

subtopic_detail: Red flag features for organic cause of constipation in an infant

stem:
A 10-month-old boy is reviewed by his GP at the routine immunisation visit. His weight today is 7.6 kg. He was born at 38+5 weighing 3.4 kg (50th centile) and tracked the 50th centile through to 6 months when he weighed 7.5 kg. He is breastfed on demand approximately 4 times a day and was started on solids at 6 months.

His mother reports he is fussy with solids and refuses most foods other than rice porridge. He has no vomiting, no diarrhoeally appropriate. Family height: mother 168 cm, father 180 cm. He has a normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination, no lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly. His length is on the 25th centile and head circumference on the 50th centile. His parents both work full-time and a grandparent provides daytime care; mealtime grazing on biscuits between meals is common.

He has had no antenatal concerns, no NICU admission, and his newborn examination was unremarkable. He has not been screened for coeliac serology, thyroid function or iron studies. His mother breastfeeds approximately 4 times in 24 hours, including overnight, and reports she does not see him take full feeds; he is often distracted at the breast. The mid-parental height projects to the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, HR 110, RR 30.
data_table.Examination: Alert, interactive. No dysmorphism. No oedema. Normal cardiorespiratory exam. No organomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart: weight has dropped from 50th to <10th centile over 4 months; length on 25th; HC on 50th. No investigations done yet.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial step?

options.text: Start an appetite stimulant such as cyproheptadine and review in one month
Admit to hospital for nasogastric feeding and observe weight gain inpatient
Order broad screen: coeliac serology, TFTs, sweat test, metabolic screen now
Refer immediately to child protection services on suspicion of parental neglect
Take a detailed feeding history and observe a feed before ordering any investigations

subtopic_detail: Assessment of inadequate weight gain in a young child

stem:
An 8-year-old boy is reviewed by a paediatrician at the request of his GP and school. For the last 18 months he has had difficulty sustaining attention to schoolwork, frequently leaves his seat, interrupts conversations, loses his pencil case daily and forgets multi-step instructions. His Year 3 teacher and his swimming coach have completed Conners questionnaires which were both above clinical cut-offs.

His mother reports similar behaviours at home, including weekends and school holidays, since pre-school. He has had no academic regression, has age-appropriate reading and numeracy, has friends but tends to fall out with them over impulsive comments, and has no features of low mood, anxiety, tics, autism or psychosis. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death, long QT or cardiomyopathy.

On examination he is well, height 50th centile, weight 60th centile, BP 100/64, HR 86 with a regular rhythm and no murmurs. There is no history of head injury, no perinatal hypoxia. He has no symptoms of restless legs, no snoring on direct questioning, and his sleep onset latency is appropriate. There is no anxiety disorder, no oppositional defiant features beyond developmental norms, and no learning disability identified on school psychometric assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 100/64, HR 86, regular rhythm.
data_table.Examination: No dysmorphism. Normal cardiovascular and respiratory exam. No tics observed.
data_table.Investigations: Conners ratings above cut-off from two informants. ECG: sinus rhythm, QTc 410 ms, no LVH, no pre-excitation.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of restricted elimination diet for 6 weeks before pharmacological therapy
Commence atomoxetine as first-line pharmacotherapy without a stimulant trial
Immediate-release methylphenidate 5 mg BD under paediatrician authorisation, behavioural strategies, monitor side effects
Watchful waiting for a further 12 months with a school behavioural plan only
Refer for cardiology review and stress echocardiogram before any pharmacotherapy now

subtopic_detail: Stimulant initiation in school-aged inattention and hyperactivity

stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to his GP by his parents for his routine check. His mother has noticed that he does not respond to his name, rarely makes eye contact, does not point to share interest, does not wave, and has only 3 single words used inconsistently. He prefers to line up his cars and becomes distressed when the line is disturbed.

He had normal hearing screening at birth, no birth complications, no significant medical illnesses, and is up to date with immunisations. His gross motor skills are typical (walks well, climbs stairs holding the rail). His paternal cousin has an autism diagnosis. Examination is unremarkable: no dysmorphic features, no neurocutaneous stigmata, no organomegaly. His M-CHAT-R/F at this visit shows a score of 8 (high risk threshold >=8).

There has been no language regression and no loss of previously acquired skills. He had a febrile illness with rash at 11 months that resolved within 48 hours. He attends a long day care 2 days per week and the educators have raised similar concerns to the parents about his lack of response to his name and limited interaction with peers, often playing in parallel rather than reciprocally.

He has had no episodes consistent with seizures, no head injuries and no recurrent ear infections. There is no maternal alcohol use during pregnancy. The parents speak English at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, growth on 50th centile across the board.
data_table.Examination: No dysmorphism. No cafe-au-lait macules. No organomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: M-CHAT-R/F score 8 (high risk). Newborn hearing screen normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and review at the 2-year check, as language development is variable
Refer to multidisciplinary autism assessment, arrange audiology, lodge NDIS Early Childhood referral
Order chromosomal microarray and Fragile X testing today, review when results return
Commence risperidone now for irritability and stereotyped repetitive behavioural features
Refer only to speech pathology and review again in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Developmental concern at 18 months with social communication features

stem:
A 15-year-old girl presents to her GP with her mother, who has found superficial linear cuts on her daughter's forearm. The patient initially declines to speak in front of her mother, so the GP sees her alone after confidentiality is explained. Over a confidential HEEADSSS interview she describes 4 months of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, fatigue, poor concentration affecting her grades, weight loss of 3 kg, and feelings of hopelessness.

She has been cutting her forearm with a razor weekly for 6 weeks for emotional relief. She reports passive thoughts that she would rather not be alive, but denies a current plan, intent, access to means, or previous attempts. There is no substance use, she is sexually inexperienced, and there is no disclosure of abuse. Her older brother has bipolar disorder.

She agrees that her mother can be involved in safety planning. Examination shows superficial linear forearm cuts, no active bleeding, no concerning weight loss on growth chart, BMI 19. There is no history of trauma, sexual abuse or domestic violence on confidential enquiry, and no eating disorder behaviours (no restriction, no binge-purge). She agrees to a follow-up plan and accepts referral to local youth mental health services.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial linear forearm cuts. Affect flat. Speech soft but coherent. No psychotic features. No infection.
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated at the initial visit.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Maintain confidentiality from the parents in all circumstances given she is a Gillick-competent minor
Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily today with no psychological referral, and review in 4 weeks
Admit involuntarily to a secure adolescent inpatient mental health unit today
Written safety plan (means restriction, supports), involve mother, GP within 1 week, refer CAMHS
Reassure that self-harm without suicidal intent is normal adolescence and review 3 months

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to ED by her parents after collapsing on standing. Over 9 months her weight has dropped from 58 kg to 38 kg; her height is 165 cm (BMI 14.0). She restricts intake to <600 kcal/day, exercises for 2-3 hours daily and induces vomiting after any meal she perceives as 'too much'. She has not menstruated for 5 months.

She insists she is fat. There has been no binge eating, no laxative use, no diuretic use, no substance use, no overt depressive symptoms beyond food preoccupation, no suicidal ideation. Examination: alert, cooperative, dry mucous membranes, lanugo on the back, BP 84/52 supine dropping to 70/40 on standing with HR 38 rising to 64, T 35.4 degC, capillary refill 3 sec, peripherally cool.

ECG shows sinus bradycardia, QTc 470 ms. Bedside investigations: Na 134, K 3.0, phosphate 0.7, magnesium 0.6, glucose 3.4, urea 6.2, creatinine 64, ALT 110. She denies laxative or diuretic use. She has no chest pain, no palpitations on exertion, no syncope episodes other than this collapse. She has no haematemesis, no diarrhoea, no constipation other than infrequent stool, and no abdominal pain. Family history: maternal aunt with bulimia nervosa, no thyroid disease, no diabetes, no coeliac disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/52 supine -> 70/40 standing, HR 38 -> 64 standing, T 35.4 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: BMI 14.0. Lanugo. Cool peripheries. Capillary refill 3 sec. No focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Na 134, K 3.0, PO4 0.7 mmol/L, Mg 0.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, ALT 110 U/L. ECG: sinus bradycardia 38, QTc 470 ms.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Discharge home with outpatient paediatric dietitian and weekly community GP review
Commence olanzapine 5 mg nightly for body image distortion and discharge home
Admit and commence high-calorie refeeding at 2000 kcal/day from day 1 to rapidly restore weight
Admit to psychiatric ward and defer medical management until psychiatric review tomorrow
Admit medical bed; cautious refeeding (~5-10 kcal/kg/day), daily electrolyte monitoring, prophylactic phosphate/thiamine, refer mental health

subtopic_detail: Severely underweight adolescent with food restriction

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is reviewed two weeks after her second culture-proven E coli febrile UTI (fever to 39 deg C) treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole per local sensitivities. The first UTI was 4 months ago. She has ongoing functional constipation well controlled with macrogol. She is otherwise well, growth on the 60th centile, with normal developmental milestones and an unremarkable antenatal renal ultrasound.

There is no family history of renal disease or VUR. Renal ultrasound after the recent admission shows mildly dilated left renal pelvis (AP diameter 8 mm), no hydroureter, no scarring, no duplex system, and normal bladder wall with no post-void residual. The GP is planning the next investigation.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile today. HR 100, RR 22, BP 96/60.
data_table.Examination: Well, abdomen soft, no flank tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: Renal USS: left renal pelvis AP 8 mm, no hydroureter, no scarring, no duplex. Urine MCS clear since treatment.

lead_in: Which next investigation is most appropriate, and when should it be performed?

options.text: Non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric nephrology referral for recurrent UTI; optimise constipation management concurrently
MCUG within the next week as the next investigation, with prophylactic trimethoprim continued until the result is reviewed in clinic
Commence nightly trimethoprim as long-term prophylaxis without further imaging to delineate cortical scarring or reflux pattern
DMSA scan in 4 to 6 months after the most recent UTI to detect cortical scarring, reserving MCUG for any abnormal DMSA result
Repeat renal ultrasound in 12 months and otherwise observe without any further imaging, with watchful waiting and return advice

subtopic_detail: Imaging after a second febrile UTI in a young girl

stem:
A 17-month-old boy attends his GP for delayed 12-month immunisations because the family has been overseas. He is well, immunocompetent, with no chronic illness. His mother is on the bone marrow transplant register and has just commenced cyclophosphamide-based conditioning for an upcoming allogeneic transplant in 4 weeks; she lives in the same household. The boy's 4-year-old sister is also up to date.

His mother is concerned about the safety of his vaccines given her own state and asks the GP for advice. His outstanding 12-month vaccines include MMR, meningococcal ACWY and the third dose of 13vPCV. He has had no recent live vaccines, no immunosuppressive therapy of his own, and no contact with active tuberculosis. The mother's transplant team has been in contact with the family GP and a written summary of household infection-control measures is being prepared.

The mother has had her own pre-transplant influenza, pneumococcal and any catch-up inactivated vaccines administered as advised by haematology. The father is asymptomatic and fully vaccinated.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, HR 108, RR 26.
data_table.Examination: Well child, no rash, no respiratory or other illness.
data_table.Investigations: None indicated for the child.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice regarding his catch-up immunisations?

options.text: Defer all of the child's vaccines until after the mother's transplant and engraftment
Give MMR and varicella as scheduled; routine isolation not required (manage rashes with aciclovir)
Replace MMR with an inactivated alternative because of household immunocompromise concerns
Give the child oral typhoid (live) vaccine prophylactically because of expected hospital visits
Give only inactivated vaccines and avoid live vaccines until mother is post-transplant immune-reconstituted

subtopic_detail: Live vaccine considerations in a household with immunocompromise

stem:
A 5-month-old breastfed boy attends his GP with his father, who has read 'a lot online' and wants to delay the 6-month vaccines. The mother is supportive of vaccination and has asked the father to discuss it with the doctor. The father is hesitant rather than refusing; his main concerns are that 'too many vaccines at once overload the immune system' and that aluminium adjuvants 'cause autism'.

The infant is otherwise well, growing on the 50th centile, with no medical issues. He had his 2 and 4-month vaccines without adverse events. There is no household medical neglect and the parents otherwise engage with primary care.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile. HR 120, RR 30.
data_table.Examination: Well, growth on 50th centile.
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated.

lead_in: Which approach is most consistent with current Australian NCIRS SKAI and RACGP guidance for vaccine hesitancy?

options.text: Refuse to provide further GP care to the family until the father agrees to the standard immunisation schedule for both of his children
Motivational-interviewing-style consultation - presumptive language, explore concerns, share tailored evidence on immune-overload and aluminium myths, offer SKAI resources
Notify child protection because vaccine refusal constitutes medical neglect under mandatory reporting obligations for treating clinicians in this family
Offer a spaced-out alternative schedule giving only one vaccine per visit to accommodate parental concerns about immune overload from co-administration
Refer to the Family Court to compel vaccination over parental objection

subtopic_detail: Parental hesitancy about routine childhood vaccination

stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to his GP by his mother because of bow legs and reluctance to walk. He was born at term, exclusively breastfed until 12 months without vitamin D supplementation, and has had limited sun exposure as the family wear concealing clothing for cultural reasons and live in a southern Australian city. His diet is otherwise low in dairy.

There is no history of diarrhoea, fatty stools, recurrent infections, fractures or a family history of metabolic bone disease. He is on the 25th centile for length and 50th for weight. On examination he has frontal bossing, widening of the wrists, palpable rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, and genu varum. He has no carpopedal spasm and no seizure activity.

His mother is otherwise well but reports myalgia and fatigue. The infant takes solids three times a day, including iron-fortified cereal, but very little dairy or oily fish. There is no family history of consanguinity, fragility fractures, or genetic bone disease. He has met expected developmental milestones for fine motor and language but has been slower to walk; he took his first independent steps at 16 months and is now unsteady, with frequent falls noticed by his mother. The wrist X-ray was ordered after the GP examined him today and the radiologist phoned through the metaphyseal findings.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, HR 108, RR 26.
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, wrist widening, rachitic rosary, genu varum. No tetany. Length 25th centile, weight 50th.
data_table.Investigations: 25-OH vitamin D 18 nmol/L, calcium 2.10 mmol/L (corrected), phosphate 0.9 mmol/L, ALP 920 U/L (markedly elevated), PTH 14.2 pmol/L (high), creatinine 24 micromol/L. Wrist X-ray: cupping and fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Bisphosphonates orally to correct the bony lower limb deformity
A single high-dose 'stoss' of colecalciferol 600,000 IU orally with no follow-up
IV calcium gluconate today and admit for cardiac telemetry monitoring
Calcitriol (1,25-OH vitamin D) 0.25 microg daily orally as first-line
Colecalciferol 1000-2000 IU daily for 3 months, optimise calcium, screen mother

subtopic_detail: Toddler with bow legs and biochemistry suggestive of metabolic bone disease

stem:
A 6-year-old boy (weight 22 kg) with known peanut allergy is brought to a tertiary ED by ambulance 25 minutes after biting a satay skewer at a family function. Within minutes he developed urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting, and audible stridor. He received IM adrenaline 300 microg into the lateral thigh by his parents at the scene and a second IM adrenaline 300 microg by paramedics 6 minutes later, with two boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg en route.

On arrival he is given high-flow oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather and a nebulised adrenaline 5 mg has just been started for persistent stridor. He has had no previous anaphylaxis admission and is not on beta-blockers. Despite these measures he remains hypotensive with ongoing wheeze, persistent stridor, and a flushed mottled appearance ten minutes after the second IM dose. The PICU registrar is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 91% on 15 L/min non-rebreather, BP 72/40 mmHg, T 36.8 deg C
data_table.Examination: Diffuse urticaria, marked lip and periorbital oedema, biphasic stridor, widespread expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 14 (drowsy but rousable)
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.29, lactate 4.4 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L; tryptase taken; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Medications received: IM adrenaline 300 microg x2, 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg x2, nebulised adrenaline 5 mg in progress, high-flow oxygen
data_table.History: Peanut allergy with prior urticaria only, no asthma, no beta-blocker use, fully immunised

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer IV hydrocortisone and IV chlorphenamine 2.5 mg, then reassess at 15 minutes
Third IM adrenaline 300 microg into lateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes
Commence an IV adrenaline infusion titrated to BP, with continuous cardiac monitoring
Give IV glucagon as a bolus to overcome adrenaline-resistant shock from beta-blockade
Give IV hydroxocobalamin for suspected concurrent cyanide-mediated vasodilation today

stem:
An 18-month-old girl (weight 11 kg) with no prior seizure history is brought to a regional ED in active generalised tonic-clonic seizure that began 28 minutes ago at home. Paramedics gave buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg at 5 minutes and a second buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg at 15 minutes without termination. On arrival at 25 minutes she remains in generalised convulsion with eye deviation, frothing, and incontinence; IV access has just been secured on the second attempt and a bedside glucose is 4.8 mmol/L.

She had a brief febrile illness with rhinorrhoea over the preceding 48 hours and a temperature of 38.6 deg C recorded today, but there is no rash, no vomiting, and no known toxic ingestion accessible in the home. There has been no prior antiepileptic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 28 /min (intermittent), SpO2 94% on 8 L/min Hudson mask, BP 96/58 mmHg, T 38.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic activity, GCS 3 during seizure, pupils 4 mm equal reactive, no neck stiffness assessable, no rash, anterior fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.20 pCO2 56 mmHg lactate 5.8 mmol/L, Na 137 mmol/L, Ca 2.30 mmol/L, FBC and CRP pending
data_table.Medications: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg at 5 min and 15 min, no other antiepileptics ever
data_table.History: First seizure, febrile URTI 48 h, fully immunised, no trauma, no toxin

lead_in: Following the APLS status epilepticus algorithm, what is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading over 20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring
IV phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading over 20 minutes with airway support ready
A third dose of buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg and continue to observe for spontaneous resolution
IV levetiracetam 40 mg/kg (max 3 g) over 5 minutes with continuous monitoring
Rapid sequence induction with thiopentone 4 mg/kg and intubation as primary seizure control

stem:
A 9-year-old boy with severe persistent asthma (one PICU admission 18 months ago for life-threatening wheeze, baseline fluticasone-salmeterol BD via spacer, salbutamol PRN) is brought to a tertiary ED after 12 hours of progressive wheeze triggered by a viral URTI in the family. In ED over the past 60 minutes he has received continuous back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 microg every 20 minutes for three doses, oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg with antiemetic cover, and high-flow oxygen at 10 L/min via nebuliser mask.

There has been no clinical improvement: he remains exhausted, leaning forward, speaking only in single words, and looks visibly tired between breaths. He has not yet received any IV bronchodilators, IV magnesium, or aminophylline. He is normotensive but markedly tachycardic with a fine tremor and palpitations from the salbutamol. There has been no fever, no foreign body history, and no preceding anaphylactic features. The PICU outreach team has reviewed at the bedside and recommends escalation but has not yet started any infusions while awaiting the ED decision.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 bpm, RR 42 /min, SpO2 88% on 10 L/min via nebuliser mask, BP 116/72 mmHg, T 37.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Tripoding, single-word speech, marked accessory muscle use, silent chest in upper zones, faint expiratory wheeze in lower zones, GCS 15 but visibly exhausted, fine tremor
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30 pCO2 50 mmHg HCO3 22 mmol/L lactate 3.8 mmol/L, K 3.0 mmol/L, glucose 9.4 mmol/L; CXR hyperinflation, no pneumothorax
data_table.Medications: Continuous nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium x3 doses, oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg given 35 min ago, no IV bronchodilator yet
data_table.History: Previous PICU admission age 7.5, fluticasone-salmeterol BD baseline, no LABA-only, no NSAID use

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg every 20 minutes and reassess in 1 hour
IV magnesium sulfate (max 2 g) over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
IV aminophylline loading over 60 minutes followed by maintenance infusion
IV salbutamol bolus over 10 minutes followed by infusion
Immediate rapid sequence intubation with ketamine and rocuronium

stem:
A 4-year-old boy (weight 16 kg) presents to a regional ED with 36 hours of fever and 6 hours of progressive lethargy following a varicella rash that began crusting 4 days ago. He has now had three 20 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride for hypotension and poor perfusion, with empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and IV clindamycin given for suspected invasive group A streptococcal septic shock.

Peripheral IV access only is available; the central line trolley has been requested but the local team is not credentialled to insert a femoral line, and the retrieval team is 45 minutes away. He remains shut down with cool mottled extremities to mid-thigh, prolonged capillary refill, narrow pulse pressure, and weak peripheral pulses. He has not yet received any inotrope or vasoactive infusion. Bedside echo by the retrieval consultant on tele-link shows a hyperdynamic underfilled left ventricle and no pericardial effusion. Lactate is rising despite ongoing resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 36 /min, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min Hudson mask, BP 74/40 mmHg, T 39.1 deg C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, cool mottled peripheries to mid-thigh, capillary refill 5 seconds, weak radial pulses, no rash beyond crusted varicella
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.21 lactate 5.6 mmol/L base excess -10, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 248 mg/L, coagulation deranged
data_table.Fluid given: 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg x3 over 45 minutes; no albumin, no inotrope yet
data_table.Access: Two peripheral IV cannulae, no central line, intraosseous available

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in haemodynamic management?

options.text: Commence peripheral IV adrenaline infusion and titrate to perfusion
Commence peripheral IV noradrenaline infusion as first-line vasopressor
Give a fourth 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride before any inotrope
Give IV hydrocortisone as the sole next haemodynamic intervention
Defer all inotrope infusion until a central venous line is inserted to avoid extravasation injury

stem:
An 11-year-old girl (weight 38 kg) is admitted to PICU with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis (initial venous pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, corrected sodium 141 mmol/L at admission). She received an initial 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride for shock and was then commenced on a deficit-plus-maintenance regimen calculated for 7% dehydration over 48 hours, with an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h started 1 hour after the fluids and added potassium 40 mmol/L once she had urinated.

Six hours into therapy the bedside nurse notes a 15-minute history of increasing headache, restlessness, and one episode of vomiting; over the past 20 minutes she has become more drowsy and confused, no longer engaging with her parents. Pre-decline GCS was 15; current GCS is 12 (E3 V3 M6). The most recent blood glucose is 14.2 mmol/L (was 32, falling at 3 mmol/L/h), sodium has fallen from 138 to 132 mmol/L despite the glucose correction (corrected sodium therefore falling), and she now has bradycardia and a rising blood pressure on the trend chart.

No focal neurology has yet been demonstrated; pupils are equal at 3 mm and reactive. The on-call PICU consultant has been called and the bed is being prepared for hyperosmolar therapy and possible intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62 bpm (was 110), RR 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 138/82 mmHg (was 102/64), T 36.8 deg C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), drowsy and irritable, no focal weakness, pupils 3 mm equal reactive, no papilloedema, Kussmaul breathing resolving
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 14.2 mmol/L, ketones 3.8 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L (corrected was 141 at admission, now ~134), K 3.6 mmol/L, pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L; head CT not yet done
data_table.Fluids/insulin: 0.9% saline + KCl 40 mmol/L at deficit + maintenance for 7% over 48 h, insulin 0.05 units/kg/h, no dextrose yet added
data_table.Trajectory: Glucose falling 3 mmol/L/h, corrected Na falling, GCS dropping over 20 minutes

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reduce insulin infusion rate and add 5% dextrose to current fluid bag, continue current rate
Increase IV fluid rate to replace deficit over 24 hours instead of 48 hours to improve cerebral perfusion
IV hypertonic 3% sodium chloride 5 mL/kg over 10 minutes, reduce fluid rate, urgent CT
IV dexamethasone for cerebral oedema and continue current fluid and insulin regimens
Intubate immediately and hyperventilate to pCO2 25-28 mmHg to lower intracranial pressure today

stem:
A 3-year-old girl (weight 14 kg) is brought into a regional ED resuscitation bay by ambulance after 6 hours of pallor, lethargy, and refusing fluids. Paramedics noted a narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 268 bpm on monitor with poor peripheral perfusion. She has had one previous documented episode of supraventricular tachycardia at age 18 months terminated by adenosine. On arrival she is pale, mottled, and increasingly drowsy.

She has poor peripheral pulses, no palpable femoral, and is barely rousable. IV access has just been obtained in the right antecubital fossa with a 22-gauge cannula on the second attempt. The rhythm strip from the ambulance shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves at a rate of 270 bpm; QRS duration 70 ms. Vagal manoeuvres (ice to face) were trialled at home by the mother and in the ambulance without effect. No drugs have yet been given in ED. The defibrillator is at the bedside with paediatric pads applied.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 270 bpm narrow complex, RR 36 /min, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min Hudson mask, BP unrecordable on cuff, T 37.0 deg C
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled to mid-thigh, capillary refill 5-6 seconds, GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5), no femoral pulse palpable, no murmurs audible
data_table.ECG: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia 270 bpm, QRS 70 ms, no visible P waves, no delta wave evident
data_table.Medications: Nil given in ED, vagal manoeuvres tried unsuccessfully
data_table.History: Prior SVT terminated by adenosine age 18 months, no structural heart disease known, no recent illness

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Rapid IV adenosine push then 10 mL saline flush via cannula
Synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 J/kg with procedural sedation if no immediate delay
Unsynchronised defibrillation at 4 J/kg as for ventricular fibrillation now
IV amiodarone loading over 20-60 minutes before any electrical therapy
IV verapamil as a slow push to break the re-entrant tachycardia

stem:
A 14-month-old boy (weight 11 kg) presents to a regional ED with 12 hours of barking cough, hoarse cry and worsening stridor at rest. He received nebulised adrenaline 5 mg (1:1000) and oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg 45 minutes ago. He had transient improvement for 20 minutes but is now again stridulous at rest with worsening recessions, increasing work of breathing, intermittent quiet episodes followed by paradoxical chest movement.

He is restless and difficult to console, and SpO2 is dropping. There is no drooling, no fever above 38.0 deg C and no foreign body history. He is fully immunised. The anaesthetic and ENT registrars have been paged and are 5 minutes away. The team is preparing the difficult-airway trolley. Current observations: HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 88 percent on 8 L/min Hudson mask, BP 102/66, T 37.6 deg C, with marked biphasic stridor, severe recessions, intermittent paradoxical chest wall movement and circumoral cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 88% on 8 L/min Hudson mask, BP 102/66 mmHg, T 37.6 deg C
data_table.Examination: Marked biphasic stridor, severe sternal and subcostal recessions, intermittent paradoxical chest wall movement, restless and not consolable, cyanosis around the lips
data_table.Treatment given: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg x1 (45 min ago), oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (45 min ago)
data_table.History: Barking cough 12 h, no drooling, no high fever, fully immunised, no FB history

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait 30 minutes for dexamethasone to take full effect before any further intervention
Repeat nebulised adrenaline 5 mg and continue ward observation; defer airway team involvement
Commence high-flow nasal cannula oxygen 2 L/kg/min and reassess at 30 minutes without airway team involvement
Repeat nebulised adrenaline as a bridge while transferring with the airway team to theatre for gas inhalational induction by anaesthetics, with ENT present and a smaller-than-predicted ETT prepared
Rapid sequence intubation in the ED with rocuronium and an age-appropriate cuffed ETT

stem:
A 13-year-old girl (weight 52 kg) is brought to ED by her parents after they found an empty 100-tablet bottle of paracetamol 500 mg in her room and a written note. She admits to taking tablets in two separate episodes over the past 18 hours: she states she took about 30 tablets approximately 14 hours ago after an argument with her sister, then a further 20 tablets about 4 hours ago when she decided she wanted to die.

She denies co-ingestion of other tablets, alcohol, or recreational drugs and there are no other empty packets in the home. She has no chronic medical illness, has a normal body mass index, is not on enzyme-inducing drugs (no carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, or isoniazid), and there is no chronic alcohol use, eating disorder, or malnutrition that would raise glutathione-depletion risk. She is fully alert with no nausea or right upper quadrant pain.

A paracetamol level taken on arrival (now 4 hours after the second ingestion and 18 hours after the first) is 320 micromol/L. ALT is 38 U/L and INR is 1.1; creatinine is 64 micromol/L; bicarbonate, lactate, and glucose are all normal. She has not vomited and has not yet received activated charcoal or N-acetylcysteine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, RR 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 118/72 mmHg, T 36.8 deg C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, no jaundice, abdomen soft and non-tender, no asterixis, mood low but engaged
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol 320 micromol/L (4 h post second ingestion / 18 h post first), ALT 38 U/L, INR 1.1, creatinine 64 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, VBG normal
data_table.Ingestion: Approx 30 x 500 mg paracetamol 14 h ago, then approx 20 x 500 mg paracetamol 4 h ago; total ~25 g ingested in staggered fashion
data_table.Other: No co-ingestants, no enzyme inducers, no chronic illness

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management decision regarding N-acetylcysteine?

options.text: Plot the 320 micromol/L level on the nomogram at 4 hours, withhold N-acetylcysteine
Withhold N-acetylcysteine because ALT and INR are normal, and arrange repeat bloods in 8 hours to reassess
Commence IV N-acetylcysteine 200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours immediately
Give activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally and reassess paracetamol level in 4 hours before deciding on N-acetylcysteine
Commence oral methionine 2.5 g every 4 hours for 4 doses as an alternative to IV N-acetylcysteine

stem:
A 7-year-old boy (estimated weight 24 kg) arrives in a tertiary trauma bay 65 minutes after being struck by a car as a pedestrian. Prehospital observations were HR 152, BP 76/40, GCS 14. He received 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride en route. FAST scan in the trauma bay is positive for free fluid in Morison's pouch and pelvis; he has an obvious right femur deformity in a traction splint, abrasions over the right chest wall, and bruising across the abdomen consistent with a seatbelt mechanism.

He is now drowsy with a GCS of 13, cool peripheries, and ongoing hypotension despite the prehospital crystalloid bolus. The on-call surgeon and interventional radiologist have been called. The blood bank has a paediatric massive transfusion pack available within 8 minutes. No tranexamic acid has yet been given. He has no known coagulopathy and no anticoagulants.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156 bpm, RR 32 /min, SpO2 96% on 10 L/min non-rebreather, BP 78/44 mmHg, T 35.6 deg C, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Bruised abdomen with seatbelt sign, positive FAST (Morison + pelvis), right femur deformity, capillary refill 4 s, cool peripheries to knees
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, base excess -8, INR 1.4, fibrinogen 1.6 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L, ionised Ca 1.05 mmol/L
data_table.Time: 65 minutes since injury, 10 mL/kg saline given prehospital, no blood products yet
data_table.History: No anticoagulants, no bleeding diathesis, fully immunised

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in haemodynamic resuscitation?

options.text: Activate paediatric massive transfusion protocol, IV tranexamic acid 15 mg/kg over 10 minutes, transfuse PRBC 10 mL/kg
Give a further 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride and reassess before activating MTP
Transfuse PRBC 20 mL/kg alone and withhold tranexamic acid until thromboelastography results are available
Withhold tranexamic acid as it is contraindicated in paediatric trauma and give cryoprecipitate 10 mL/kg first to correct fibrinogen
Commence peripheral noradrenaline to maintain perfusion and defer blood products until SBP is restored

stem:
A 5-month-old male infant (not yet sitting independently or rolling consistently) is brought to ED by his mother for a frenulum tear noted during a feed. Mother states he banged his face on the cot 2 days ago but the lip injury was only seen today. The father is a step-father who was alone with the infant on the day of the injury.

There is no past medical history of bleeding or bruising disorders. On examination there is a torn upper lip frenulum with surrounding bruising on the upper gum and a small yellow bruise over the left pinna. He is otherwise alert, well-perfused, feeding adequately on review, and has no acute distress. A previous ED record from 6 weeks ago notes a presentation for a left thigh bruise of unclear mechanism, dismissed as a possible cot-rail injury at the time. The Department of Communities and Justice has not previously been involved.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm, RR 36 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 90/56 mmHg, T 36.9 deg C
data_table.Examination: Torn upper lip frenulum with gum bruising, small yellow bruise over left pinna, no other external bruising on full skin exam, no torticollis, no head swelling, anterior fontanelle soft, retinal exam not performed
data_table.Development: Not yet rolling consistently, not sitting independently; pre-mobile per WHO milestones
data_table.Past presentation: ED visit 6 weeks ago for left thigh bruise, dismissed as cot-rail injury
data_table.Social: Mother and step-father carers, no prior child protection involvement

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that frenulum tears are common in this age group, GP review in 1 week
Send coagulation studies and FBC today, discharge home if all results are normal
Refer to outpatient paediatrics in 2 weeks for assessment, with no statutory notification at this stage
Discharge with father supervised by mother only, after a verbal safety plan with mother
Admit, mandatory child protection notification, skeletal survey, ophthalmology fundoscopy, plain CT head

stem:
A 4-year-old unimmunised boy presents to a regional ED with 6 hours of high fever to 39.4 deg C, painful drooling, refusal to swallow and a muffled hot-potato voice. He sits forward on his mother's lap in a tripod posture with his neck extended. There has been no preceding barking cough and no hoarseness; the parents describe rapid onset over a single afternoon.

There is no history of choking on a small object, no recent dental work, and no preceding pharyngitis. He has not received nebulised adrenaline or steroid. The ED consultant has asked the team to avoid distressing the child and to call anaesthetics and ENT immediately. He is alert but anxious and looks toxic. HR 148, RR 32, SpO2 95 percent on room air, BP 102/64, T 39.4 deg C, with tripoding, drooling, mild inspiratory stridor and no barking cough.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 bpm, RR 32 /min, SpO2 95% on room air, BP 102/64 mmHg, T 39.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Tripoding, drooling, muffled voice, mild inspiratory stridor, no barking cough, no hoarseness, neck extended, anxious but alert
data_table.History: Unimmunised, no preceding URTI, rapid onset over hours, no FB choking event, no dental procedure
data_table.Treatments given: Nil so far; team avoiding distress and calling airway team

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and immediate next step (without distressing examination) is most appropriate?

options.text: Acute epiglottitis (most likely Haemophilus influenzae type b given non-immunisation); keep the child calm on the parent's lap and proceed to theatre with anaesthetics and ENT for gas inhalational induction and definitive airway before any blood tests or imaging
Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup); give oral dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline in ED
Inhaled foreign body; arrange urgent rigid bronchoscopy in theatre
Bacterial tracheitis complicating viral croup with Staphylococcus aureus; intubate in theatre with copious tracheal toilet
Retropharyngeal abscess; arrange contrast neck CT before airway management

stem:
A 6-year-old boy (weight 22 kg) with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is admitted to the paediatric oncology ward 12 hours after starting induction with high-dose steroid and his first dose of rasburicase. The bone marrow blast count at diagnosis was 92%, white cell count 142 x10^9/L, with bulky mediastinal disease on imaging. He has been on hyperhydration with 2.5 L/m2/day of isotonic fluid without potassium since admission.

Over the last 4 hours he has become increasingly nauseated and reports muscle cramps and tingling around the mouth, and is now passing only small volumes of dark urine. A repeat biochemistry panel ordered after the nursing staff noted reduced urine output shows the changes below. A 12-lead ECG performed because of the potassium result shows peaked T waves in the precordial leads and a PR interval of 220 ms. The renal registrar has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 124/78 mmHg, T 37.0 deg C
data_table.Examination: Mild Chvostek sign, no carpopedal spasm, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: K 6.9 mmol/L, urate 0.62 mmol/L, phosphate 3.4 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.78 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 48), urea 12.2 mmol/L, pH 7.31, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, urine output 0.3 mL/kg/h
data_table.ECG: Peaked T waves V2-V5, PR 220 ms, QRS 90 ms, no widening yet
data_table.Treatment so far: Hyperhydration without K, rasburicase 12 h ago, no calcium given, no insulin-glucose, no salbutamol

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg as the first agent to shift potassium intracellularly, then reassess ECG in 15 minutes
Sodium bicarbonate IV bolus as primary therapy to drive potassium intracellularly today
IV 10% calcium gluconate over 5-10 minutes, then insulin-dextrose infusion, urgent dialysis
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate as the first intervention while ECG changes resolve spontaneously
IV furosemide as primary therapy to enhance renal potassium excretion in this oliguric child

stem:
A 6-day-old male term infant (birth weight 3.4 kg, now 3.2 kg) is brought to a regional ED with 12 hours of poor feeding, lethargy and grey colour. He was born at 39+4 weeks with Apgars 9 and 9 and discharged at 36 hours after a normal newborn examination. The newborn pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours was normal. There is no family history of congenital heart disease.

He is grey-mottled with cool peripheries and weak femoral pulses bilaterally. Four-limb BPs: right arm 78/50, right leg 52/30. Pre-ductal SpO2 (right hand) 92 percent, post-ductal SpO2 (foot) 78 percent. The precordium is hyperdynamic with a single loud S2 and no audible murmur. VBG: pH 7.18, lactate 6.2, BE -12, glucose 3.1, Na 136, K 4.6, Hb 168. Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary plethora. Echocardiography reveals critical coarctation with a closing PDA.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 64 /min, SpO2 pre-ductal 92% / post-ductal 78%, BP RA 78/50, RL 52/30, T 36.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Grey-mottled, cool to mid-thigh, weak femoral pulses, hyperdynamic precordium, single loud S2, no murmur, hepatomegaly 3 cm
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.18 lactate 6.2 mmol/L base excess -12, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, Na 136 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L, Hb 168 g/L; CXR cardiomegaly + pulmonary plethora; echo: critical coarctation with closing PDA

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention and oxygen target?

options.text: IV indometacin to close the patent ductus arteriosus and reduce the right-to-left shunt across the ductal lesion immediately
Adenosine rapid IV push for suspected supraventricular tachycardia, bypassing prostaglandin while awaiting paediatric cardiology review
Oral sildenafil to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance instead of maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin in this duct-dependent infant
IV prostaglandin E1 infusion 10-50 ng/kg/min titrated to effect, airway support ready for apnoea; target pre-ductal SpO2 ~85-92% and avoid high FiO2
Commence head-box oxygen at FiO2 1.0 to maximise systemic saturations, with continuous pre- and post-ductal SpO2 and serial ABG monitoring

stem:
A 14-year-old boy (weight 60 kg) with a mechanical mitral valve replacement on long-term anticoagulation is brought to ED 90 minutes after coming off his bicycle without a helmet. He had a brief loss of consciousness at the scene and one episode of vomiting. He is on dabigatran 110 mg twice daily (switched from warfarin 6 months ago due to INR variability); his last dose was 2 hours pre-injury.

On arrival his GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6) and dropping; he has a scalp haematoma over the right parietal area, equal but sluggish pupils, and a non-contrast CT head shows an acute right-sided subdural haematoma with 6 mm of midline shift. Neurosurgery plans urgent operative evacuation within the hour. INR is 1.2; aPTT 58 s; the thrombin time is markedly prolonged. He has no other major injuries on secondary survey.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, RR 18 /min, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, BP 132/82 mmHg, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Right parietal scalp haematoma, equal sluggish pupils, no focal limb weakness, no other injuries
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast CT head: right subdural haematoma with 6 mm midline shift; neurosurgery for urgent evacuation
data_table.Anticoagulant: Dabigatran 110 mg BD, last dose 2 hours before injury (so ~3.5 h pre-decision)
data_table.Coags: INR 1.2, aPTT 58 s, thrombin time markedly prolonged

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate reversal strategy before craniotomy?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus prothrombinex-VF as for warfarin reversal
Andexanet alfa 400 mg IV bolus then 4 mg/min infusion as specific reversal
Fresh frozen plasma infused over 1 hour as the primary reversal
Recombinant activated factor VII IV as a universal haemostatic agent
Idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g doses 15 minutes apart) as specific dabigatran reversal

stem:
An 8-year-old boy presents to a regional ED with 3 weeks of polyuria, nocturia, polydipsia and 3 kg unintentional weight loss. He has been tired but is still attending school and eating normally. He has had no abdominal pain, no vomiting and no Kussmaul respiration. He has no past medical history, takes no medications, is fully immunised and has a maternal aunt with T1DM.

He is alert and well perfused with no signs of dehydration. Fingerprick glucose 22 mmol/L, capillary blood ketones 1.8 mmol/L. VBG: pH 7.35, HCO3 19. Na 138, K 4.2. He has no acetone breath and no abdominal tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 108/66 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, mucous membranes moist, capillary refill <2 seconds, no acetone breath, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 22 mmol/L, blood ketones 1.8 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.35, HCO3 19 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with urine dipstick and GP referral for fasting glucose and HbA1c tomorrow
Commence IV 0.9% saline at twice maintenance and a fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour as per the inpatient ketoacidosis protocol
Admit under the paediatric diabetes team for diagnosis confirmation (HbA1c, type 1 antibodies), subcutaneous insulin initiation (basal-bolus), and structured family education with dietetics
Single oral dose of metformin 500 mg and paediatric endocrinology outpatient follow-up
Observe in short stay for 4 hours and discharge if glucose falls below 15 mmol/L

stem:
A 12-year-old girl weighing 40 kg with a 2-week history of polyuria and polydipsia presents to a tertiary paediatric emergency department after a day of vomiting and abdominal pain. She is drowsy but rousable, with deep sighing respirations and acetone breath. Capillary glucose is 32 mmol/L and blood ketones are 5.8 mmol/L. A venous blood gas shows pH 7.08, HCO3 7 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L and creatinine 88 micromol/L.

She has not previously been diagnosed with diabetes and is not on any chronic medication. There is no recent head injury, no seizure activity, and no concurrent gastrointestinal infection in the family. The senior registrar has commenced a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 30 minutes for clinically estimated 8 percent dehydration, an indwelling urinary catheter has been placed for hourly urine output measurement, and a second wide-bore IV cannula has been sited. The on-call paediatric endocrinologist and the PICU team have been informed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 36 /min Kussmaul, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% on RA, T 37.0 deg C, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, abdomen soft mildly tender, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: BSL 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, VBG pH 7.08, HCO3 7, Na 132, K 4.4, Cl 102, urea 9.8, creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate insulin and fluid management plan immediately after the resuscitation bolus?

options.text: Insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h immediately with the bolus, maintenance fluids only after the second hour
IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg followed by infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h, deficit over 24 hours
Use 5% dextrose with 0.45% saline from outset plus insulin infusion at 0.15 units/kg/h immediately
Start 0.9% saline maintenance plus deficit over 48 hours, insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h after 1-2 hours
Replace deficit with 0.9% saline over 6 hours, insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h after bolus

stem:
A 9-year-old boy weighing 30 kg is 6 hours into treatment of newly diagnosed diabetic ketoacidosis in a paediatric high dependency unit at a tertiary children's hospital. His initial pH was 7.02 with HCO3 5 mmol/L, glucose 38 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L (corrected sodium 142 mmol/L), potassium 4.6 mmol/L and chloride 100 mmol/L. He received a single 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 30 minutes, then maintenance fluid plus 48-hour deficit replacement using 0.9% saline with potassium chloride 40 mmol/L, and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h started 90 minutes after fluids commenced.

He has not received any sodium bicarbonate. Glucose is now 16 mmol/L, pH 7.18 and HCO3 11 mmol/L, and the nurses have just transitioned the fluid to 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose. Over the last 30 minutes the bedside nurse has noted progressively increasing irritability, a new complaint of headache, and now a single episode of non-bilious vomiting. On urgent reassessment his GCS has fallen from 15 to 11 (E3 V3 M5), with a heart rate that has slowed from 120 to 78 bpm and a rising blood pressure of 138/92 mmHg.

Pupils are 4 mm and sluggish bilaterally with no focal motor deficit and no posturing. The bedside glucose is 14 mmol/L and the most recent potassium was 3.9 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm (down from 120), BP 138/92 mmHg (up from 108/66), RR 14 /min, SpO2 98% on RA, T 36.9 deg C, GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5)
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, headache, one vomit, pupils 4 mm sluggish bilaterally, no focal neurology, fontanelle closed, no papilloedema visible
data_table.Investigations: BSL 14 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, last VBG pH 7.18 HCO3 11, urine output 1.5 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Increase IV fluid rate to twice maintenance and rebolus 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline to address suspected hypovolaemia
Stop the insulin infusion and give an IV bolus of 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia
3% hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg IV over 15 minutes, reduce IV fluid rate by a third, urgent CT brain
IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg infused over 30 minutes to correct the residual acidosis safely
Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis as cause of the altered consciousness today

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with T1DM diagnosed 8 months ago is found by her father unresponsive in bed at 06:30. She is on basal-bolus insulin glargine 8 units at dinner and aspart with meals; she had a heavier than usual swimming session yesterday afternoon. Her father estimates her current weight at 22 kg. Capillary glucose 1.6 mmol/L. She is breathing normally with a strong pulse but does not respond to her name, withdraws only to a sternal rub, and is having intermittent generalised tonic-clonic jerking.

There is no IV access at home. He has an in-date glucagon hypokit and an oral glucose gel in the fridge. Ambulance is 12 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 97% on RA, T 36.4 deg C
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive to voice, withdraws to pain, intermittent generalised tonic-clonic activity, airway patent
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate action by her father?

options.text: Place oral glucose gel between her cheek and gum and roll her onto her side
Administer IM glucagon 1 mg AND inject 2 units of insulin aspart to stabilise the response
Wait for the ambulance and let paramedics administer glucagon in 12 minutes
Administer IM glucagon 0.5 mg from the hypokit (because she weighs under 25 kg) and place her in the recovery position; recheck glucose after 10-15 minutes and call paramedics to confirm next steps
Give buccal midazolam to terminate the seizure before glucose correction

stem:
A 12-day-old male term infant presents to a regional ED with 3 days of poor feeding, vomiting and increasing lethargy. He was born at 39+2 NVD, birth weight 3.4 kg, exclusively breastfed, discharged at 48 hours with a normal newborn examination. The heel-prick screen has not yet returned. He has lost 14 percent of birth weight. There is no diarrhoea or fever.

He is pale, peripherally cool with CRT 4 seconds, sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. Genitalia are normal male with bilaterally descended testes and no hyperpigmentation. On arrival: HR 188, RR 56, SpO2 96 percent on room air, T 36.2, BP 62/38. Bloods: Na 124, K 7.2, glucose 2.4, urea 11, creatinine 62, pH 7.22, HCO3 14.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188 bpm, RR 56 /min, SpO2 96% on RA, T 36.2 deg C, BP 62/38 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, normal male external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L, K 7.2 mmol/L, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, urea 11 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and most discriminating biochemical signature is correct?

options.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and projectile non-bilious vomiting in the first 6 weeks of life
Late-onset group B streptococcal sepsis with septic shock and acute kidney injury rather than any primary adrenal or mineralocorticoid dysfunction
Urea cycle defect with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy; the discriminating signature is raised ammonia with a respiratory alkalosis on blood gas

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 with systemic mineralocorticoid resistance; the discriminating signature is hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + metabolic acidosis with normal cortisol and elevated aldosterone
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) with neonatal salt-wasting crisis; the signature is hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia + metabolic acidosis day 7-14

stem:
A 4-year-old girl with classical salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia is brought to the paediatric emergency department by her parents with 24 hours of fever, vomiting and reduced oral intake during a gastroenteritis outbreak at her childcare centre. Her regular medications are hydrocortisone 5 mg in the morning, 2.5 mg at midday and 5 mg at night, plus fludrocortisone 100 microg daily.

Her parents administered an extra oral hydrocortisone dose 6 hours ago but she vomited it back within 10 minutes and has not tolerated anything orally since. They did not have an in-date intramuscular hydrocortisone ampoule at home. On arrival she is drowsy and pale with markedly delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool peripheries and a thready pulse. Her body surface area is calculated at 0.7 m^2 and her weight today is 16 kg. Bedside glucose is 2.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 98% on RA, T 38.7 deg C, BP 78/44 mmHg, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 2.8 mmol/L, point-of-care Na 130 mmol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L, weight 16 kg, BSA 0.7 m^2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 20 mg with oral rehydration solution and observe in short-stay for 4 hours
IV dexamethasone, 10 mL/kg Hartmann's solution and IV ceftriaxone
IV hydrocortisone 50 mg bolus, 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose
IM hydrocortisone 100 mg and oral fludrocortisone 100 microg as a double daily dose
IV methylprednisolone and a 20 mL/kg 3% saline bolus for presumed cerebral oedema

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is referred by her GP for short stature. Her height has been below the 1st centile since age 5, and over the last 12 months her growth velocity has been 3 cm/year, having previously tracked along the 3rd centile. Her mid-parental height projects to the 25th centile. Her mother had menarche at age 13 and her father had a normal pubertal timing.

She has no chronic medications, no fatigue, and no family history of coeliac disease, IBD or thyroid disease. She has not yet had any breast development and there is no axillary or pubic hair. Her weight is on the 10th centile and BMI is normal. Examination shows a normal cardiovascular system with no radio-femoral delay or murmur, no goitrerological examination. Bone age performed last week is 9 years.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg, T 36.6 deg C, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Height below 1st centile, weight 10th centile, Tanner stage 1 breast and pubic hair, no dysmorphic features, no goitre, no cubitus valgus
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 9 years (chronological 11), MPH 25th centile, growth velocity 3 cm/year

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line investigation panel?

options.text: Growth hormone provocation testing with clonidine and arginine stimulation alone today
FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH/free T4, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), IGF-1, and karyotype
MRI brain with pituitary protocol plus dynamic GnRH stimulation testing now
Random cortisol, ACTH and short Synacthen test to exclude Addison's as cause
Faecal calprotectin and upper GI endoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease cause

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is referred by her GP for breast development first noticed by her mother 8 months ago. Her mother also reports the recent appearance of fine axillary hair, mild adult-type body odour, and accelerated linear growth (she has crossed two centile lines on the height chart in the past year, from 50th to 90th centile). She has had no headaches, no visual symptomsleeding.

There is no neonatal history of seizures or hypothalamic insult. There is no exposure to topical oestrogen, no parental medications she could be accessing, no oestrogen-containing supplements in the household, and no soy-heavy diet. On examination she has Tanner stage 3 breast development with palpable glandular tissue, Tanner stage 2 pubic hair, fine axillary hair on inspection of the underarm, no acne, no cafe-au-lait maculesaly.

Bone age performed today is 9 years. Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterine length of 4.2 cm with an endometrial echo and bilateral ovaries with multiple small follicles and no ovarian cyst or mass.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84 bpm, BP 102/62 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, height 90th centile, weight 75th centile
data_table.Examination: Tanner B3 P2, fine axillary hair, mild body odour, no acne, no clitoromegaly, no abdominal mass, no cafe-au-lait macules
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 9 (chronological 6), pelvic US: uterus 4.2 cm with endometrial echo, ovaries bilateral follicles

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation to distinguish central from peripheral precocious puberty?

options.text: Pelvic MRI to look for an ovarian sex cord-stromal tumour producing oestradiol
GnRH (or analogue) stimulation test measuring LH and FSH at 0, 30 and 60 minutes
Serum 17-OH progesterone and DHEAS to exclude non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Empirical commencement of a GnRH analogue (leuprolide) and monitor for breast regression
MRI brain with pituitary protocol to look for a hypothalamic hamartoma before any biochemical testing

stem:
A 9-day-old female infant has a positive newborn screening result from the Victorian newborn bloodspot screening program, with a TSH of 92 mIU/L on the day-2 sample (the laboratory cut-off used in Victoria is >=15 mIU/L on the dried bloodspot). She was born at 39+5 by uncomplicated NVD with a birth weight of 3.2 kg and Apgar scores of 9 and 9, has been exclusively breastfed every 3 hours, is feeding well, has had appropriate weight gain since the initial physiological loss and has passed meconium normally.

She has mild prolonged jaundice with a transcutaneous bilirubin of 180 micromol/L at day 9 but is otherwise well, with no lethargy, no constipationdistress reported by her parents. On examination she is alert, has an open posterior fontanelle of 1 cm, no umbilical hernia, no macroglossia and no palpable goitre or anterior neck mass. Confirmatory venous bloods drawn today show TSH 88 mIU/L, free T4 5 pmol/L and thyroglobulin 12 microg/L, with maternal thyroid antibodies still pending. A thyroid ultrasound and Tc-99m pertechnetate scan are being arranged through the nuclear medicine department.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 100% on RA, T 36.8 deg C, weight 3.25 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly jaundiced, posterior fontanelle 1 cm, no macroglossia, no umbilical hernia, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Bloodspot TSH 92 mIU/L, venous TSH 88 mIU/L, free T4 5 pmol/L, thyroglobulin 12 microg/L, bilirubin 180 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the bloodspot TSH at 4 weeks of age and only treat if it remains elevated
Commence oral levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day within 2 weeks of birth and review TFTs in 2 weeks
Commence oral levothyroxine 2 microg/kg/day to avoid overtreatment and review in 6 weeks
Defer treatment pending the result of the thyroid scan to determine the underlying aetiology
Commence intravenous liothyronine (T3) 2 microg/kg/day in preference to oral levothyroxine for faster onset

stem:
A 14-year-old girl is brought by her mother to the GP because of a 6-month history of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, gradual weight gain of 4 kg with no change in appetite, and a recent slowing of menstruation since menarche at age 12. She has had no neck pain or dysphagia. There is a family history of autoimmune disease, with her aunt having coeliac disease and her grandmother having vitiligo.

On examination she has a smooth, mildly enlarged, non-tender goitre approximately twice the normal size, dry skin, a delayed relaxation phase of the ankle reflex, and a heart rate of 56 bpm. Her height has tracked along the 25th centile but her growth velocity has fallen to 3 cm in the last year. Bloods today show TSH 78 mIU/L, free T4 6 pmol/L, anti-TPO antibodies 480 IU/mL (reference <35), anti-thyroglobulin antibodies 240 IU/mL, normal full blood count and normal electrolytes. Coeliac serology is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 56 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, T 36.1 deg C, BMI 70th centile
data_table.Examination: Smooth diffuse non-tender goitre, dry skin, delayed ankle reflex relaxation, no exophthalmos, Tanner B4 P4
data_table.Investigations: TSH 78 mIU/L, free T4 6 pmol/L, anti-TPO 480 IU/mL, anti-Tg 240 IU/mL, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oral levothyroxine 100 microg daily and recheck thyroid function tests in 6-8 weeks
Commence carbimazole 15 mg daily plus propranolol 20 mg three times daily orally
Arrange thyroid ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration of the goitre before any treatment
Defer treatment for 3 months to allow for possible spontaneous resolution of subclinical disease
Commence oral levothyroxine 50 microg daily and recheck TFTs in 6-8 weeks

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric endocrinology outpatient clinic by her GP with a 3-month history of progressive unintentional weight loss of 6 kg despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, fine tremor, palpitations, mild anxiety, oligomenorrhoea and poor sleep, and a recent decline in academic performance noted by her teachers. Her mother has noticed that her eyes appear more prominent and that she has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and a tendency to fidget.

There is no recent viral illness, no anterior neck paindine-containing medication exposure, and no family history of thyroid disease, although a maternal cousin has type 1 diabetes mellitus and her grandmother has vitiligo. On examination she has a smooth diffuse non-tender goitre approximately twice normal size with an audible bruit on auscultation, mild bilateral proptosis with lid lag and lid retraction, fine resting tremor, warm sweaty palms, and a resting heart rate of 124 bpm in sinus rhythm.

Her bloods show TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L (reference 9-19), free T3 18 pmol/L (reference 3.5-6.5), anti-TSH receptor antibody 12 IU/L (reference <1.75), and a normal full blood count including a neutrophil count of 4.2 x 10^9/L with normal LFTs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124 bpm sinus, BP 138/72 mmHg with wide pulse pressure, T 37.4 deg C, RR 18 /min
data_table.Examination: Smooth goitre with bruit, mild bilateral proptosis with lid lag, fine tremor, warm sweaty palms, no pretibial myxoedema
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L, free T3 18 pmol/L, anti-TSHR Ab 12 IU/L, neutrophils 4.2 x 10^9/L, LFT normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line medical management?

options.text: Propylthiouracil 5-10 mg/kg/day orally as preferred thionamide due to peripheral T4-to-T3 block
Definitive radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation as initial therapy without a trial of thionamide
Total thyroidectomy under general anaesthesia as first-line definitive therapy now
Carbimazole 0.5-1 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses plus propranolol 1-2 mg/kg/day, monitor FBC/LFT
Lugol's iodine 5-10 drops three times daily as monotherapy until normalisation of free T4

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is referred from his GP for evaluation of polyuria and polydipsia of 4 months' duration. His parents estimate his fluid intake at approximately 4 litres per day, including overnight water bottles, and he is waking 3-4 times nightly to drink and urinate, with secondary nocturnal enuresis after being dry at night for the previous 18 months. He has had a 1 kg weight loss but is otherwise growing on the 25th centile and his pubertal stage is Tanner 1 as expected.

There is no history of head injury, no headachesetes mellitus such as polyphagia. His past history includes Langerhans cell histiocytosis diagnosed 18 months ago at age 3 with cutaneous and bony involvement, treated with vinblastine and prednisolone, that has been in apparent remission on surveillance imaging. On examination he is alert, well perfused, with normal vital signs and an unremarkable systemic examination, including normal fundoscopy and visual field examination by confrontation.

Bloods today show Na 148 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, urea 6.2 mmol/L, creatinine 38 micromol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, calcium 2.4 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 305 mOsm/kg with a paired urine osmolality of 110 mOsm/kg measured on a morning sample.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mucous membranes moist, no visual field defect, no papilloedema, no skin lesions visible
data_table.Investigations: Na 148 mmol/L, plasma osm 305 mOsm/kg, urine osm 110 mOsm/kg, SG 1.002, glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Formal water deprivation test with paired plasma and urine osmolality, then desmopressin challenge
Desmopressin trial with measurement of urine osmolality response, followed by MRI brain with pituitary protocol
Renal ultrasound and urinary tract DMSA scan to assess for medullary cystic disease
Oral glucose tolerance test to exclude type 1 diabetes mellitus as the cause
24-hour urinary calcium and serum parathyroid hormone to exclude hypercalciuric nephrogenic DI

stem:
A 7-year-old girl is on day 3 of admission for culture-proven Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis. She is receiving IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily, has had dexamethasone for the first 4 doses, and is on maintenance IV fluids with 0.9% saline plus 5% dextrose at 70 mL/hour. Her GCS has improved from 12 on admission to 14 today. Overnight the nurse notes her urine output has fallen to 1.2 mL/kg/h and her morning bloods show Na 124 mmol/L (down from 137 yesterday), K 3.8, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, plasma osmolality 252 mOsm/kg.

A paired urine sample shows urine sodium 78 mmol/L and urine osmolality 510 mOsm/kg. On clinical examination she is alert, euvolaemic with capillary refill of 2 seconds, moist mucous membranes, no peripheral oedema, JVP not raised, and no postural drop. She has had a mild morning headache but no vomiting, no seizure activity and no focal neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, T 37.0 deg C, GCS 14, weight 25 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, euvolaemic clinically, no oedema, JVP not raised, no focal neurology, fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L, K 3.8, urea 3.2, plasma osm 252 mOsm/kg, urine Na 78 mmol/L, urine osm 510 mOsm/kg, urine output 1.2 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluid restriction to approximately two-thirds maintenance with daily electrolytes and strict fluid balance
3% hypertonic saline 3-5 mL/kg IV bolus to correct sodium 5 mmol/L over 30 min
Increase maintenance fluid to 1.5 times maintenance with 0.9% saline to replace renal sodium losses
Commence oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily for selective V2 receptor antagonism today
Administer furosemide IV with potassium chloride supplementation and continue current fluids

stem:
A 14-year-old boy is referred to a paediatric weight management clinic with a BMI of 36 kg/m^2 (>99.9th centile), with weight gain accelerating since age 9. He was a normally grown infant with a healthy weight until age 8. He has no syndromic features, normal growth velocity, normal pubertal progression, and no developmental delay. He has obstructive sleep apnoea (AHI 18 events/h on polysomnography 6 months ago), insulin-resistant acanthosis nigricans at the neck, persistent right knee pain on impact, and self-reported low mood with school avoidance for the last 6 months.

His mother and uncle have type 2 diabetes; his father has had bariatric surgery. Investigations show fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.9%, fasting insulin elevated, ALT 78 U/L with hepatic steatosis on ultrasound, normal TSH and free T4, normal cortisol with no Cushingoid features, normal calcium and phosphate, and normal renal function. He attends a structured family-based lifestyle program weekly. His parents ask whether medication should be added.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg, T 36.7 deg C, BMI 36 kg/m^2 (>99.9th centile)
data_table.Examination: Acanthosis nigricans neck and axillae, no striae, normal pubertal stage (Tanner G4 P4), no goitre, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.9%, fasting insulin raised, ALT 78 U/L, US: hepatic steatosis, TSH/free T4 normal, cortisol normal, AHI 18/h

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence oral metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1000 mg BD as adjunct to lifestyle
Commence orlistat 120 mg three times daily with meals as the preferred pharmacotherapy for adolescent obesity
Refer immediately for sleeve gastrectomy without any further trial of medical therapy
Commence liraglutide 3 mg subcutaneously daily as TGA-approved first-line adolescent obesity pharmacotherapy
Add a low-dose thyroid hormone supplement to increase basal metabolic rate today

stem:
A 4-year-old girl with confirmed trisomy 21 attends her annual general paediatric review at a metropolitan outpatient clinic. She had a complete repair of a complete AVSD at age 7 months and has no residual significant intracardiac shunt on her most recent echocardiogram 6 months ago. She is in mainstream preschool with aide support, has gained 1.4 kg over the past year along her usual centile on the Down syndrome growth chart, and her parents have no specific concerns.

She is on no regular medications. Her most recent TSH 12 months ago was 4.2 mIU/L with a free T4 of 14 pmol/L, both within laboratory reference range. She has had no audiology concerns since her last test, no constipation, no cold intolerance, and her energy levels are normal for her. Her general examination today is unremarkable apart from typical syndromic facies, no goitre, and a flat well-healed midline sternotomy scar. Her mother asks specifically about routine bloods.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, T 36.7, BP 95/60, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Growth: Weight 14.8 kg (50th centile on T21 chart), Height 95 cm (25th centile on T21 chart)
data_table.Examination: Typical T21 features, no goitre, well-healed sternotomy, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Previous investigations: TSH 4.2 mIU/L, fT4 14 pmol/L (12 months ago)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate thyroid screening plan for this child?

options.text: Repeat TSH and free T4 only if symptoms of hypothyroidism develop
Repeat TSH and free T4 every 6 months until age 5, then annually
Annual TSH (with free T4 if TSH abnormal) lifelong
TSH, free T4 and thyroid autoantibodies every 3 years
Refer to paediatric endocrinology for routine surveillance

subtopic_detail: Down syndrome - atlantoaxial instability and sport clearance
stem:
