A 9-year-old boy with trisomy 21 attends his paediatrician for clearance to join a local junior trampolining club, having previously only participated in school swimming. His parents are keen because of his social benefit but want a clear answer on safety. He had a balanced AVSD repair at 5 months with no residual lesion and has been discharged from cardiology.

He has had no neck pain, no torticollisills, and no clumsiness compared with his usual baseline. His neurological examination today shows the expected mild generalised hypotonia of trisomy 21, symmetric reflexes with no clonus or upgoing plantars, normal tone in all four limbs, and a gait that is age-typical for him with no ataxia. He has never had a cervical spine X-ray. His mother asks whether he requires imaging or specialist review before starting trampolining, swimming and football at his new school.

data_table.Examination: Typical T21 features, mild generalised hypotonia, no torticollis, symmetric reflexes, plantars downgoing, no clonus, age-appropriate gait

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step before he begins trampolining?

options.text: Order routine flexion-extension and lateral cervical spine radiographs before clearing him for any sport participation
Clinical screen with focused history and neurological examination, and counsel that trampolining is high-risk and best avoided
Refer urgently for MRI of the cervical spine before clearing him for any sport participation
Clear him for trampolining and all contact sports given the entirely normal neurological examination today
Restrict him from all organised competitive sport until a paediatric orthopaedic spine specialist review

stem:
A 3-year-old boy with trisomy 21 (AVSD repair at 6 months, normal TSH 5 months ago, fully immunised) is brought to the GP with 3 weeks of progressive lethargy, intermittent low-grade fevers without an obvious source, and new bruising over shins and trunk that he does not recall sustaining. He has been on no medications and has had no preceding viral illness.

On examination he is pale, has a smooth firm spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin, generalised non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy with the largest node 2 cm, multiple bruises in non-traumatic distribution and palatal petechiae. He is haemodynamically stable. Capillary FBC: Hb 68, WCC 22 with blasts on film, platelets 28. He is not febrile to a level requiring urgent neutropenic sepsis protocol but the GP wants the appropriate disposition.

data_table.Examination: Pale, splenomegaly 3 cm BLCM, generalised lymphadenopathy (largest 2 cm), bruising on shins and trunk, palatal petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L (blasts on film), platelets 28 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure as likely viral illness and repeat FBC in 2 weeks
Empirical oral antibiotics for presumed occult bacterial infection and review at 48 hours without addressing the abnormal blast cells on the film today
Same-day transfer to a tertiary paediatric oncology service for marrow assessment, supportive care and isolation; confirm trisomy 21-specific TMD/ML-DS pathway awareness
Order ferritin, B12 and folate to investigate the anaemia in primary care before any involvement of haematology-oncology services at this stage
Refer to outpatient general paediatrics for the next available clinic without same-day haematology-oncology involvement

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with karyotypically confirmed 45,X Turner syndrome is reviewed in a tertiary endocrinology and general paediatric clinic. She was diagnosed in the newborn period after she presented with lymphoedema and a webbed neck; echocardiogram in the neonatal period showed a normally functioning bicuspid aortic valve with no coarctation. She is on subcutaneous growth hormone and her height has tracked along the Turner syndrome centile chart since starting therapy 18 months ago.

Her parents ask about the schedule of ongoing heart investigations because they have read about aortic complications in adult women with Turner syndrome. She is asymptomatic, has no exertional symptoms, plays normally with peers, and has no chest pain, syncope, or palpitations. On examination she has the expected Turner phenotype, a normal cardiac auscultation with no murmur today, and equal brachial and femoral pulses with no inter-limb blood pressure differential. Her last echocardiogram was 18 months ago and was unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 20, BP right arm 102/65, right leg 104/68, no inter-limb gradient
data_table.Examination: Turner phenotype, no murmur, S1 S2 normal, femoral pulses equal to brachial
data_table.Imaging: Bicuspid aortic valve known, last echo 18 months ago - no aortic dilatation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate ongoing cardiac surveillance plan?

options.text: Repeat the echocardiogram only if a new cardiac murmur or new symptom develops in future
Echocardiogram every 5 years through childhood, then transition imaging to the adult cardiology service
Annual blood pressure measurement and ECG without further imaging unless symptoms arise
Serial childhood echocardiography (typically every 3 to 5 years) with a baseline cardiac MRI at adolescent transition
Cardiac MRI annually from age 6 onwards regardless of cardiac symptoms or echo findings

stem:
A 16-month-old girl with genetically confirmed Williams syndrome (7q11.23 microdeletion on chromosomal microarray) is reviewed in a tertiary metabolic clinic after a routine annual calcium check showed an elevated corrected calcium. She has known supravalvular aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 22 mmHg under cardiology follow-up, the characteristic elfin facies, and a sociable, indiscriminately friendly behavioural profile. Over the past 6 weeks her parents describe increased irritability, constipation despite adequate dietary fibre, polyuria with new night-time wetting after months of dry nappies, and reduced appetite.

She has been receiving a standard infant multivitamin including 400 IU/day vitamin D and her formula has been a regular age-appropriate cows-milk-based formula. She has had no recent vitamin D loading, no thiazide diuretic exposure, and no excessive sun exposure unusual for Brisbane.

data_table.Examination: Elfin facies, no goitre, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft, no palpable mass, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.10 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.55 mmol/L, PTH suppressed 0.4 pmol/L, 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L, phosphate 1.2 mmol/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, urinary calcium:creatinine ratio elevated
data_table.Imaging: Renal ultrasound: mild bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis
data_table.Medications: Multivitamin with 400 IU vitamin D daily

lead_in: Which single intervention is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase her oral fluid intake only and recheck the serum calcium in 6 weeks without other change
Commence oral prednisolone daily and continue her current diet and vitamin D supplements unchanged
Commence a single intravenous infusion of pamidronate in the day-stay unit and continue current diet
Admit for intravenous fluid rehydration and intravenous furosemide infusion to promote urinary calcium excretion
Stop the vitamin D-containing multivitamin and start a low-calcium, vitamin D-free formula with endocrine input

subtopic_detail: Noonan syndrome - feeding and cardiac surveillance
stem:
An 8-month-old boy referred from a regional paediatrician now has a confirmed PTPN11 pathogenic variant consistent with Noonan syndrome. His parents are seen in a metropolitan multidisciplinary Noonan clinic. He has known mild-to-moderate valvular pulmonary stenosis on his most recent echocardiogram with a peak gradient of 35 mmHg and no clinical decompensation. He has been a slow and reluctant feeder since birth, taking 60 to 90 minutes for a bottle, with frequent posseting, occasional choking on thin fluids, and a weight tracking along the 3rd centile despite caloric fortification advice.

He has had no aspiration pneumonias to date. He has the typical Noonan facies with hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, a webbed neck, and a pectus carinatum-excavatum combination. Developmentally he is mildly delayed in gross motor but has age-appropriate social engagement. Bleeding history is unremarkable with no easy bruising and no prolonged bleeding from heel pricks. His parents ask which specialist input is most important to add now to address the issue limiting his weight gain.

data_table.Growth: Weight 6.4 kg (3rd centile), Length 65 cm (10th centile)
data_table.Examination: Noonan facies, 3/6 ESM at upper LSE radiating to back, normal femoral pulses, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Echo: valvular PS, peak gradient 35 mmHg, normal RV function; FBC normal; coagulation screen pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next addition to his multidisciplinary management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric feeding service for multidisciplinary assessment with speech pathology and dietetics
Refer urgently to cardiology for balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty to relieve the pulmonary stenosis gradient
Commence subcutaneous growth hormone therapy now to address his persistent short stature and weight
Refer to paediatric haematology now for prophylactic platelet transfusions and ongoing infusion planning
Refer the parents to clinical genetics for counselling alone, without further specialist clinical input

stem:
A 12-year-old girl is referred by her GP to a paediatric cardiology and genetics service because her father was recently diagnosed with Marfan syndrome at age 41 after an acute type A aortic dissection that he survived following emergency surgery. A pathogenic FBN1 variant was identified on his diagnostic genetic panel. She is asymptomatic, plays netball at school, and has no chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or visual symptoms.

She has never had an ophthalmology slit-lamp examination or an echocardiogram. On clinical examination today she is tall for her age and family (height 168 cm, 95th centile; mid-parental centile 50th), with a moderate pectus excavatum, mild thoracolumbar scoliosis on standing radiograph (Cobb 18 degrees), a positive Steinberg sign on the right, and an arm span to height ratio of 1.04. She has no spontaneous pneumothorax history, no skin striae beyond unremarkable post-pubertal striae, and no dural ectasia symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Tall, pectus excavatum, mild scoliosis (Cobb 18), positive right Steinberg, arm span:height 1.04, no Walker-Murdoch, no high-arched palate, no skin hyperextensibility
data_table.Family history: Father - pathogenic FBN1 variant, type A dissection at 41 (survived)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order whole-exome sequencing now as the first-line genetic investigation for this asymptomatic teenager
Order a full multi-gene aortopathy panel (FBN1, TGFBR1/2, ACTA2, MYH11) as first-line genetic testing
Reassure that her habitus is familial and rescreen only if she later develops cardiovascular symptoms
Refer for empirical prophylactic beta-blocker therapy without genetic testing or baseline aortic imaging today
Targeted cascade FBN1 testing for the familial variant, plus baseline echocardiogram and ophthalmology slit-lamp assessment

subtopic_detail: Marfan syndrome - aortic protection and activity
stem:
A 15-year-old boy with previously diagnosed Marfan syndrome on the basis of revised Ghent criteria and a confirmed FBN1 pathogenic variant attends his annual paediatric cardiology review at a tertiary centre. He plays competitive rowing five times per week, including ergometer sessions involving repetitive Valsalva. His most recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows an aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva of 4.0 cm with a Z-score of 3.2 indexed to body surface area, increased from a Z-score of 2.5 one year ago.

There is mild aortic regurgitation. He has no history of dissection, no syncope, and no documented hypertension. He is currently not on any cardiovascular medications, having declined them previously because his aortic root was within range. His mother died of a presumed type A dissection in her late 30s.

data_table.Examination: Tall Marfanoid habitus, soft early diastolic murmur at LSE consistent with mild AR, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Imaging: Aortic root 4.0 cm, Z-score 3.2 (was 2.5 one year ago), mild aortic regurgitation, no dissection

lead_in: Which single management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue the current competitive rowing program, defer medication, and review again in 12 months' time
Commence beta-blocker (or losartan if intolerant), restrict competitive isometric and contact sport, repeat imaging every 6 months
Refer immediately for prophylactic aortic root replacement surgery at the current aortic root diameter
Commence a beta-blocker but allow unrestricted rowing and rugby resistance work because medication is fully protective
Stop all exercise indefinitely and avoid any organised or recreational physical activity going forward

stem:
A 17-year-old woman is referred to a paediatric genetics service from a regional clinic for assessment of suspected Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Her sister, aged 21, was recently admitted to a metropolitan tertiary hospital after a spontaneous splenic artery rupture and underwent emergency embolisation; sister's subsequent connective tissue gene panel confirmed a pathogenic COL3A1 variant. The patient herself has generalised joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 7/9, soft velvety skin, easy bruising in unusual locations (forearms, thighs) that her mother has long attributed to clumsiness, and translucent skin over the chest wall with prominent visible veins.

She has had no major vascular events, but reports two episodes of mild epistaxis in the past year and a self-resolving spontaneous left-sided pneumothorax aged 14 (managed conservatively). She has thin lips, a thin nose, and prominent eyes. She has no marfanoid habitus, no aortic root dilatation on a recent echocardiogram (root 2.6 cm, Z-score 0.4), no ectopia lentis, no scoliosis, and a normal palate.

data_table.Examination: Beighton 7/9, soft velvety translucent skin, visible chest wall veins, easy bruising, thin lips, thin nose, prominent eyes; no marfanoid habitus, no aortic root dilatation
data_table.Family history: Sister with confirmed COL3A1 pathogenic variant, splenic artery rupture
data_table.History: Spontaneous pneumothorax age 14, recurrent epistaxis

lead_in: Which single statement most accurately reflects the most likely diagnosis and the best next step?

options.text: Hypermobile EDS - reassure and focus on physiotherapy and pain management, with no genetic testing arranged
Vascular EDS - cascade COL3A1 testing, baseline non-invasive vascular imaging, celiprolol if confirmed, plus pregnancy counselling
Marfan syndrome - arrange FBN1 testing and commence losartan empirically while awaiting confirmation of the diagnosis
Classical EDS - send COL5A1 and COL5A2 testing rather than the COL3A1 gene that her sister carries
Confirmed vascular EDS - proceed directly to catheter arteriography to comprehensively map the entire arterial tree

subtopic_detail: Fragile X - inheritance and carrier counselling
stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends a genetics outpatient clinic for counselling after her 5-year-old son was diagnosed with Fragile X syndrome on a clinically indicated FMR1 molecular test showing a full mutation expansion of approximately 380 CGG repeats. Her son has moderate intellectual disability, autistic features, and the classic phenotype. Targeted FMR1 testing of the patient herself reveals a premutation in the 80 CGG repeat range.

She is currently considering a second pregnancy and asks specifically about the risk to her future biological children, the implications for her own health, and the implications for her younger brother (aged 28) and her elderly father. Her brother and father are clinically asymptomatic. She has had no fertility issues to date and her menstrual cycles are regular.

data_table.Genetics: Index case (son): FMR1 full mutation (~380 CGG repeats); Mother (patient): FMR1 premutation (~80 CGG repeats)
data_table.Family history: Maternal grandfather alive aged 72, no known clinical issues; brother 28 - asymptomatic

lead_in: Which single statement is the most accurate counselling point?

options.text: Any future daughter who inherits her premutation will definitely develop full-syndrome Fragile X in childhood
Fragile X is autosomal recessive and her brother must be tested before he plans any pregnancy
Premutation alleles do not expand on transmission and never cause clinical disease in any carrier
Her father almost certainly carries the full mutation and has a 50% transmission risk to children
Each future biological son has a 50% inheritance risk, and female-line premutations can expand to full mutation

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to her GP because her mother has noticed an increasing number of pale brown skin patches over 2 years. There is no family history of neurofibromatosis or unexplained tumours. She is developmentally appropriate, fully immunised and otherwise well. On full examination today she has 7 well-demarcated cafe-au-lait macules across her trunk and limbs, all greater than 5 mm in longest diameter, and bilateral axillary freckling clearly visible.

She has no Lisch nodules visible on bedside ophthalmoscopy, no plexiform neurofibroma, no cutaneous neurofibroma, no symptoms of optic glioma, and no skeletal dysplasia. Growth is on the 50th centile (head circumference 75th). Vision and developmental screening today are normal.

data_table.Examination: 7 cafe-au-lait macules >5 mm, bilateral axillary freckling, no neurofibromas, no Lisch nodules on bedside exam, no skeletal abnormality

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate conclusion-and-next-step pair under the 2021 revised NIH/NF1 criteria?

options.text: She does not meet criteria because skin findings alone can never be diagnostic of NF1; do not refer to paediatric genetics or arrange surveillance
She meets criteria only if molecular NF1 gene testing returns a pathogenic variant; do not diagnose NF1 without sequencing confirmation first
She does not meet criteria because the cafe-au-lait macule threshold is at least 10 lesions over 15 mm in size in this prepubertal age group
She meets criteria (>=6 cafe-au-lait over 5 mm PLUS axillary freckling = two 2021 criteria); refer to paediatric genetics for NF1 surveillance pathway
She meets criteria only if a first-degree relative also has clinically confirmed NF1 with documented genetic testing for a pathogenic variant

stem:
A 3-year-old boy with clinically diagnosed neurofibromatosis type 1 (multiple cafe-au-lait macules, bilateral axillary freckling, affected mother) is seen at his general paediatric clinic for a routine review. He is developmentally appropriate, has no headaches, no vomiting, and no obvious visual complaints. He has had no prior dedicated ophthalmology assessment. His mother has been told that NF1 children are at risk of optic pathway glioma but is unclear when surveillance should start and how often it should occur.

On examination today he has no obvious visual abnormality on bedside testing, no proptosis, normal pupils, and a fundus that is difficult to assess in clinic. There is no precocious puberty, no growth failure, and no new neurological deficit.

data_table.Examination: Multiple CALMs, bilateral axillary freckling, no proptosis, no precocious puberty, no focal neurology

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate surveillance plan for optic pathway glioma in this child?

options.text: MRI brain and orbits every 6 months as routine surveillance until age 8 regardless of symptoms
Refer only if visual symptoms develop, with no scheduled ophthalmology or imaging surveillance
Annual paediatric ophthalmology review (acuity, visual fields, fundus) until around age 7 to 8
GP-led bedside visual acuity check at each routine immunisation visit only
Annual CT brain and orbits with intravenous contrast as routine optic pathway surveillance

stem:
A 7-month-old infant girl is brought to a regional paediatric ED with a 5-day history of new clusters of stereotyped flexion movements occurring on waking and after feeds. The clusters consist of brief symmetrical flexion of the neck, trunk, and arms occurring every 5 to 10 seconds for up to 2 minutes, after which she appears distressed and then drowsy.

Her mother has captured a video showing typical infantile spasms. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, but a fetal MRI at 30 weeks performed because of a cardiac rhabdomyoma seen on antenatal scan showed multiple cortical tubers. A postnatal genetic panel confirmed a pathogenic TSC2 variant. On general examination today she has 3 hypopigmented ash-leaf macules on her trunk and a developmental regression noted by her parents - she had been babbling and reaching for objects 6 weeks ago but is now less responsive and no longer reaches. EEG performed today shows hypsarrhythmia.

data_table.Examination: 3 ash-leaf macules, regression of social and motor milestones, no focal neurology
data_table.Imaging: Multiple cortical tubers on prior MRI; cardiac rhabdomyoma stable

lead_in: Which single first-line therapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Levetiracetam monotherapy
Oral prednisolone monotherapy
Sodium valproate monotherapy
Vigabatrin monotherapy
Ketogenic diet (first-line)

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 woman is referred to tertiary fetal medicine after a 28-week scan showed a 14 mm well-circumscribed echogenic mass on the fetal interventricular septum and a second 8 mm mass on the LV free wall. Fetal cardiac function is preserved, there is no hydrops, no significant outflow obstruction and normal amniotic fluid volume. The woman has no personal history of seizures, facial angiofibromas or hypopigmented macules, and a normal renal ultrasound last year.

There is no family history of tuberous sclerosis. Dedicated reassessment of the fetal brain, kidneys and skeleton shows no other anomalies (acknowledging antenatal imaging limits).

data_table.Imaging: Fetal echo: 14 mm IVS rhabdomyoma + 8 mm LV free wall rhabdomyoma, preserved function
data_table.Family history: No known TSC; maternal clinical examination unremarkable

lead_in: Which combination of counselling, antenatal investigation and postnatal plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Multiple fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas are strongly linked to TSC (~75-80%); arrange fetal MRI for cortical tubers, plan TSC1/TSC2 sequencing postnatally
Cardiac rhabdomyomas are almost always isolated benign tumours unrelated to any syndromic diagnosis; no further postnatal evaluation or genetic testing required
Antenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma is essentially diagnostic of Williams syndrome; arrange 7q11.23 microarray and avoid further multisystem surveillance investigations
Antenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma is most commonly associated with Noonan syndrome (RASopathy); arrange a RASopathy gene panel and skip the fetal MRI now
Lesions typically grow rapidly after birth and require surgical excision in the neonatal period without any further syndromic evaluation or follow-up

subtopic_detail: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome - hypocalcaemia and immune workup
stem:
A 5-day-old term male neonate is reviewed on the postnatal ward after a 90-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure that terminated spontaneously. He was born at 38+5 weeks by uncomplicated NVD. Antenatal scans identified interrupted aortic arch type B for which he is scheduled for repair next week. Examination shows hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears with deficient ear lobes, and a small mouth with high-arched palate.

The postnatal CXR shows no clear thymic shadow. Investigations: ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L (low), magnesium 0.85 (normal), glucose 3.4, PTH inappropriately low for the calcium. There has been no maternal calcium-altering medication exposure.

data_table.Examination: Hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears, high-arched palate; cardiac murmur of IAA-B
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 1.62 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L, magnesium 0.85 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, PTH inappropriately low
data_table.Imaging: No clear thymic shadow on CXR; IAA-B confirmed on echo

lead_in: Which combination of first-line genetic investigation and live-vaccine planning is most appropriate?

options.text: Chromosomal microarray as first-line genetic test for 22q11.2 microdeletion; withhold live vaccines pending T-cell subset confirmation
Standard G-banded karyotype looking for trisomy 22 or other numerical aneuploidies as the first-line genetic test
Repeat newborn bloodspot screening card focused on congenital hypothyroidism as the first-line diagnostic workup
Maternal serum vitamin D level only as the first-line investigation before any other targeted genetic or immune testing
Trans-fontanelle cranial ultrasound at the cotside as the next investigation before any further genetic or immune workup

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born male is brought to the ED with a 10-day history of vomiting after every feed, now forceful and arching over the shoulder. The vomit is milky, never green or blood-stained. He is hungry immediately after vomiting and feeds vigorously. Birth was 39+4 NVD, weight 3.6 kg. Today his weight is 3.5 kg (50th to 3rd centile cross), capillary refill 3 seconds, anterior fontanelle slightly sunken.

A 1 cm mobile firm mass is palpable in the right epigastrium after a test feed, with visible peristalsis crossing the upper abdomen left to right. Venous blood gas: pH 7.51, pCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3 38 mmol/L, Na 134, K 3.1, Cl 89, glucose 4.2 mmol/L. The paediatric surgical registrar wants to know the next step.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 44, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 98%, weight 3.5 kg.
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, CRT 3 s, mucous membranes dry. Soft abdomen, palpable olive RUQ, visible peristalsis.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.51, pCO2 50, HCO3 38, Na 134, K 3.1, Cl 89, glucose 4.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for Ramstedt pyloromyotomy after a single saline bolus, with electrolyte correction deferred to the postoperative period

Resuscitate with 0.9% saline, then maintenance and replacement with 0.45% saline plus 5% dextrose plus potassium until Cl over 100, HCO3 under 30, K over 3.5 mmol/L; confirmatory ultrasound; then pyloromyotomy
Commence omeprazole orally and review in clinic in one week as outpatient reflux management
Request urgent upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation before any fluid resuscitation or surgical referral
Trial extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 weeks as cow's milk protein allergy is the most likely diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Infant with non-bilious projectile vomiting and electrolyte disturbance

stem:
A 14-month-old previously well boy presents with an 8-hour history of episodic screaming in 15-20 minute cycles, drawing his knees up to his chest, with pallor and limpness between episodes. His mother describes one stool 90 minutes ago that was dark red and mucousy, like jam. There has been one episode of non-bilious vomiting. He had a viral URTI 5 days ago.

There has been no foreign travel and no unwell contacts. On examination he is now quiet and pale, HR 152, CRT 3 seconds, T 37.1 degC. The abdomen is soft with a vague sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant and an empty right iliac fossa. There is no peritonism, no guarding. Bedside ultrasound performed by the paediatric registrar shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant with concentric rings of bowel wall. A surgical registrar and an interventional radiologist are both immediately available.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152 bpm, RR 32, BP 92/58, T 37.1 degC, SpO2 99%, CRT 3 s.
data_table.Examination: Pale, lethargic between episodes. Sausage mass RUQ, empty RIF (Dance sign). No peritonism, no guarding.
data_table.Investigations: POCUS: target sign RUQ, concentric rings of bowel-within-bowel.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and arrange outpatient paediatric review the following day given the absence of frank peritonism on examination
Resuscitate with IV fluid and antibiotics, NG decompression, air-contrast enema with surgery on standby
Proceed directly to laparotomy for open manual reduction without attempting radiological reduction first
Perform contrast CT abdomen to confirm the diagnosis before any therapeutic intervention is undertaken
Admit for observation overnight on clear fluids and re-image with ultrasound the following morning

subtopic_detail: Toddler with intermittent colicky pain and bloody stool

stem:
A 38-hour-old term male born at 39+5 by NVD to a G2P1 mother with an uneventful pregnancy is brought to the special care nursery by the midwife. He has had three episodes of vomiting in the last 90 minutes, the most recent two clearly bilious (bright green) and photographed on the midwife's phone for the registrar to review. He passed meconium at 18 hours of age and has been breastfeeding poorly since the second feed, latching but suckling weakly and falling asleep.

Birth weight 3.4 kg, current weight 3.25 kg, representing a 4% drop. On examination he is irritable with HR 178, RR 62, CRT 3 seconds, T 36.4 degC, SpO2 96% in room air. The abdomen is mildly distended in the upper abdomen without obvious mass, soft, with sluggish bowel sounds. There is no inguinal hernia, no anal stenosis, and no perianal abnormality.

Antenatal scans had not commented on intra-abdominal anatomy beyond reporting a normal anatomy scan at 20 weeks, with no polyhydramnios noted. An NG tube is placed and immediately drains 25 mL of bilious fluid with relief of distension. The neonatal registrar has IV access through a peripheral cannula and is preparing maintenance fluids and a 10 mL/kg saline bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 62, T 36.4 degC, SpO2 96% RA, CRT 3 s, weight 3.25 kg.
data_table.Examination: Irritable, mildly distended abdomen, soft, no mass, sluggish bowel sounds. No hernia, normal anus.
data_table.Investigations: NG aspirate 25 mL bilious. IV access x 1, fluids being prepared.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Upper GI contrast study within the next hour, paediatric surgical team aware and theatre standby
Conservative management with NG decompression and IV fluids overnight, with reassessment in the morning
Abdominal ultrasound looking for the whirlpool sign before considering further imaging today
Plain supine abdominal radiograph alone to exclude duodenal atresia as the diagnosis
Contrast enema looking for microcolon to exclude meconium ileus as diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in the first 48 hours of life

stem:
An 8-year-old boy presents with a 22-hour history of central abdominal pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa 8 hours ago. He has vomited twice, has not eaten since lunch yesterday, and has a temperature of 38.1 deg C. He is reluctant to walk and held his right hip flexed on arrival. There is no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms, no foreign travel and no sick contacts.

He is not on medication and is fully immunised. On examination HR 112, RR 22, BP 108/68, abdomen with localised tenderness at McBurney point, voluntary guarding without rebound, positive cough sign. There is no generalised peritonism. Bloods: WCC 14.8 x10^9/L (neutrophils 11.2), CRP 38 mg/L. Urinalysis is negative. Paediatric Appendicitis Score is 7/10. Radiology offers an ultrasound within the hour.

data_table.Examination: Reluctant to walk, McBurney tenderness, voluntary guarding, positive cough sign, no rebound.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.8 (neutrophils 11.2), CRP 38, urinalysis negative. PAS 7/10.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step, and what is the appropriate plan if ultrasound is non-visualising?

options.text: Discharge home with simple analgesia and safety-net advice given the absence of rebound peritonism
Order contrast CT abdomen and pelvis as the first-line imaging investigation

Ultrasound RIF first; if positive (non-compressible blind-ending tubular structure over 6 mm with hyperaemia) proceed to laparoscopic appendicectomy with IV pre-operative antibiotics; if non-visualising, admit for serial clinical reassessment with repeat ultrasound or CT escalation as needed
Treat with IV cefotaxime and metronidazole as antibiotic-only therapy without surgical intervention
Order MRI abdomen and pelvis as the first-line investigation to avoid ionising radiation

subtopic_detail: School-age child with right iliac fossa pain

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to a regional emergency department at 03:00 with sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 4 hours ago, associated with one episode of vomiting. There is no dysuria, no urethral discharge. He is not sexually active. On examination he is in significant pain, the left hemiscrotum is swollen, erythematous and tender, the left testis is high-riding with a transverse lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left.

Prehn sign is negative (lifting the testis does not relieve pain). The right testis is normal. Urinalysis is negative for leucocytes and nitrites. The nearest paediatric surgical service is 90 minutes away by road. The local on-call general surgeon is in-house. Bedside Doppler ultrasound is not immediately available; the sonographer is on call from home and estimates a 45-minute arrival time.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn sign.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative. Doppler USS not available for 45 minutes.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait for the on-call sonographer to arrive and perform Doppler ultrasound before any surgical decision
Commence IV ceftriaxone and doxycycline for presumed bacterial epididymo-orchitis without surgical exploration
Proceed immediately to scrotal exploration with consent for bilateral orchidopexy or orchidectomy if non-viable
Attempt manual detorsion in the open-book direction (lateral rotation) then discharge home with urology outpatient follow-up
Transfer the patient by road to the paediatric surgical service 90 minutes away for definitive management

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with acute unilateral scrotal pain

stem:
A 12-hour-old term female born by elective lower-segment caesarean for breech presentation at 39+2 weeks has had two episodes of bright-green vomiting after attempted breastfeeding. Antenatal scans at 12 and 20 weeks were reported as normal; nuchal translucency was low risk. Birth weight 3.1 kg, Apgars 9 and 9. She has not yet passed meconium. On examination HR 162, RR 56, T 36.8 deg C, SpO2 97% on room air.

The abdomen is mildly distended in the upper abdomen with a flat lower abdomen and visible epigastric fullness. There is no obvious mass, no inguinal hernia, and the anus is patent on inspection. A nasogastric tube is placed and aspirates 30 mL of bilious fluid. The on-call paediatric registrar is reviewing the supine abdominal radiograph and considering whether the appearance is consistent with duodenal atresia rather than malrotation with midgut volvulus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 56, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: Upper abdominal distension, flat lower abdomen, patent anus, no hernia. NG bilious aspirate 30 mL.
data_table.Investigations: Supine AXR pending interpretation.

lead_in: Which radiographic finding most reliably differentiates duodenal atresia from malrotation with midgut volvulus, and what is the implication for next investigation?

options.text: Multiple dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and soap-bubble appearance, suggesting meconium ileus and prompting contrast enema
Pneumatosis intestinalis with portal venous gas, suggesting necrotising enterocolitis
Double bubble sign with absent distal bowel gas, supporting duodenal atresia; proceed to fluid resuscitation and surgical referral without urgent upper GI contrast
Free intraperitoneal gas under the diaphragm with a football sign, suggesting perforation
Corkscrew appearance of the duodenum visible on the supine plain film

subtopic_detail: Neonate with green vomiting on day 1 - differential framework

stem:
A 16-month-old boy of Anglo-Australian background presents with severe constipation since the second week of life. His mother reports he passed meconium at 52 hours of age, required digital stimulation to pass stool for the first 6 months, and was breastfed exclusively until 6 months when solids were introduced uneventfully. He now stools once every 5-7 days, with explosive decompression when finally passing.

His growth has crossed centiles downwards from the 50th at birth to the 9th today. He is now febrile at 38.6 degC, lethargic, with foul-smelling green-tinged diarrhoea overnight, mild abdominal distension, and tachycardia at 148. His abdomen is distended and tympanic, with no obvious mass and no organomegaly. PR examination is performed gently by the paediatric registrar and produces an explosive release of gas and liquid stool with relief of distension.

He has had multiple aperient trials including macrogol and lactulose without sustained improvement, and dietary fibre optimisation through the maternal and child health nurse. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis or thyroid disease. Newborn screening for cystic fibrosis was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, RR 32, T 38.6 degC, weight on 9th centile (was 50th at birth).
data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen, explosive PR release. Lethargic.
data_table.Investigations: Pending.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate definitive investigation?

options.text: Sweat chloride test to exclude cystic fibrosis as the cause of meconium delay
Anorectal manometry alone as the single definitive diagnostic test for this
Contrast enema with assessment for transition zone, followed by trial of laxatives
Full-thickness rectal suction biopsy with assessment for ganglion cells and acetylcholinesterase staining
Faecal calprotectin and stool MCS as the initial diagnostic test

subtopic_detail: Toddler with delayed meconium and chronic constipation

stem:
A 28+5 week preterm female born at birth weight 1.05 kg is now on day 11 of life in the neonatal intensive care unit. She was extubated to CPAP on day 4 and trophic feeds of expressed breast milk were introduced on day 5 and advanced to 60 mL/kg/day by day 10. Over the last 12 hours she has had two large bilious gastric aspirates, abdominal distension increasing from 25 cm to 28.5 cm girth, and one episode of bright red blood in the stool.

She has become apnoeic with three desaturations to less than 80% in the last hour requiring stimulation. HR has risen from 145 to 178. T is 36.0 degC, BP 48/22 mmHg with mean arterial pressure 30. CRT is 4 seconds. The abdominal wall is shiny with bluish discolouration over the right flank. WCC has fallen from 9.2 to 4.1 x10^9/L, platelets from 224 to 86, CRP risen from less than 5 to 92 mg/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L.

The supine abdominal radiograph shows multiple dilated loops of bowel with intramural gas (pneumatosis intestinalis) and a curvilinear lucency over the liver consistent with portal venous gas. There is no free intraperitoneal gas on a left lateral decubitus film. The paediatric surgical service has been consulted by phone.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 70, T 36.0 degC, BP 48/22 (MAP 30), SpO2 88% on CPAP, CRT 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Distended shiny abdomen with bluish flank discolouration. PR bright red blood.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.1, platelets 86, CRP 92, lactate 4.8. AXR: pneumatosis + portal venous gas, no free gas.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until blood culture results are available to avoid promoting antibiotic resistance and unnecessary coverage
Continue enteral feeds at current volume and add oral probiotics to reduce bacterial gut translocation
Proceed immediately to laparotomy regardless of radiographic findings of pneumatosis or perforation
Nil by mouth, OG free drainage, IV benzylpenicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole, TPN, serial films, paediatric surgical involvement
Place a peritoneal drain at the bedside as definitive treatment without commencing antibiotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Preterm infant with feed intolerance and abdominal distension

stem:
A 22-month-old girl is brought to a rural emergency department 70 minutes after her older brother saw her swallow a small shiny disc that he had taken from a household remote control. He believes she put it directly in her mouth and swallowed it. She is now drooling slightly, refuses to drink, has had one episode of non-bloody vomiting but is not in respiratory distress.

There is no stridor, no wheeze, no blood in the saliva. HR 134, RR 28, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99% in room air. Examination of the oropharynx is unremarkable; the abdomen is soft and non-tender. The mother brings the empty battery compartment of the remote and the parents identify the missing battery as a CR2032 lithium coin cell (20 mm diameter).

The emergency department has plain radiography but no on-site paediatric endoscopy. The nearest paediatric centre with interventional endoscopy is 2 hours by road or 45 minutes by retrieval helicopter (currently available). A chest and abdominal radiograph shows a round radio-opaque disc with a double-rim (halo) appearance at the level of T2-T3 in the oesophagus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 134, RR 28, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Drooling, refuses fluids, no stridor, no respiratory distress.
data_table.Investigations: CXR/AXR: 20 mm disc with double-rim sign at T2-T3 oesophagus.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer by road over 2 hours; no oral honey as child is under 24 months
Discharge home with safety-net advice to return if symptoms worsen, given the child appears clinically stable on arrival
Induce vomiting with oral ipecac syrup at the bedside now to expel the swallowed battery
Wait 4 hours and repeat radiograph to see whether the battery has spontaneously passed the lower oesophageal sphincter
Activate retrieval for endoscopic battery removal within 2 hours; oral honey en route if age >12 months and airway intact

subtopic_detail: Toddler with witnessed coin-like object ingestion

stem:
A 4-month-old formula-fed infant is brought to the GP with a 6-week history of frequent posseting, irritability and back-arching after feeds, and intermittent streaks of fresh blood and mucus in the stool that the mother has photographed on her phone. He has mild atopic eczema on the cheeks and antecubital fossae. He was born at term, weight at birth 3.5 kg (50th centile).

At 6 weeks his weight was on the 50th centile; today at 4 months he is on the 9th centile, having crossed two major centiles downward over 10 weeks. He is exclusively fed standard cow-milk-based formula and has never had any breastmilk feeds since the second week of life. There is a family history of asthma in the mother and peanut allergy in an older sibling.

He is otherwise well, with no fever, no dehydration, normal urine output, and a normal abdominal examination with no distension or tenderness. The mother has tried thickened formula, smaller more frequent feeds, and head-up positioning after feeds for 30 minutes, without improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 36, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Mild facial eczema. Soft non-tender abdomen. Weight crossed from 50th to 9th centile over 10 weeks.
data_table.Investigations: Stool with visible blood and mucus streaks. No fever.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral omeprazole daily for a 4-week trial as the most likely diagnosis is GORD-related vomiting
Switch to extensively hydrolysed formula for 2-4 weeks, monitor symptoms/growth, re-challenge to confirm; allergy referral if severe
Switch directly to soy-based formula as the first-line alternative formula without considering hydrolysate today
Order skin-prick testing and specific IgE to cow's milk to confirm the diagnosis before any dietary change
Advise the mother to dilute the formula with extra water and add infant gripe water at each feed

subtopic_detail: Infant with vomiting, eczema and stool changes

stem:
A 10-week-old infant is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of poor feeding for the last 24 hours. He is not yet rolling and is not yet sitting. Examination is unremarkable except for a 2 cm bluish bruise over the left cheek and a 1 cm bruise on the right ear pinna. The mother offers no clear mechanism but mentions that her partner reported the baby may have rolled off the couch, although the baby has never previously rolled.

On further examination there is a small frenular tear under the upper lip and the anterior fontanelle is full but not tense. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. His older sibling, aged 3, was treated for a spiral femur fracture last year that was attributed to a fall from a slide. The family is known to community services for housing instability.

The mother has a history of intimate-partner violence in a previous relationship. The current partner is not the biological father and is not present. Birth was at term, NVD, with no perinatal concerns, and the baby is up to date with immunisations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 38, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: 2 cm cheek bruise, 1 cm ear pinna bruise, frenular tear, full fontanelle. Pre-mobile.
data_table.Investigations: Pending. Family known to community services.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Notify the police but not the statutory child protection service, as bruising alone does not meet child protection thresholds
Reassure and discharge home with feeding advice, given that the bruises are small and the mother provided a plausible explanation today
Order coagulation studies in isolation to exclude haemophilia and discharge if all results return normal
Admit for full child protection workup (skeletal survey, CT, fundoscopy, FBC, coags, LFTs, urine drug screen) and notify statutory service
Wait 48 hours to see if the bruising evolves clinically before deciding whether to make any report

stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a GP clinic alone requesting the combined oral contraceptive pill. She is sexually active with one partner who is also 15 and is in the same year at school. She has had a normal menarche at 12, regular cycles every 28-30 days, no medical comorbidities, no migraine with aura of VTE, and a normal blood pressure of 110/68.

Her BMI is 22. She does not want her parents told because she is worried they will react badly even though she trusts them on most other matters. She lives at home with both parents and an older sister, attends school regularly, is performing well academically, plays competitive netball, and has no signs of coercion, grooming, intimate-partner violence, mental illness, or substance misuse on a HEEADSSS assessment conducted by the GP at this consultation.

She asks the GP directly whether the GP must tell her parents, and demonstrates a clear understanding of how the pill works, the failure rate, the risk of VTE, and the importance of barrier protection for STI prevention. Her partner is not present and has not been mentioned in any concerning way.
lead_in: Which is the most appropriate response by the GP?

options.text: Defer all decisions until a Medicare-rebated specialist adolescent gynaecology review, which typically takes 3 to 6 months in public clinics
Decline to prescribe and require the patient to return with a parent before any consideration of contraception
Mandatorily notify DCJ because any sexual activity by a 15-year-old is reportable in all Australian jurisdictions
Prescribe the COCP but inform the parents by telephone after the consultation for safety reasons and ongoing supervision
Assess Gillick competence, document understanding, prescribe COCP without parental notification, encourage but do not require disclosure to a trusted adult

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to a paediatric outpatient clinic with a 4-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain that is worse after meals, non-bloody loose stool 4 to 6 times daily including overnight episodes that wake him from sleep, intermittent low-grade fevers, recurrent painful mouth ulcers on the inner lip, and 5 kg of weight loss. He has fallen from the 75th to the 25th height centile over the last year and pubertal development is at Tanner 2 when his peers are at Tanner 3 to 4.

There is a paternal uncle with Crohn disease and a maternal grandmother with rheumatoid arthritis. On examination he is pale, BMI 17, with mild RIF tenderness, no palpable mass, a perianal skin tag, and a small fistulous opening at the 7 o'clock position with no active discharge. Bloods show Hb 102 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 8 microg/L, platelets 482, CRP 48 mg/L, ESR 56 mm/hr, albumin 28 g/L.

Faecal calprotectin is 1850 microg/g (reference less than 50). Stool MCS and PCR for bacterial pathogens, C. difficile and parasites are negative. Coeliac serology is negative with normal total IgA. He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 110/70, T 37.4 degC, BMI 17.
data_table.Examination: Pale, RIF tender, perianal skin tag, fistulous opening at 7 o'clock.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102, MCV 76, ferritin 8, platelets 482, CRP 48, albumin 28. Faecal calprotectin 1850 microg/g. Coeliac neg, stool MCS neg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trial of empirical 6-week elimination diet before any invasive endoscopic investigation today
Empirical 4-week course of oral metronidazole then reassessment of faecal calprotectin levels
Capsule endoscopy as the first-line investigation to assess the small bowel mucosa
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast as the imaging modality of choice for diagnosis
Ileocolonoscopy with terminal ileal and colonic segmental biopsies plus upper GI endoscopy with MR enterography

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss

stem:
A 22-month-old girl is referred by her maternal and child health nurse for faltering growth. Her birth weight was on the 75th centile after an uncomplicated term pregnancy and NVD. She was exclusively breastfed until 6 months when solids were introduced including wheat-based cereals, pasta and bread, with normal progression of feeding milestones over the next several months. She is now on the 9th centile for weight and 25th for height, having crossed two major weight centiles downward over the last 8 months.

Her mother reports chronic loose, bulky, pale, foul-smelling stools 3 to 5 times daily that float in the toilet, marked abdominal distension that develops over the course of the day, irritability particularly in the late afternoon, and a recent reduction in appetite. The paternal grandmother has type 1 diabetes mellitus and an older sibling aged 7 has confirmed coeliac disease diagnosed two years ago on duodenal biopsy.

On examination today she is pale, thin, with mild abdominal distension, no organomegaly, no clubbing, and reduced subcutaneous fat over the buttocks and proximal thighs. The GP orders anti-tTG IgA and total IgA as the initial screen. Anti-tTG IgA returns at 230 U/mL (reference less than 20, more than 10 times upper limit), total IgA is 1.6 g/L (normal for age, excluding IgA deficiency), endomysial antibody is positive, and HLA-DQ2 is positive.

The mother attends to discuss the results and asks the GP what should happen next. She is keen to start a strict gluten-free diet immediately because she has already done so for the older sibling and knows the supermarket products.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, RR 26, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale, thin, distended abdomen, reduced buttock fat pads, no organomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: anti-tTG IgA 230 U/mL (less than 20), total IgA 1.6 g/L (normal), EMA positive, HLA-DQ2 positive.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue gluten, refer paediatric gastroenterology for duodenal biopsy, only start gluten-free after histology; baseline nutritional studies; screen relatives
Commence a strict gluten-free diet immediately given the strongly positive serology and family history, with no further investigation needed
Discontinue gluten for 4 weeks then perform a gluten challenge with repeat serology and biopsy
Repeat anti-tTG IgA in 6 months and only proceed to further investigation if titres remain elevated
Order an IgG-based gliadin antibody panel and faecal fat studies as the next investigations

subtopic_detail: Toddler with faltering growth and loose stools
Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis - initial management
stem:
A 7-year-old boy with known HbSS sickle cell disease presents to a metropolitan ED with 6 hours of severe pain in both thighs and the lower back. He has had three similar admissions in the past 18 months. He is afebrile, with no cough, no chest paindominal pain. He takes daily penicillin V prophylaxis, folic acid and hydroxycarbamide, and his vaccinations including conjugate pneumococcal, meningococcal B and ACWY, Hib and annual influenza are up to date.

He last had a transfusion 9 months ago. On examination he is alert and engaged, tearful with pain, with no scleral icterus, a soft non-tender abdomen, no chest signs and no neurological deficit. There is no swelling of joints, no warmth and no focal tenderness over long bones beyond diffuse muscular tenderness. Initial observations: T 36.9 degC, HR 118 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 108/64 mmHg.

Bedside SpO2 trend over the last 30 minutes is stable. He has not taken any analgesia at home and is rating his pain 9 out of 10.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 degC, HR 118, RR 22, SpO2 98% RA, BP 108/64.
data_table.Examination: Distressed by pain, no chest signs, no focal bony tenderness, no scleral icterus, no neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed.
data_table.Medications: Penicillin V prophylaxis, folic acid, hydroxycarbamide.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral ibuprofen alone, then reassess pain at 60 minutes
IV saline bolus 20 mL/kg, observe without giving analgesia
IV morphine plus paracetamol and ibuprofen, maintenance fluids
Empirical IV ceftriaxone, blood cultures and ward admission
Urgent exchange transfusion via the on-call haematologist

subtopic_detail: Acute chest syndrome recognition in sickle cell disease
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with HbSS sickle cell disease was admitted 36 hours ago with a vaso-occlusive crisis affecting her back and hips, and has been on IV morphine via PCA, regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, and maintenance fluids at 100% maintenance. Pain has improved from 9 to 5 out of 10. Overnight she developed a new dry cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain on inspiration.

This morning her temperature is 38.4 degC, HR 132 bpm, RR 36, SpO2 91% on room air rising to 95% on 2 L nasal prongs, BP 104/62 mmHg. On auscultation she has reduced air entry and crackles at the right base. She has had no vomiting, no recent travel, and no sick contacts. She is fully vaccinated and on penicillin V prophylaxis and hydroxycarbamide.

Her last transfusion was 8 months ago. A chest X-ray performed in the last hour shows a new right lower zone consolidation that was not present on admission. Repeat FBC shows Hb 71 g/L (baseline 88), WCC 19.4 x10^9/L, platelets 312, reticulocytes 320 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degC, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 91% RA / 95% on 2 L NP, BP 104/62.
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry and crackles right base, distressed by pain and dyspnoea.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 71 g/L (baseline 88), WCC 19.4, platelets 312, CRP 96. CXR: new right lower zone consolidation.
data_table.Medications: IV morphine PCA, paracetamol, ibuprofen, penicillin V, hydroxycarbamide, maintenance saline.

lead_in: Which is the single best next step?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, oxygen, incentive spirometry, urgent haematology call regarding transfusion
Increase morphine PCA background rate and continue current ward management
Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and repeat the chest X-ray in 6 hours
Stop ibuprofen, give nebulised salbutamol and observe on the ward
Arrange urgent CT pulmonary angiogram before any further therapy

subtopic_detail: Discriminating sickle crisis types - sequestration vs aplastic
stem:
A 3-year-old girl with known HbSS sickle cell disease, on daily penicillin V prophylaxis and folic acid, is brought to a regional ED by her mother. Over the last 24 hours she has become progressively lethargic, with poor oral intake but no vomiting or diarrhoea. Her older brother had a febrile illness with a malar rash one week ago. She has not had any cough, dyspnoea, chest or limb pain, no preceding bony pain and no haematuria.

She is afebrile today, but two days ago had a low-grade temperature. On examination she is pale and tired, alert but quiet, with no scleral icterus, no rash, clear chest and no neurology. Her abdomen is soft with a non-tender spleen palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, unchanged from her baseline. Observations: T 36.7 degC, HR 142, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA, BP 92/56, capillary refill 2 s. Bedside bloods: Hb 48 g/L (baseline 85), WCC 6.8 x10^9/L, platelets 256, reticulocytes 12 x10^9/L (baseline approximately 300), bilirubin 24 micromol/L, LDH mildly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 degC, HR 142, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA, BP 92/56, cap refill 2 s.
data_table.Examination: Pale, alert, spleen 2 cm below costal margin (baseline), no jaundice, no haemodynamic compromise.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 48 g/L (baseline 85), reticulocytes 12 x10^9/L (baseline ~300), WCC 6.8, platelets 256, bilirubin 24 micromol/L.

lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

options.text: Acute splenic sequestration crisis
Hyperhaemolytic crisis from delayed transfusion reaction
Iron deficiency anaemia from poor dietary intake
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 infection
Vaso-occlusive bone marrow infarction

subtopic_detail: Acute childhood ITP - watchful waiting threshold
stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to the GP after her parents noticed widespread petechiae on her shins and a few bruises on her trunk that appeared over 48 hours. She had a coryzal illness 10 days ago that has now resolved. She is otherwise well, eating, drinking, and playing normally. There has been no fever in the past week, no bone pain.

She has no significant past medical history, no recent travel and her vaccinations are up to date. Family history is negative for bleeding disorders. On examination she is well, alert and playful. Temperature is 36.8 degC, HR 102, RR 22, BP 96/58, capillary refill 2 s. She has scattered petechiae on both lower legs and four bruises 1-2 cm across on the trunk and arms in non-suspicious distributions.

There is no mucosal bleeding, no epistaxis and no lymphadenopathy. There is no hepatosplenomegaly and no joint swelling. Bedside FBC: Hb 124 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L with normal differential, neutrophils 3.4, lymphocytes 3.1, platelets 18 x10^9/L. Blood film shows large platelets with otherwise normal red and white cell morphology.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 degC, HR 102, RR 22, BP 96/58, cap refill 2 s.
data_table.Examination: Well, playful. Petechiae shins, scattered trunk bruises. No mucosal bleeding, no lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L, WCC 7.2 (normal diff), platelets 18 x10^9/L. Film: large platelets, otherwise normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit and infuse IV immunoglobulin now
Reassure, give safety advice and arrange paediatric follow-up
Commence oral prednisolone daily for two weeks
Transfuse a single unit of pooled adult platelets
Refer for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine

subtopic_detail: ITP with wet purpura - IVIG vs steroids decision
stem:
A 6-year-old boy presents to ED with worsening epistaxis lasting 35 minutes despite firm nasal pinching, and new oral blood blisters noted by his mother this morning. Petechiae appeared over the legs and trunk 3 days ago. He had a mild diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago that resolved without antibiotics. He is otherwise well, with no fever, weight loss, night sweats or bone pain, and no joint swelling.

Past history is unremarkable, vaccinations are up to date and he takes no medications. On examination he is alert, slightly pale, with active oozing from the left anterior nare, multiple buccal haemorrhagic bullae, scattered petechiae and bruising over the trunk and lower limbs, but no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly. Observations: T 36.9 degC, HR 118, RR 24, BP 102/64, SpO2 99% RA, capillary refill 2 s.

FBC: Hb 102 g/L, WCC 8.0 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 4 x10^9/L. Coagulation: PT 12 s, APTT 32 s, fibrinogen 3.1 g/L. Blood film shows isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets and otherwise normal cells. There has been no haematuria, no melaena and no neurological symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 degC, HR 118, RR 24, BP 102/64, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Active epistaxis 35 min, oral haemorrhagic bullae, petechiae and bruises. No lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, WCC 8.0 (normal diff), platelets 4 x10^9/L. Coags normal. Film: isolated thrombocytopenia, large platelets.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Continue nasal pressure and discharge with outpatient haematology follow-up
IV immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg with admission for observation
Pooled platelet transfusion (one adult dose) and admit
Oral tranexamic acid alone with review in 48 hours
Splenectomy after initial haemodynamic stabilisation

stem:
An 8-year-old boy with newly-diagnosed acute ITP (platelets 6 x10^9/L on a community FBC two days ago) is brought to a tertiary ED at 22:00 after a witnessed fall from standing height onto a tiled floor. He struck the back of his head and had immediate vomiting, followed by 15 minutes of drowsiness. On arrival he is rousable to voice with a GCS of 12 (E3 V4 M5), HR 122, RR 22, BP 116/72, SpO2 99% room air, T 36.8 degC, pupils 3 mm equal and reactive, with no focal neurological deficit.

He has scattered petechiae and bruising over the trunk and limbs, oozing from the gums, and a 3 cm haematoma over the right occiput. There is no other injury. He was not taking any antiplatelet or anticoagulant medication. CT head obtained 20 minutes ago shows a small right parietal acute subdural haematoma without midline shift. Repeat FBC in ED: Hb 108 g/L, WCC 7.4 with normal differential, platelets 5 x10^9/L. Coagulation: PT 12 s, APTT 30 s, fibrinogen 3.0 g/L. The neurosurgical registrar has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 degC, HR 122, RR 22, BP 116/72, SpO2 99% RA, GCS 12.
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, occipital haematoma, gum ooze, petechiae and bruising. No focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108, WCC 7.4 (normal diff), platelets 5 x10^9/L. Coags normal. CT: small acute right parietal SDH, no mass effect.

lead_in: Which combination of immediate interventions is most appropriate?

options.text: IVIG 1 g/kg alone with observation in a paediatric high-dependency bed
Platelet transfusion alone, admit for neurosurgical observation
IV tranexamic acid bolus followed by infusion as principal therapy
Platelet transfusion plus IV methylprednisolone plus IVIG, urgent neurosurgical review
Immediate emergency splenectomy for rapid platelet response

subtopic_detail: Definition and recognition of febrile neutropenia
stem:
A 9-year-old boy on maintenance chemotherapy for B-cell ALL (14 months into therapy) is brought to a metropolitan paediatric ED 2 hours after a single recorded oral temperature of 38.4 deg C at home. He has had mild coryza but no localising features, no rigors, and no diarrhoea. He took oral paracetamol 1 hour ago. He has a tunnelled central venous access device with no overlying erythema or tenderness, and no recent admissions.

He is fully immunised for age and has no known drug allergies. On arrival his temperature is 37.9 deg C, HR 116, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent room air, BP 104/64, capillary refill 2 seconds, and he looks well and is interacting normally. An FBC taken 3 days ago at clinic showed Hb 102 g/L, WCC 1.2, neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 138, and a repeat is in progress now.

He meets the RCH definition of febrile neutropenia (single temperature 38.0 deg C or higher with ANC under 0.5). Peripheral and central line cultures are being collected.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.9 degC (38.4 at home), HR 116, RR 22, SpO2 98% RA, BP 104/64.
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, central line site clean, mild coryza, no localising features.
data_table.Investigations: FBC 3 days ago: Hb 102, WCC 1.2, neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 138.
data_table.Medications: Maintenance chemotherapy for ALL (oral 6-MP, weekly oral methotrexate, intermittent vincristine and steroid pulses).

lead_in: Which empirical antibiotic regimen and timing target is most appropriate?

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam within 60 minutes of arrival, adding vancomycin only if shock, suspected line infection, severe mucositis, or known resistant colonisation
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily empirically within 60 minutes of arrival, with no anti-pseudomonal cover added
IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus empirical IV vancomycin and IV gentamicin within 60 minutes given the indwelling central line in situ
Withhold antibiotics pending the repeat FBC to confirm ongoing neutropenia and pending the blood culture preliminary results
Discharge home on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin with outpatient FBC review tomorrow, given he is well and afebrile

subtopic_detail: Septic workup priorities in febrile neutropenia
stem:
A 12-year-old girl with AML in induction (day 11) presents to ED 90 minutes after a recorded oral temperature of 39.1 degC at home. She has a tunnelled central line in situ and at the exit site there is new erythema and tenderness. She has had one episode of vomiting and feels weak but reports no respiratory, urinary or abdominal symptoms.

Triage observations: T 39.0 degC, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 96% RA, BP 88/46, capillary refill 4 s. She appears pale and slightly mottled peripherally and is sleepy but rousable. Her most recent FBC, taken 24 hours ago, showed Hb 84, WCC 0.3, neutrophils 0.05 x10^9/L, platelets 28. She has no documented antibiotic allergies. She last had piperacillin-tazobactam 8 days ago for a previous febrile episode that was culture-negative.

The PEWS triggers immediate review and the unit's paediatric sepsis pathway is activated. Repeat venous lactate at the bedside is 3.6 mmol/L and capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. Her parents have a copy of her oncology plan listing penicillin tolerance and recent antibiotic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0 degC, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 96% RA, BP 88/46, cap refill 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Sleepy, mottled, central line exit site erythema and tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84, WCC 0.3, neutrophils 0.05, platelets 28. Lactate 3.6 mmol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: AML induction chemotherapy (day 11). Previous pip-tazo course 8 days ago.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate priority?

options.text: Remove central venous line immediately and culture catheter tip before any antibiotics
Paired cultures plus IV meropenem and vancomycin with 20 mL/kg saline bolus, within 60 minutes
Urgent CT abdomen and pelvis to exclude typhlitis before commencing any antibiotics
IV piperacillin-tazobactam alone, then reassess at 30 minutes before any escalation
Give granulocyte colony-stimulating factor immediately to raise the neutrophil count first

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome - recognition and initial step
stem:
A 7-year-old girl with newly diagnosed B-cell ALL is admitted to the paediatric oncology ward. Her presenting WCC was 180 x10^9/L with bulky mediastinal disease and tender hepatosplenomegaly. She has not yet received any chemotherapy. Pre-treatment workup is in progress. She has been on IV hyperhydration with 0.45% saline at 3 L/m^2/24 hours for 6 hours. She is well, alert, with no muscle weakness, no chest pain.

Observations: T 37.2 degC, HR 110, RR 22, BP 108/64. Initial biochemistry, returned just now, shows urea 8.6 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (above the upper limit for age), potassium 5.8 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.05 mmol/L, phosphate 2.4 mmol/L, urate 0.62 mmol/L (upper limit 0.36), LDH 1850 U/L. Urine output over the last 6 hours has been 1.2 mL/kg/hour. ECG shows peaked T waves in V2-V4 without QRS widening. No allopurinol has been given. The consultant is on the phone for the next-step discussion before induction is started.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.2 degC, HR 110, RR 22, BP 108/64. ECG: peaked T waves V2-V4.
data_table.Examination: Alert, no muscle weakness, hepatosplenomegaly tender, mediastinal mass on CXR.
data_table.Investigations: Urea 8.6, creat 78, K 5.8, Ca corrected 2.05, phosphate 2.4, urate 0.62 mmol/L, LDH 1850.
data_table.Medications: IV hyperhydration 3 L/m^2/24 h with 0.45% saline. No chemotherapy yet.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Oral allopurinol three times daily plus add potassium to fluids
IV rasburicase, continue hyperhydration, frequent biochemistry, PICU/nephrology input
IV calcium gluconate 10% and proceed with induction chemotherapy now
Urgent urine alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate to pH above 7.5
Withhold further IV fluids and observe to avoid cardiac strain

subtopic_detail: When to investigate iron deficiency further
stem:
A 4-year-old girl previously diagnosed with iron deficiency anaemia has returned to the GP for a routine review. Three months ago her haemoglobin was 88 g/L with ferritin 7 micrograms/L. She was started on oral elemental iron 4 mg/kg/day with cow's milk reduced to 400 mL/day and was reported by her mother to be taking the iron consistently. Over the last three months she has had two short episodes of loose stools she attributed to gastroenteritis circulating at daycare, and her mother has noted ongoing tiredness and intermittent abdominal bloating.

There is no overt blood in the stool, no haematuria. Vaccinations are up to date and growth has dropped from the 25th to the 10th centile for weight over the past year. On examination she looks slim but well, with no lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly and no joint swelling. Observations are within normal limits for age. Repeat FBC today: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 67 fL, RDW 17%, platelets 388, WCC normal. Ferritin 9 micrograms/L. Iron has been continuously prescribed and adherence is reported as good.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal for age.
data_table.Examination: Slim, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy. Weight centile dropped 25th to 10th.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 (was 88), MCV 67, ferritin 9 microg/L (was 7), platelets 388. Loose stools intermittently.
data_table.Medications: Oral elemental iron 4 mg/kg/day for 12 weeks.

lead_in: Which investigation is most appropriate now?

options.text: Continue current oral iron and re-test FBC in another 3 months
Upper GI endoscopy as the first-line investigation
Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies plus total IgA
Haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude beta-thalassaemia trait
Meckel scan with technetium-99m pertechnetate

stem:
A 14-year-old previously well girl presents to her GP with a 6-week history of a painless lump in the left side of her neck that has gradually enlarged. She also describes intermittent night sweats requiring change of clothing and a 3 kg unintentional weight loss over the same period. There has been no preceding sore throat, no dental infection and no foreign travel.

She has had no fevers documented at home, no cough. She has had no contact with tuberculosis or unwell pets and consumes no unpasteurised dairy. She is HPV-vaccinated and otherwise immunised. On examination she is well, afebrile, with a 3 cm firm, rubbery, non-tender, mobile node in the left posterior triangle, with a second 1.5 cm node deeper in the supraclavicular fossa on the same side.

There is no other regional or generalised lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly and no skin changes. Bedside FBC shows Hb 118 g/L, WCC 7.4 with normal differential, platelets 280. CRP is 14, LDH 320 U/L (upper limit 250). ESR is 56. A bedside ENT examination of the oropharynx is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile, otherwise normal.
data_table.Examination: 3 cm rubbery non-tender mobile left posterior triangle node + 1.5 cm left supraclavicular node, no organomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118, WCC 7.4 (normal diff), platelets 280, CRP 14, LDH 320, ESR 56.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial 2 weeks of oral cefalexin and clinical review
Ultrasound of the neck nodes only, review in 6 weeks
Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the largest neck node
Bartonella, EBV, toxoplasma serology with review in 4 weeks
Urgent paediatric oncology referral for excisional node biopsy and staging

subtopic_detail: SCID red flags - recognition and urgent investigation
stem:
A 4-month-old boy is brought to a regional ED for his third admission, this time with 10 days of persistent oral thrush despite two courses of oral nystatin, an erythematous nappy-area candidiasis, and a 5-week history of chronic non-bloody diarrhoea with poor weight gain (current weight on the 3rd centile, having tracked along the 50th at birth). His past admissions in the last 6 weeks have been for pneumocystis-like interstitial pneumonia requiring nasal high-flow and one episode of CMV viraemia.

He was born at term to non-consanguineous parents; his mother had a brother who died of an unexplained pneumonia at 7 months of age. He received BCG at birth in his country of birth, and rotavirus oral vaccine at 6 weeks in Australia. On examination he is small and pale, with oral plaques, perineal candidiasis, no thymic shadow on a recent chest X-ray, no palpable lymph nodes or tonsillar tissue, and bilateral fine inspiratory crackles.

T 37.4 degC, HR 152, RR 50, SpO2 94% RA. FBC today: Hb 96, WCC 5.2 with absolute lymphocyte count 0.6 x10^9/L (well below the age-specific lower limit of around 3.0). Total IgG, IgA, IgM are all low.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 degC, HR 152, RR 50, SpO2 94% RA.
data_table.Examination: Failure to thrive, oral thrush, perineal candidiasis, no thymic shadow on CXR, absent tonsils/lymph nodes, bilateral crackles.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96, WCC 5.2, ALC 0.6 x10^9/L, IgG / IgA / IgM all low.
data_table.Medications: Recent rotavirus oral vaccine, BCG at birth overseas.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate single next step?

options.text: Empirical oral fluconazole and clinic review in 4 weeks
Same-day immunology referral, lymphocyte subsets, isolation, no live vaccines
Reassure parents that recurrent infections are normal at 4 months
Give routine 6-month MMR catch-up vaccination at this visit
Send HIV antibody (not PCR) and clinic review in 2 weeks

stem:
A previously well 4-year-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric ED by ambulance after 12 hours of escalating fever, headache and vomiting. He is fully immunised on the current Australian schedule including 13vPCV and Hib. On arrival he is photophobic, has neck stiffness on passive flexion, and a positive Kernig's sign. There is no purpuric rash. He becomes briefly drowsy during examination with a GCS of 13 (E3 V4 M6) and his right pupil is noted to be 4 mm and the left 3 mm, both still reactive.

Fundoscopy is attempted but the view is limited. His mother reports no recent head injury, no foreign travel and no known sick contacts. He has had no seizures and no recent antibiotics. The ED registrar is preparing to perform an urgent lumbar puncture before commencing antibiotics. The paediatric registrar has been called and IV access has been obtained, with bloods including blood culture, FBC, EUC, CRP, coagulation and venous gas already drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 142 bpm, RR 28 /min, BP 112/74 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck stiff, photophobic, anisocoria 4 mm right vs 3 mm left, no purpura, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 22.4, neutrophils 18.6 x 10^9/L, CRP 184 mg/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, INR 1.0, platelets 188 x 10^9/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Proceed with LP now and start IV ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone after CSF
Give IV ceftriaxone at the standard sepsis dose, defer LP, and arrange urgent neuroimaging only after antibiotics are running
Give IV dexamethasone then IV ceftriaxone at the CSF-penetrating dose, defer LP, arrange CT brain after stabilisation
Give IV benzylpenicillin alone, defer LP, and observe in resuscitation for 30 minutes
Perform CT brain first, then LP if the scan is normal, then commence antibiotics once CSF is obtained

subtopic_detail: Bacterial meningitis workup in the preschool child

stem:
A 5-week-old term male infant is brought to a regional ED by his parents after a single rectal temperature of 38.4 deg C taken because he was unsettled and feeding poorly for the last 8 hours. He was born by normal vaginal delivery at 39+2 weeks with no risk factors for early-onset sepsis: maternal GBS swab negative at 36 weeks, no prolonged rupture of membranes, no intrapartum fever.

He had an unremarkable nursery course and went home on day 2. He is exclusively breastfed and has been gaining weight along the 50th centile. He has had no cough, no diarrhoea, and there are no sick contacts. He has not yet received any immunisations as his 6-week appointment is next week. On examination he is mottled peripherally, with a soft anterior fontanelle, no focus of infection, and a capillary refill of 3 seconds. He has been crying weakly but is consolable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 deg C rectal, HR 184 bpm, RR 56 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 76/42 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries, CRT 3 s, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no focal infection, no rash, weak cry
data_table.History: Term NVD, GBS negative, no maternal fever, exclusively breastfed, not yet immunised

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen after blood, urine and CSF are obtained?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg eight-hourly as initial empirical monotherapy with no other antibiotic added at this stage
Intravenous benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin as the Australian regimen, adding cefotaxime at meningitic doses if meningitis is suspected
Intravenous ampicillin 50 mg/kg plus intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg without gentamicin, as per the US AAP febrile-infant pathway
