Intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg plus intravenous gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg eight-hourly to cover Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative pathogens
Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg as a single dose with planned review in 4 hours pending blood and urine results before further escalation

subtopic_detail: Sepsis evaluation in the febrile young infant

stem:
A 7-year-old previously well boy is brought to the ED at 0200 hours with a 14-hour history of fever, lethargy, leg pain and a rash that started 3 hours ago. His mother says he received his 4vMenACWY vaccine at 12 months and a MenB vaccine privately at age 3, but no booster since. He attends a metropolitan primary school and a 9-year-old classmate was hospitalised yesterday with a similar illness.

On arrival he is mottled with cold peripheries and a capillary refill of 4 seconds. There is a non-blanching purpuric rash on both shins and the buttocks with several lesions over 4 mm and one early ecchymotic lesion of about 1 cm. He is rousable but irritable, with a GCS of 14, and complains of severe calf pain. The ED registrar gives IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg and a 20 mL/kg fluid bolus.

A lumbar puncture is deferred because of his haemodynamic instability and an emerging coagulopathy on the venous gas (lactate 4.2 mmol/L). Blood culture and a meningococcal PCR (EDTA) are obtained. The infectious diseases registrar asks about public health management of close contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 deg C, HR 168 bpm, RR 36 /min, BP 86/48 mmHg, SpO2 95% on room air, CRT 4 s
data_table.Examination: Mottled cold peripheries, purpuric rash shins/buttocks, one 1 cm ecchymotic lesion, irritable, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.2 (neutrophils 1.1) x 10^9/L, platelets 84 x 10^9/L, INR 1.6, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, CRP 96 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate public-health and contact-management action?

options.text: Notify the local public health unit only after the meningococcal PCR returns positive, and prescribe ciprofloxacin only to household contacts
Notify public health immediately, give ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally as a single dose to all the boy's school classmates and teachers
Notify public health within 5 working days, no chemoprophylaxis needed because he received MenACWY and MenB vaccines
Notify public health immediately on clinical suspicion; ciprofloxacin 250 mg orally as single dose for household and close contacts
Notify public health immediately and give rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 4 days to household contacts

subtopic_detail: Identification and public-health response to invasive meningococcal disease

stem:
A 9-year-old previously well girl presents to the tertiary paediatric ED with 3 days of fever, headache and confusion, and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes at home that resolved spontaneously without intervention. Her mother describes intermittent inappropriate laughter and word-finding difficulty for the last 24 hours and a sense that the child has been smelling something burnt that nobody else in the household can smell.

There is no rash and no neck stiffness, and she has had no foreign travel, no mosquito-exposed regional travel to northern Australia or to Murray-Darling river settings, and no animal bites or scratches. Her immunisations are up to date for the standard NIP schedule (no Japanese encephalitis vaccine because of no risk exposure recorded). On examination she has a low-grade fever, her GCS fluctuates between 13 and 15, she has subtle right-sided pronator drift and expressive dysphasia, and the rest of the cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examinations are normal.

There are no purpuric lesions on full skin survey. CT brain is unremarkable. MRI is scheduled for the morning. LP is performed: opening pressure 22 cm H2O, CSF clear, WCC 96 x 10^6/L (90% lymphocytes), protein 0.92 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L (paired serum 5.1), Gram stain negative; CSF HSV, VZV, enterovirus and meningococcal PCR are pending, and an autoimmune encephalitis panel including anti-NMDAR antibodies has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 deg C, HR 108 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating GCS 13 to 15, expressive dysphasia, right pronator drift, no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (WCC 96, 90% lymphs), protein 0.92 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, CT brain normal, MRI pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management decision?

options.text: Commence IV aciclovir at the paediatric encephalitis dose q8h empirically while awaiting CSF HSV PCR
Commence high-dose IV methylprednisolone for presumed anti-NMDAR encephalitis pending antibody results today
Commence IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone, withhold antivirals until PCR results
Arrange urgent EEG and defer all therapy until non-convulsive status epilepticus is fully excluded
Commence IV ribavirin for suspected Japanese encephalitis given the recent Murray Valley exposure risk

subtopic_detail: Encephalitis with focal neurology in a school-aged child

stem:
A previously well 5-year-old boy presents to his GP with 4 days of fever, productive cough and reduced activity. He is fully immunised on the Australian NIP including 13vPCV, and has had no foreign travel or sick contacts. He is alert, well perfused, taking oral fluids and about 75 percent of usual food, with no recessions or grunting. SpO2 is 96 percent on room air.

Auscultation reveals bronchial breathing and crackles in the right lower zone. A chest X-ray performed because of the persistent fever shows right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. His weight is 18 kg. He has no known drug allergies and has not received antibiotics in the previous 3 months.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 deg C, HR 112 bpm, RR 28 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 100/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breath sounds and crackles right lower zone, no recessions, no grunting, alert and active
data_table.Investigations: CXR right lower lobe consolidation, no effusion

lead_in: Which oral antibiotic regimen is most appropriate as outpatient first-line therapy?

options.text: Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days
Amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) eight-hourly for 5 days
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days as first-line monotherapy
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5/3.2 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days
Cefalexin 25 mg/kg six-hourly for 7 days

subtopic_detail: First-line antibiotic for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with right lower lobe pneumonia diagnosed 5 days ago by her GP has been on oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg q8h but is brought to the tertiary paediatric ED after 48 hours of persistent high fevers, increasing respiratory effort, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and a new reluctance to lie on her left side. She is fully immunised including 13vPCV.

On arrival she is febrile to 39.6 deg C, has a respiratory rate of 38 /min with mild subcostal recessions, SpO2 91% on room air, and dullness to percussion with reduced breath sounds over the right lower and mid zones with bronchial breathing above. She is tolerating sips of fluid only and is reluctant to take deep breaths. A chest X-ray shows a right-sided opacification of the lower two-thirds of the hemithorax with blunting of the costophrenic angle and a meniscus sign suggestive of a moderate effusion.

Bloods show WCC 24 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 21), CRP 268 mg/L, and a normal lactate. Blood cultures are taken and IV flucloxacillin and cefotaxime are commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 deg C, HR 138 bpm, RR 38 /min, SpO2 91% on room air, BP 104/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recessions, dull right base, reduced breath sounds, bronchial breathing above, splinting on right
data_table.Investigations: CXR right effusion two-thirds hemithorax with meniscus, WCC 24 (N 21) x 10^9/L, CRP 268 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide drainage decisions?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT chest to assess for necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess
Repeat plain chest X-ray in lateral decubitus position for layering effusion
Diagnostic thoracocentesis only, with pleural fluid pH, LDH, glucose and Gram stain
Bedside chest ultrasound to characterise effusion (size, septation, loculation) and guide drainage
Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage for microbiology and cytology of fluid

stem:
A 9-week-old infant is brought to the ED by her parents after three brief cyanotic episodes at home, the last preceded by a paroxysm of coughing that ended in a deep gasping noise. She has been coryzal for 10 days and her cough has worsened in the last 4 days with occasional post-tussive vomiting. She has not received any immunisations because her parents have been delaying the 6-week schedule.

Her mother completed a course of antibiotics 2 weeks ago for a chest infection diagnosed at the GP as pertussis. The infant was born at 38 weeks and her mother did not receive a pertussis vaccine in pregnancy. On examination she is afebrile, has minimal increased work of breathing between paroxysms, and her chest is clear. SpO2 between coughing episodes is 97% on room air but dropped to 78% during the cough observed in ED.

There is a single sub-conjunctival haemorrhage. Bloods show WCC 38 x 10^9/L with an absolute lymphocytosis of 28 x 10^9/L. Nasopharyngeal aspirate for Bordetella pertussis PCR has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 152 bpm, RR 44 /min between paroxysms, SpO2 97% baseline (78% with cough)
data_table.Examination: Sub-conjunctival haemorrhage, paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop, otherwise well between episodes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 38 (lymphocytes 28) x 10^9/L, CXR clear, NPA pertussis PCR pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate antibiotic regimen for this infant?

options.text: Oral roxithromycin 4 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days, admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring
Oral azithromycin once daily for 5 days, admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole twice daily for 14 days, admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring
IV ceftriaxone once daily for 7 days continuously
Withhold antibiotics; they do not change clinical course once paroxysms have begun

subtopic_detail: Pertussis in the unimmunised young infant

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the GP after his father, a recently arrived migrant from a high-tuberculosis-incidence country in South-East Asia, was diagnosed last week with smear-positive cavitating pulmonary tuberculosis sensitive to all first-line drugs on rapid molecular testing. The boy has been well, has no cough, no feversht along the 50th centile on his growth chart. He has not received BCG vaccination as it is not on the routine Australian schedule.

He shares a bedroom with his father and has slept in the same bed during the 8 weeks prior to his father's diagnosis. On examination he is well, alert and interactive, with no peripheral or cervical lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, and a clear chest on auscultation. The local public health unit asks the GP to coordinate his contact assessment. A chest X-ray is performed and is reported as normal.

A Mantoux tuberculin skin test using 0.1 mL of 10 TU/mL purified protein derivative is placed in the left forearm and read by the public health nurse at 72 hours, showing an induration of 12 mm with surrounding erythema. HIV serology is non-reactive. The mother asks whether an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) such as QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus would be more accurate in her son and whether he needs treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, clear chest, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CXR clear, Mantoux 12 mm induration at 72 h, HIV non-reactive, no BCG history

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the Mantoux in 8 weeks because 12 mm without BCG may be non-specific
Reassure that the Mantoux is negative because it is under 15 mm and discharge with no further investigation
Order IGRA (QuantiFERON or T-SPOT) instead because it is more specific and avoid further skin testing
Start a 6-month course of rifampicin monotherapy without isoniazid today
Diagnose latent TB and commence isoniazid daily for 9 months with pyridoxine

subtopic_detail: Latent and contact tuberculosis investigation in a young child

stem:
A 16-year-old male attends the GP alone requesting a confidential review after an episode of condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new partner 18 hours ago. He says the partner has subsequently disclosed by message that he is HIV positive but has been on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load for 2 years. The patient is otherwise well, has no symptoms, has had no other recent sexual exposures, is up to date with hepatitis B vaccination, and has not used injecting drugs.

He has heard about post-exposure prophylaxis online and asks whether he needs it. He is afraid of his parents finding out. He is articulate, demonstrates clear understanding of confidentiality, his health, and the implications of testing and treatment. He says he is willing to attend the local sexual health clinic but only if his Medicare claim history will not appear on his parents' Medicare statement.

There are no concerns about coercion or capacity. He has no penicillin or other drug allergies, and his renal function is normal on a recent school medical.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 76 bpm, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, no rash, no mucosal lesions, normal external genitalia
data_table.History: Condomless receptive anal intercourse 18 h ago; partner HIV positive on ART with undetectable VL for 2 yr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Document Gillick competence and refer to sexual health clinic same day; PEP not indicated as source confirmed undetectable (U=U); baseline HIV/HBV/syphilis serology
Prescribe a 28-day course of tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir empirically and arrange baseline HIV testing at the GP
Defer all testing and management until the parents are informed because the patient is still a minor under 16
Perform an HIV antibody-only test today and reassure that, if it returns negative, he does not need PEP
Inform the patient that PEP is no longer available in Australia and that PrEP is the only option for future exposures

subtopic_detail: HIV testing and post-exposure prophylaxis in the adolescent

stem:
A 13-month-old infant has been brought to the GP 60 hours after she shared a paediatric outpatient waiting room for 90 minutes with a child later confirmed by PCR to have measles. She was due to receive her first MMR vaccine at the 12-month visit but it was deferred 2 weeks ago because of an intercurrent febrile illness. Her older sister, aged 4, is in the same household and is fully immunised.

Her mother is 22 weeks pregnant and her serological status for measles is unknown. The household also includes her grandmother, aged 68, who was born in 1958 in Australia and has no recorded MMR doses, and an uncle with cystic fibrosis (post-lung-transplant 4 years ago, on tacrolimus and prednisolone). The GP confirms the public health unit has already issued a contact-tracing alert. The infant is currently well, afebrile, and has no rash, no coryza and no conjunctivitis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 124 bpm, RR 28 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no rash, no Koplik spots, no conjunctivitis, no coryza
data_table.History: Exposure 60 h ago, due first MMR but deferred 2 weeks ago, household includes pregnant mother, unvaccinated grandmother, immunosuppressed transplant uncle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate post-exposure measure for the index 13-month-old infant?

options.text: Give intramuscular normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG) because she is under 9 months
Administer MMR now (within 72 hours of exposure), notify public health, repeat MMR at 18 months
Withhold post-exposure prophylaxis because she is currently asymptomatic; arrange measles serology day 14
Administer MMR vaccine plus oral ribavirin for 7 days starting today
Reassure that maternal antibody will protect her until she is 12 months old

stem:
An 8-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, currently in the consolidation phase of a Berlin-Frankfurt-Munster protocol and on dexamethasone, vincristine and intrathecal methotrexate, is brought to the day oncology unit after a confirmed face-to-face household exposure to his 5-year-old sister, who developed a vesicular varicella rash on her trunk and face this morning. He has not had clinical varicella infection at any time in the past, did not complete the varicella vaccination schedule because of his oncology diagnosis at the time of his routine 18-month appointment, and was last on the day oncology ward yesterday for his scheduled intrathecal chemotherapy.

The patient is currently afebrile and entirely asymptomatic, with no rash, no oral lesions and no respiratory or constitutional symptoms; his most recent full blood count 2 days ago showed a WCC of 1.8 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.7 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.9 x 10^9/L, and platelets 84 x 10^9/L. His baseline varicella IgG taken at diagnosis was negative. The exposure occurred 36 hours ago, and the local paediatric oncology consultant is available by phone.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 92 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Well, no rash, no oral lesions, no respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: WCC 1.8 (neutrophils 0.7) x 10^9/L, platelets 84 x 10^9/L, varicella IgG negative on baseline

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate intervention for this patient?

options.text: Live attenuated varicella vaccine 0.5 mL subcutaneously within 5 days of exposure
Oral valaciclovir q8h for 7 days starting from day 7 after exposure
Oral aciclovir six-hourly for 5 days starting immediately today
Observation only and IV aciclovir q8h if a rash develops
Zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) intramuscularly within 96 hours of exposure (up to 10 days)

subtopic_detail: Varicella post-exposure prophylaxis in the immunocompromised host

stem:
A 3-year-old previously well, fully immunised girl is brought to her GP with 12 hours of right ear pain and a mild fever. She has been clingy but is eating and drinking normally with no vomiting and no neck stiffness. This is her first episode and she has no high-risk background (no cleft palate, no immunodeficiency, not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander).

On examination her left tympanic membrane is normal and her right tympanic membrane is erythematous and bulging with the membrane intact and no otorrhoea. She is afebrile in clinic at 37.8 deg C. Her mother reports she settles with paracetamol.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 deg C, HR 110 bpm, RR 24 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 100/62 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right TM erythematous and bulging, intact, no otorrhoea, left TM normal, no mastoid tenderness, no neck stiffness
data_table.History: First episode, fully immunised, no high-risk background, eating/drinking normally

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Regular analgesia (paracetamol with or without ibuprofen) and safety-net advice to return or recommence antibiotics if not improving at 48 to 72 hours
Immediate oral amoxicillin at half the standard AOM dose three times daily for 5 days
Immediate oral amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for 7 days
Immediate oral cefaclor three times daily for 7 days
Topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops twice daily for 7 days

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the ED with 24 hours of progressive right eyelid swelling and redness on a background of 4 days of purulent nasal discharge and intermittent facial pain. He is fully immunised including 13vPCV and Hib. He has had a temperature of up to 39.2 deg C at home. On examination the right upper and lower eyelids are warm, erythematous and tense; the eye itself is closed by swelling but can be opened with gentle effort.

The conjunctiva is mildly injected. He reports pain when asked to move the eye and has restricted upgaze and lateral gaze on the right with a sense of pressure. Visual acuity in the affected eye is reduced to 6/18 from a documented 6/6 at school screening 4 months ago, and there is a relative afferent pupillary defect on swinging-flashlight testing. He has no proptosis measured by Hertel exophthalmometry. The left eye is normal. He has no neck stiffness and no focal neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 deg C, HR 128 bpm, RR 24 /min, BP 108/66 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Right eyelid swelling, painful EOM with restricted upgaze and lateral gaze, RAPD, VA 6/18 right vs 6/6 left, no proptosis on Hertel
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 15), CRP 142 mg/L, blood culture taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin q6h for 7 days and review by GP in 48 hours
IV flucloxacillin q6h monotherapy and ophthalmology review in the morning
MRI orbits in the morning before any antibiotics, to confirm the diagnosis
Urgent contrast CT sinuses/orbits, admit, IV ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin + metronidazole, urgent ophthalmology and ENT
Single dose of oral prednisolone and observation, on the assumption of allergic angioedema

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is brought to a tertiary paediatric ED by her parents on day 10 of consolidation chemotherapy with high-dose methotrexate and cytarabine. She has a tunnelled Hickman line in situ for 4 months, has been febrile for 4 hours with a single reading of 38.6 deg C documented at home by her parents, has had new rigors over the last 30 minutes, and her parents report increasingly rapid breathing and that she has been progressively more lethargic over the last hour with reduced eye contact.

On arrival to the resuscitation bay she is mottled with cold peripheries and a capillary refill of 5 seconds, BP 78/40 mmHg, HR 162 bpm, RR 40 /min, SpO2 94% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, T 39.4 deg C. There is no obvious focus of infection on rapid head-to-toe examination, the Hickman exit site is clean and not erythematous, her chest is clear, and there is no abdominal tenderness or perianal lesion.

Her full blood count two days ago showed neutrophils 0.2 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.4 x 10^9/L, haemoglobin 92 g/L, and platelets 28 x 10^9/L. A repeat FBC, blood cultures drawn from both Hickman lumens and a peripheral site simultaneously, venous lactate, VBG, EUC, LFTs, coagulation, group and screen, urinalysis and a portable CXR are being arranged in parallel with resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 162 bpm, RR 40 /min, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 94% on 4 L/min, CRT 5 s
data_table.Examination: Mottled cold peripheries, lethargic, no rash, no mucositis bleeding, Hickman line site clean, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Recent neutrophils 0.2 x 10^9/L, platelets 28 x 10^9/L, lactate pending, no known resistant organisms

lead_in: After 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus is initiated, what is the single most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: IV cefepime 50 mg/kg q8h monotherapy
IV ceftriaxone daily plus IV vancomycin six-hourly
IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus IV gentamicin, add vancomycin if line infection suspected or shock persists
IV meropenem 20 mg/kg eight-hourly as broad-spectrum monotherapy
Delay antibiotics until blood cultures return positive to ensure organism-directed therapy today

subtopic_detail: Febrile neutropenia with septic shock in the immunocompromised child

stem:
A 5-year-old previously well boy is brought to a metropolitan paediatric emergency department because of right hip pain and refusal to weight-bear for the past 18 hours. His mother reports a coryzal illness that resolved 10 days ago and no history of trauma. Immunisations are up to date and he is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. On arrival he is alert, holds his right hip in slight flexion, abduction and external rotation, and cries with passive internal rotation.

He has no rash, no other joint involvement and no overlying erythema or warmth at the hip. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and peripheral pulses are normal. He was given paracetamol 2 hours ago at triage. The ED registrar performs an ultrasound which demonstrates a moderate right hip effusion. Bloods and a plain pelvic radiograph have been arranged. The orthopaedic registrar asks for risk stratification using the Kocher criteria before deciding on theatre versus observation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 deg C, HR 128 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Holds right hip in flexion / abduction / external rotation, painful log-roll, no overlying erythema, refuses to bear weight even with paracetamol on board
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.8 x10^9/L (neutrophils 9.6), CRP 38 mg/L, ESR 52 mm/h, blood culture pending, pelvic XR no fracture or SUFE, hip US moderate effusion

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and ibuprofen for simple analgesia and arrange GP review in 48 hours for a likely post-viral self-limiting hip presentation with planned reassessment
Admit for observation and serial examinations with maintenance IV fluids, withholding empirical antibiotics until a repeat CRP and full blood count at 12 hours have been reviewed
Commence empirical oral flucloxacillin six-hourly and arrange outpatient orthopaedic clinic review the following week with safety-net advice for parents
Arrange urgent ultrasound-guided hip aspiration in theatre, send synovial fluid for cell count and culture, then commence empirical IV flucloxacillin after sampling
Order an urgent contrast MRI of the hip and pelvis and defer joint aspiration and antibiotics until imaging has formally excluded coexisting osteomyelitis or pelvic abscess

subtopic_detail: Paediatric orthopaedics - septic arthritis vs transient synovitis

stem:
A 12-year-old boy with a BMI of 30 kg/m^2 presents to his GP with a 6-week history of intermittent left knee and anterior thigh pain that has progressed over the past week to an antalgic limp. He denies any specific injury and has been otherwise well. He is in the early stages of puberty (Tanner 2 pubic hair). On examination the left lower limb is held in slight external rotation with the patient supine.

When the GP attempts to flex the left hip, the leg obligately externally rotates. Hip internal rotation and abduction are reduced compared with the right side, but there is no joint warmth, no effusion clinically and no overlying erythema. He is afebrile with normal observations. He weighs 78 kg. Plain anteroposterior pelvic radiographs are obtained and reported by the radiologist as showing a widened, irregular left proximal femoral physis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 86 bpm, RR 16 /min, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait, externally rotated left lower limb at rest, obligate external rotation on hip flexion, reduced internal rotation and abduction, no warmth or effusion
data_table.Investigations: AP pelvis - widened irregular left proximal femoral physis; frog-lateral pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the family, advise simple oral analgesia with paracetamol and review the child in clinic in 6 weeks if symptoms persist or worsen with ongoing activity
Refer for routine paediatric orthopaedic outpatient assessment within the next 2 weeks and allow continued partial weight-bearing on the affected limb in the interim period
Order an outpatient MRI of the left hip within the next 7 days to exclude an idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis before any orthopaedic referral or non-weight-bearing measures
Make the child strictly non-weight-bearing (wheelchair or crutches), arrange immediate transfer to the nearest paediatric orthopaedic unit and request a frog-lateral pelvic radiograph
Arrange an outpatient MRI of the left knee given the predominant knee pain to exclude meniscal injury or osteochondritis dissecans before any hip-focused intervention

stem:
A 13-year-old male competitive basketballer presents to his GP with a 6-week history of bilateral anterior knee pain that is worse during and after training, jumping and stair climbing, and that settles with rest. He denies any acute injury and has had no swelling, locking or giving way. He has had a recent growth spurt of 8 cm over the past 12 months.

On examination both knees show localised tenderness and a palpable bony prominence at the tibial tuberosity, with reproduction of pain on resisted knee extension and on direct pressure over the tuberosity. There is no joint effusion, no warmth, no ligamentous laxity and no patellar grind. He has full painless range, no nocturnal pain, no constitutional symptoms and no inguinal lymphadenopathy. He is afebrile with normal observations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 78 bpm, RR 14 /min, BP 112/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bilateral tibial tuberosity tenderness with prominent bony enlargement, pain on resisted knee extension, no effusion, full ROM, stable ligaments
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure with the clinical diagnosis of Osgood-Schlatter, advise relative activity modification, ice and simple analgesia, and continue sport within pain tolerance
Order bilateral knee MRI to exclude osteochondritis dissecans and refer to paediatric orthopaedics
Apply long-leg plaster casts bilaterally for 6 weeks then reassess for ongoing apophyseal fragmentation
Inject intralesional corticosteroid into the tibial tuberosity bilaterally to reduce inflammation
Arrange plain knee radiographs in both AP and skyline views to confirm the diagnosis and exclude tibial tuberosity avulsion fracture

stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to her GP after a school nurse noticed asymmetry of her back during a routine screening assessment. She has no back pain, no neurological symptoms and no functional limitation, and dances three times a week without difficulty. She had menarche 6 months ago. On examination, when she bends forward (Adams forward bend test) there is a clearly visible right thoracic rib prominence.

Standing posture shows a right shoulder higher than the left and asymmetric flank crease. There is no leg-length discrepancy on examination. Neurological examination is normal, including abdominal reflexes and lower limb tone, power, reflexes and sensation. There are no skin stigmata of spinal dysraphism (no hairy patch, lipoma or sacral dimple). A standing posteroanterior spinal radiograph is ordered and reports a right thoracic curve with a Cobb angle of 28 degrees and Risser stage 2.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 deg C, HR 72 bpm, RR 14 /min, BP 108/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right thoracic rib prominence on Adams forward bend, right shoulder elevation, no leg length inequality, normal neurology, no cutaneous spinal stigmata, Tanner 4
data_table.Investigations: Standing PA spine - right thoracic curve, Cobb 28 degrees, Risser 2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the patient and family, discharge with no follow-up arrangements as she is currently asymptomatic and reports no functional or postural concerns
Arrange routine GP review in 6 months with a repeat standing posteroanterior spinal radiograph at that time to reassess Cobb angle and Risser stage progression
Refer to a paediatric orthopaedic / spinal surgeon for consideration of bracing given a Cobb angle of 28 degrees in a skeletally immature patient
Refer urgently to spinal surgery for posterior spinal instrumentation and fusion given the visible deformity, asymmetric shoulders and a 28-degree thoracic Cobb angle
Order an urgent whole-spine MRI under sedation to exclude syringomyelia given the visible right thoracic curve and shoulder-height asymmetry on standing examination

stem:
A term female infant is being examined on day 2 of life on the postnatal ward. She was born by elective caesarean at 39+1 weeks for breech presentation that did not respond to external cephalic version. Birthweight was 3520 g. There is a family history of developmental dysplasia of the hip in her older sister who required a Pavlik harness.

She is breastfeeding well and has passed urine and meconium. On hip examination today, the Ortolani manoeuvre on the left hip elicits a palpable clunk as the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum with abduction. The right hip is stable. There is no leg-length discrepancy or asymmetric thigh skin creases. Neurological examination including primitive reflexes is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 142 bpm, RR 46 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Positive Ortolani sign on left hip (clunk on abduction reduction), Barlow negative on right, no leg length discrepancy, normal Moro and tone
data_table.Risk factors: Female, breech to term, first-degree family history of DDH

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that hip clunks at this age are usually benign and arrange a routine 6-week paediatric review without specialist input or imaging today
Order an immediate plain anteroposterior pelvic radiograph to assess acetabular index and the Shenton line before referral
Refer to paediatric orthopaedic surgery now for assessment and Pavlik harness application, and arrange a static and dynamic hip ultrasound
Apply double nappies between the legs to maintain abduction and review the infant in 4 weeks
Arrange an outpatient hip ultrasound at 6 weeks as standard risk-factor screening

subtopic_detail: Developmental dysplasia of the hip - neonatal exam

stem:
An 8-month-old girl is brought to her GP because her parents have noticed her left leg appears shorter than the right when they change her nappy. She was born at term, was not breech, and the newborn check was documented as normal. There is no family history of hip problems and she had no hip ultrasound. She is meeting developmental milestones, including sitting independently, and has not yet started cruising.

On examination, with the infant supine and hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees, the left knee sits lower than the right (positive Galeazzi sign). Hip abduction is reduced on the left (60 degrees versus 80 degrees on the right). There is asymmetry of the thigh and gluteal skin creases. There is no warmth or tenderness and the infant is afebrile with normal neurology. The mother asks whether ultrasound is still useful at 8 months and is anxious about radiation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 126 bpm, RR 32 /min
data_table.Examination: Positive Galeazzi (apparent shortening of left thigh), reduced left hip abduction (60 vs 80 deg), asymmetric skin creases, no warmth, normal neurology
data_table.Past: Normal newborn examination, no neonatal hip ultrasound, no risk factors documented

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Static and dynamic Graf-classified hip ultrasound
MRI pelvis under general anaesthetic
Plain anteroposterior pelvic radiograph
CT pelvis with three-dimensional reconstruction
Bone scintigraphy with Tc-99m MDP

stem:
A 3-year-old previously well boy is brought to ED with a 4-day history of a painless intermittent limp affecting the right leg. He had a coryzal illness 2 weeks ago that has now resolved. He has had no fevers, no rashes and no recent trauma. He is fully immunised and not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. On examination he ambulates with a Trendelenburg gait favouring the right side.

Hip abduction and internal rotation are mildly reduced on the right compared with the left. He is afebrile and there is no warmth, swelling or tenderness at the right hip, knee, ankle or foot. He will bear weight, although with a limp, and engages happily with the toys in the cubicle. Bloods show WCC 8.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 4.2), CRP 6 mg/L. Bedside hip ultrasound shows a small right hip effusion. The mother asks whether ALL or Perthes need to be excluded today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 104 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Trendelenburg gait, mild reduction in right hip abduction and internal rotation, no warmth or swelling, weight-bearing, afebrile, alert and playful
data_table.Investigations: WCC 8.4 (N 4.2), CRP 6, ESR 18, hip US small right effusion, AP pelvis pending

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Septic arthritis of the right hip joint with bacterial synovitis
Transient (irritable hip) synovitis following recent viral upper respiratory tract illness
Perthes disease of the right femoral head with early epiphyseal involvement
Slipped upper femoral epiphysis of the right hip in an obese child
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting with limp and disproportionate bone pain

stem:
A 4-year-old Aboriginal girl living in a remote Northern Territory community presents to the clinic with 36 hours of right ear pain and fever. Her mother reports that she has had three episodes of ear discharge in the past year and frequent colds. She is up to date with immunisations including PCV. On examination she is alert, well-perfused and tolerating oral fluids.

Otoscopy of the right ear shows a bulging, opaque, erythematous tympanic membrane with no perforation and no visible discharge. The left tympanic membrane is dull but intact with a visible air-fluid level. There is no mastoid tenderness, no facial nerve palsy and no postauricular swelling. She has no penicillin allergy. The clinic nurse has commenced paracetamol and the doctor is choosing antibiotic therapy in line with the current eTG and CARPA Standard Treatment Manual. The clinic nurse asks whether watchful waiting is appropriate.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 deg C, HR 118 bpm, RR 22 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Right TM bulging, opaque, erythematous, intact; left TM dull with air-fluid level; no mastoid tenderness; oropharynx clear
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Watchful waiting with regular paracetamol for analgesia and structured otoscopic review in 48 hours
Oral amoxicillin three times daily for 7 days
Oral cefuroxime axetil twice daily for a 3-day short course
Topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops two drops twice daily for 7 days
Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin single weight-based dose at the clinic today

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media - Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander child duration

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents to a tertiary paediatric ED with a 5-day history of left ear pain initially diagnosed as AOM by the GP and treated with oral amoxicillin. Over the past 24 hours her mother reports new posterior auricular swelling, displacement of the pinna and worsening fever despite the antibiotics. There is no history of recent travel and immunisations are up to date.

On examination the left auricle is protruding outwards and downwards. There is a fluctuant, erythematous, tender swelling behind the left ear that obliterates the post-auricular sulcus. Otoscopy shows a bulging, erythematous left tympanic membrane with pus visible behind it; the right ear is normal. There is no facial nerve palsy, no neck stiffness deficit. She is alert and interactive but in pain.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 152 bpm, RR 28 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Left auricle protruding outwards and downwards, fluctuant tender postauricular erythematous swelling obliterating sulcus, bulging erythematous left TM with pus, GCS 15, no neck stiffness, no facial nerve palsy
data_table.Investigations: WCC 21.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 16.4), CRP 162 mg/L, blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Change current oral amoxicillin to oral amoxicillin/clavulanate twice daily for 10 days and arrange GP review in 48 hours to assess for improvement
Admit, commence intravenous flucloxacillin six-hourly as monotherapy and arrange routine outpatient ENT clinic review within 1 week of discharge home
Admit, commence IV ceftriaxone, request urgent CT temporal bones with contrast and urgent ENT review for consideration of cortical mastoidectomy and myringotomy
Perform urgent lumbar puncture in ED for cell count, protein, glucose and culture and commence empirical IV ceftriaxone for suspected intracranial extension from the ear
Arrange urgent MRI brain with MR venography to exclude lateral sinus thrombosis and intracranial abscess before commencing any intravenous antibiotic therapy or surgical input

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media complications - acute mastoiditis

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to his GP by his mother because his preschool teacher reports he frequently says "what?" and is increasingly inattentive in group sessions. He has had four episodes of GP-diagnosed acute otitis media in the last 12 months, all treated and resolved. He has had no ear pain or discharge for the past 3 months. His speech and language are mildly behind peers but he is using full sentences.

He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and lives in a household with no smokers. On otoscopy both tympanic membranes appear retracted and dull with visible air-fluid levels and reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Tympanometry performed in the rooms shows bilateral type B (flat) tracings. The mother brings audiology results performed last week showing a bilateral conductive hearing loss of 35 dB. His mother asks whether antibiotics or a steroid spray could resolve the effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 deg C, HR 92 bpm, RR 18 /min
data_table.Examination: Bilateral retracted dull TMs with air-fluid levels, reduced TM mobility, no perforation, no discharge, mildly delayed expressive language
data_table.Investigations: Tympanometry bilateral type B (flat); audiology bilateral conductive hearing loss 35 dB

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin three times daily for 10 days as empirical treatment for chronic middle ear effusion and review at the end of the course
Prescribe intranasal fluticasone 50 microgram daily plus oral cetirizine 5 mg daily for 3 months to address presumed allergic contribution to chronic middle-ear effusion
Watchful waiting for a further 6 months without repeat audiology, tympanometry or specialist review given the absence of acute ear pain or discharge
Refer to ENT for consideration of bilateral grommet insertion given persistent bilateral OME >3 months with bilateral conductive hearing loss >25 dB and emerging language and behavioural impact
Refer to a paediatric audiologist for hearing aid fitting as definitive long-term management of the bilateral conductive hearing loss without ENT or grommet consideration

subtopic_detail: Otitis media with effusion - referral threshold

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the GP after the third episode of right-sided epistaxis this month. Each episode has been brief (5 to 10 minutes), stopped with pressure, and has occurred when he was picking his nose. He is otherwise well, with no bruising, no bleeding from other sites and no family history of bleeding disorders. He is on no medication.

Anterior rhinoscopy reveals a small visible vessel and a crust over the right Little area, with no active bleeding; the left nasal cavity is clear. There is no septal haematoma, no mass and no facial deformity. He has full eye movements, no proptosis, no neck masses and no lymphadenopathy. Full blood count and coagulation screen are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 86 bpm, RR 18 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Visible vessel and crust at right Little area, no septal haematoma, no mass, no proptosis, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, coagulation screen normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to ENT for examination under general anaesthetic to exclude juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
Apply topical antiseptic ointment (Naseptin or paraffin) twice daily for 2 weeks plus reinforce first aid technique (pinch the soft part of the nose, lean forward, 10 to 15 minutes)
Perform bedside silver nitrate cautery bilaterally to Little area today with topical antibiotic ointment for 1 week
Insert an anterior Merocel nasal pack into the right nostril and remove at 48 hours in the GP rooms
Commence oral tranexamic acid three times daily for 6 weeks as antifibrinolytic prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Paediatric epistaxis - first aid and management

stem:
A 4-year-old girl presents to her GP with a 3-day history of a tender red swelling in front of the right ear. Her mother reports a small pit in front of the right ear since birth that has occasionally discharged a small amount of fluid but has never been red or swollen before. On examination there is a 1.5 cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant swelling immediately anterior to the right ear at the level of the helical root, centred over a visible pit.

The pinna, ear canal and tympanic membrane are normal. There is no facial nerve weakness, no cervical lymphadenopathy and no parotid swelling. She is afebrile and otherwise well. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 22 /min
data_table.Examination: 1.5 cm tender erythematous fluctuant swelling over visible right preauricular pit; normal pinna, EAC and TM; no facial nerve weakness; no parotid swelling

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan now, and what is the appropriate timing of definitive surgery?

options.text: Oral di/flucloxacillin six-hourly for 7 days now, with incision and drainage if not settling at 48 to 72 hours; refer to ENT for elective complete sinus excision once the acute infection has fully resolved (typically 6 weeks)
Urgent total parotidectomy on suspicion of an infected first branchial cleft anomaly with facial nerve involvement
Reassurance and review only if the lesion enlarges or discharges further
Express the sinus contents by firm squeezing today plus topical mupirocin 2% three times daily for 7 days
Same-day complete excision of the sinus tract under general anaesthesia with antibiotic cover

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the GP with his fourth episode of severe sore throat in 8 months. Each episode has lasted 5-7 days with fever above 38.5 deg C, white tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. In total over the past 12 months he has had four documented episodes of tonsillitis. Each episode has been seen by a clinician with positive examination findings consistent with bacterial tonsillitis and treated with a course of oral antibiotics (phenoxymethylpenicillin).

The family reports significant school absence and parental work disruption. There is no history of obstructive sleep apnoea, no failure to thrive and no immunodeficiency. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Examination today shows large, partially scarred tonsils with no acute exudate. He is afebrile. The family asks specifically about tonsillectomy referral now, long-term penicillin prophylaxis, a throat swab for asymptomatic strep, and immunology workup for recurrent infections.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 88 bpm, RR 18 /min
data_table.Examination: Large scarred tonsils, no acute exudate, no cervical lymphadenopathy, well grown along 50th centile
data_table.Past history: Four documented episodes of tonsillitis in last 12 months, each clinician-confirmed and antibiotic-treated

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ENT for elective tonsillectomy given that he meets Paradise criteria for surgical management of recurrent severe bacterial tonsillitis in childhood
Continue watchful waiting with documented sore throat diary, treat acute episodes with phenoxymethylpenicillin and reassess against Paradise criteria over the next 12-24 months
Commence long-term oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily prophylaxis for 12 months to suppress recurrent group A streptococcal pharyngitis episodes
Take a throat swab today for group A streptococcus PCR and treat with phenoxymethylpenicillin if positive
Refer to paediatric immunology for assessment of suspected primary immunodeficiency given the four episodes of bacterial tonsillitis in the past 12 months

stem:
A 9-month-old girl is brought to the GP after her grandmother noticed that the left pupil appeared white in a recent flash photograph. The mother reports the eye otherwise looks normal, the baby fixes and follows in good light and reaches for toys with both hands. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth with an unremarkable antenatal course.

The parents do not recall whether the red reflex was specifically examined on the newborn check. There is no family history of retinoblastoma or other eye disease. On examination with an ophthalmoscope held at arm's length the right pupil shows a normal red reflex but the left pupil shows a clearly visible white reflex (leukocoria). There is no strabismus, no nystagmus and no proptosis. The cornea is clear and the anterior chamber appears normal. Visual behaviour is reduced when the right eye is occluded.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 122 bpm, RR 30 /min
data_table.Examination: Left leukocoria with absent red reflex on direct ophthalmoscopy; right red reflex normal; no strabismus; clear cornea; normal anterior chamber

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that white reflex on flash photographs is usually benign and review at the routine 12-month immunisation visit
Refer to a community optometrist for paediatric vision testing in 4 to 6 weeks
Refer urgently (within 24 to 48 hours) to a paediatric ophthalmologist for examination under anaesthetic to assess for retinoblastoma and other causes of leukocoria
Order outpatient MRI brain and orbits under GA as the initial investigation to characterise any intraocular mass before specialist ophthalmology referral
Patch the right (unaffected) eye for 2 hours daily for amblyopia management of the left eye and review in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Red reflex abnormality - leukocoria and retinoblastoma

stem:
A 3-day-old term male infant is brought to ED by his parents because of bilateral profuse purulent eye discharge that began 24 hours ago and is rapidly increasing. He was born by normal vaginal birth at 39+2 weeks weighing 3220 g. The pregnancy was unbooked because the mother (a 19-year-old who recently migrated and was lost to antenatal care) presented in labour at the nearest hospital.

Antenatal STI screening was not performed. The baby has otherwise been feeding and behaving normally. On examination there is profuse yellow-green purulent discharge from both eyes with marked eyelid oedema (chemosis) so pronounced that the lids cannot be readily opened. The cornea on the small visible portion looks slightly hazy on the right. He is afebrile with normal observations. There is no other rash, no hepatosplenomegaly and no other focus of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 148 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral profuse purulent eye discharge, marked chemosis preventing easy lid opening, possible right corneal haze, no rash, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Maternal history: Unbooked pregnancy, no antenatal STI screening, age 19, recently migrated

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Send eye swab for Gram stain, bacterial culture and Chlamydia / Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR, admit, commence IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, perform saline eye irrigation and request urgent paediatric ophthalmology review
Prescribe topical chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops one drop to each eye six-hourly for 7 days and review at the GP clinic the following day to assess improvement
Commence oral azithromycin once daily for 3 days as empirical therapy for likely Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis without admission or specialist input
Reassure the parents that this is most likely chemical (silver nitrate) conjunctivitis from birth, irrigate with normal saline, and review in 48 hours
Apply topical aciclovir 3% eye ointment five times daily for suspected neonatal herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis and arrange paediatric review the following day

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to her GP with 24 hours of progressive left eyelid swelling and redness that started after an insect bite on the eyelid the previous afternoon. She has been afebrile, well, eating and drinking normally. There is no preceding sinusitis and no recent dental infection. On examination she has erythema and swelling of the left upper and lower eyelid with localised tenderness at the bite site, but she can open the eye spontaneously.

Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes, pupillary responses are equal and brisk with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and full eye movements are present with no pain on movement. There is no proptosis, no chemosis and the conjunctiva is white. Otoscopy and oropharyngeal examination are normal. There is no facial nerve weakness and the contralateral eye is normal. The mother specifically asks whether admission for IV antibiotics is needed today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 96 bpm, RR 20 /min
data_table.Examination: Left upper and lower eyelid erythema and swelling, eye opens spontaneously, VA 6/6 bilateral, equal pupils no RAPD, full eye movements painless, no proptosis, no chemosis, white conjunctiva
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone daily, flucloxacillin six-hourly and metronidazole eight-hourly with urgent contrast CT of sinuses and orbits

Commence oral cefalexin or amoxicillin/clavulanate and review at 24 hours with explicit safety-netting for pain on eye movement, restricted movement, proptosis, reduced visual acuity, fever or unwell appearance
Apply warm compresses to the eyelid four-hourly and prescribe topical chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment three-hourly to the affected lid for 7 days without systemic antibiotics
Refer urgently to paediatric ophthalmology for surgical incision and drainage of a suspected lid abscess
Prescribe oral prednisolone daily for 5 days alongside oral antibiotics to reduce eyelid swelling more rapidly and accelerate symptom resolution

subtopic_detail: Periorbital cellulitis - Chandler I outpatient management

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to her GP because her grandmother thinks she has a squint. The mother is unsure. She was born at term, met milestones and has otherwise been well. There is no family history of strabismus, amblyopia or significant refractive error. On examination she has a broad nasal bridge and prominent epicanthic folds. Hirschberg corneal light reflex test is centred symmetrically in both pupils.

The cover-uncover test reveals no movement of either eye when the other is occluded. Eye movements are full in all directions of gaze. Red reflex is normal bilaterally and visual behaviour is age-appropriate with good fixation and following.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 108 bpm, RR 24 /min
data_table.Examination: Broad nasal bridge with prominent epicanthic folds; symmetric Hirschberg corneal light reflex; cover-uncover test no movement; full eye movements; bilateral normal red reflex

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric ophthalmology for examination under anaesthesia and consideration of strabismus surgery

Reassure that this is pseudoesotropia from epicanthic folds, document normal Hirschberg and cover-uncover testing, and book the routine 4-year preschool vision screen; advise return if any new objective squint is noted
Patch the left eye for 2 hours daily for 3 months to prevent amblyopia
Commence topical atropine 1% to the right eye to penalise the dominant eye for presumed left amblyopia
Order outpatient MRI brain and orbits under sedation to exclude a sixth nerve palsy

subtopic_detail: Childhood strabismus - true esotropia versus pseudoesotropia

stem: A 22-month-old boy refuses to crawl after 24 hours of fever and irritability. He is fully immunised. He lies still with the left hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and screams on any movement of it.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 degrees C, HR 178 /min, BP 78/40 mmHg, capillary refill 4 s
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 198 mg/L, hip ultrasound large effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Sepsis pathway, cultures, antibiotics, urgent hip washout
Fluids, vancomycin and meropenem, admit to intensive care
Red cells and urgent contrast MRI before any antibiotic
Paracetamol and reassessment in 4 hours in the resus bay
Ceftriaxone alone, with an arterial line before surgery

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis in unwell child - resuscitation and source control

stem:
A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community presents to the local clinic with a 10 day history of migratory arthritis affecting his right knee, then left ankle and now both wrists. The pain is severe enough to limit weight-bearing. He recalls a sore throat 3 weeks ago that resolved without medical review. He has not had any rash, no nodules and no chorea.

On examination he has warm, tender, swollen wrists bilaterally with limited range of movement; the knee and ankle are no longer involved. There is no rash, no subcutaneous nodules and no abnormal involuntary movements. Cardiovascular examination reveals a soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla that has not previously been documented. Investigations are back. The clinic team asks whether this could be post-streptococcal reactive arthritis, JIA, HSP or Lyme arthritis given the migratory pattern and remote setting.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 deg C, HR 124 bpm, RR 22 /min, BP 102/62 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bilateral warm tender swollen wrists; cardiac apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla; no rash; no nodules; no chorea
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.6, CRP 78 mg/L, ESR 64 mm/h, ASOT 850 IU/mL (elevated), anti-DNase B elevated, echocardiogram shows mild mitral regurgitation with no chamber dilatation
data_table.Past: No previous documented ARF, fully immunised, no penicillin allergy

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis affecting multiple joints in additive pattern without convincing evidence of carditis on echocardiogram in this Aboriginal child from a remote community
Acute rheumatic fever fulfilling Australian modified Jones criteria for a high-risk population with carditis and migratory polyarthritis as a definite first episode in this Aboriginal child
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis polyarticular subtype with incidental cardiac murmur and elevated streptococcal serology unrelated to the migratory arthritis presentation in this school-aged child
Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) presenting with arthritis as the dominant initial feature ahead of any palpable purpuric rash, abdominal pain or renal involvement
Lyme arthritis from Borrelia burgdorferi infection acquired locally in the remote Australian setting

subtopic_detail: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis versus acute rheumatic fever

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to his GP with recurrent severe right-sided epistaxis over 4 months. Each episode lasts over 20 minutes and on two occasions has required ED attendance for anterior packing. He also reports 3 months of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and intermittent right cheek fullness. There is no history of trauma, no significant nose picking and no family history of bleeding disorders.

He is on no medication. He is otherwise well and growing along the 50th centile. Anterior rhinoscopy reveals a pink-grey mass filling the posterior right nasal cavity that bled briskly on attempted swab. Full blood count and coagulation screen are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 84 bpm, RR 16 /min, BP 116/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right posterior nasal pink-grey mass, brisk bleeding on touch, right-sided nasal obstruction, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no facial nerve weakness
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, coagulation screen normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure as benign anterior Little area epistaxis and prescribe topical Naseptin twice daily for 2 weeks with first-aid advice
Attempt bedside biopsy of the visible posterior mass with cup forceps under topical lidocaine to confirm histology before imaging or specialist referral
Refer urgently to ENT and arrange contrast-enhanced MRI or CT of the nasopharynx without biopsy in clinic
Apply silver nitrate cautery to both sides of the nasal septum at Little area today plus topical antibiotic ointment and GP review in 2 weeks
Commence oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily for 6 weeks as definitive antifibrinolytic therapy

subtopic_detail: Adolescent epistaxis - red flags for juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

stem:
A term male infant born at 39+4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth is reviewed on the postnatal ward at 72 hours of age. Birthweight was 3460 g and current weight is 3260 g (5.8 percent loss). He is exclusively breastfed and feeding 3 hourly with audible swallowing, has had 4 wet nappies in the last 24 hours and passed meconium and changing stools.

Mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the cord direct antiglobulin test was negative and cord bilirubin was 38 micromol/L. Maternal serology was unremarkable and there is no family history of haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency or significant neonatal jaundice. The midwife notes that the baby looks visibly yellow to the mid-thigh and orders a serum bilirubin which returns at 340 micromol/L total, with a conjugated fraction of 8 micromol/L. The baby is alert, has a normal Moro and suck, no hepatosplenomegaly, and is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 138 bpm, RR 44 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Visibly jaundiced to mid-thigh, alert, normal tone and Moro, no hepatosplenomegaly, anterior fontanelle soft, no petechiae or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 340 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, Hb 175 g/L, reticulocytes 3 percent, blood group A positive, DAT negative
data_table.Maternal history: Group O positive, antibody screen negative, no maternal infection, no medication exposure

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure, continue breastfeeding on demand and repeat serum bilirubin within 24 hours
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and substitute formula to exclude breast milk jaundice before treating
Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat SBR in 6 hours, exchange if rising towards 450 micromol/L
Arrange immediate double-volume neonatal exchange transfusion in the neonatal unit today
Order abdominal ultrasound and split bilirubin trend to investigate biliary atresia first

stem:
A male infant born at 36+2 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a mother with gestational diabetes on diet control is reviewed on the postnatal ward in a level 4 maternity unit. Birthweight is 2640 g (25th centile). He had skin-to-skin contact from delivery and a first breastfeed at 40 minutes of life. The local hypoglycaemia protocol mandates 3 hourly prefeed BSLs for the first 12 hours in at-risk infants.

At 2 hours of age the prefeed heelprick capillary blood glucose, confirmed on a calibrated point-of-care device, is 1.8 mmol/L. He latches briefly but tires quickly and falls asleep at the breast within 2 minutes. He is pink, has a strong cry on handling, normal tone, and a normal newborn examination with no dysmorphic features, no hepatomegaly, and no respiratory distress.

He has had no jitteriness, no apnoea, and no seizures. He has not yet received expressed colostrum or formula top-up. The mother's last HbA1c was 5.6 percent and she had no insulin during labour. Maternal observations are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C axillary, HR 142 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 98 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink, normal tone, no jitteriness, no respiratory distress, no hepatomegaly, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 1.8 mmol/L at 2 hours of age, prefeed
data_table.Risk factors: Late preterm 36+2, infant of diet-controlled GDM mother, birthweight 25th centile, breastfeeding established but ineffective

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding on demand and recheck BSL in 3 to 4 hours before the next feed
IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus, 10% dextrose infusion at 80 mL/kg/day, continue feeds, recheck BSL 30 min
Offer 5 mL/kg of expressed breast milk or formula by cup and recheck BSL in 30 minutes
Administer IM glucagon 30 microg/kg as a single bolus dose and continue exclusive breastfeeding without recheck
Apply 40 percent buccal dextrose gel 0.5 mL/kg and continue exclusive breastfeeding without recheck

stem:
A 38-year-old G3P2 woman at 41+3 weeks is in second-stage labour when the obstetric team note thick meconium-stained liquor after artificial rupture of membranes. She had two previous uncomplicated vaginal births at term and her current antenatal course was unremarkable with normal serial growth scans and normal screening serology. CTG is reassuring with normal baseline variability and no late or variable decelerations.

The baby is born vaginally 12 minutes later with a single nuchal cord that was easily reduced. At delivery the baby cries vigorously within the first 15 seconds, has good tone with flexed limbs, is pink centrally with peripheral cyanosis, and has a heart rate above 100 bpm by auscultation. There is visible thick meconium on the perineum, on the baby's skin and around the mouth. The neonatal team is present at delivery with a prepared resuscitaire, the radiant warmer is on, and suction is checked. No previous obstetric complications.

data_table.Birth details: Term plus, 41+3 weeks, vaginal birth, thick meconium-stained liquor
data_table.Examination at 30 seconds: Vigorous cry, good tone, HR > 100 bpm, peripheral cyanosis only, visible meconium on skin

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Routine newborn care: drying, warmth, ongoing observation, keep mother and baby together
Direct laryngoscopy with tracheal suction before drying or stimulation today
Bag-mask ventilation with 21 percent oxygen for 60 seconds and reassess heart rate
Intubate, suction the trachea and transfer to NICU for prophylactic CPAP
Bulb suction the oropharynx and nasopharynx on the perineum before delivery of the shoulders

stem:
A male infant born at 28+1 weeks by emergency caesarean for severe pre-eclampsia and absent end-diastolic flow on Doppler is now day 7 of life in the level 3 NICU of a tertiary perinatal centre. Mother received a full course of antenatal betamethasone and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection. Birthweight was 1040 g (25th centile for gestation). He has been receiving minimal enteral feeds of expressed breast milk at 20 mL/kg/day for 4 days, advanced cautiously, and parenteral nutrition via a peripherally inserted central catheter; umbilical lines were removed on day 4.

He is on nasal CPAP with FiO2 0.21 after extubation from surfactant therapy on day 2. Over the last 6 hours the nurses note new abdominal distension, two episodes of bilious aspirate, a single small bloody stool and a temperature instability with a low of 36.1 deg C. On examination he is mottled with a capillary refill of 4 seconds, the abdomen is tense and tender with visible bowel loops, and there is mild erythema of the abdominal wall.

The treating team obtains a supine abdominal radiograph and a left lateral decubitus film, plus blood cultures, a venous gas and a full blood count.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.1 deg C, HR 178 bpm, RR 70 /min on CPAP FiO2 0.21, SpO2 91 percent
data_table.Examination: Mottled, tense distended tender abdomen, visible bowel loops, abdominal wall erythema, lethargic
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.2 x10^9/L, platelets 78 x10^9/L, CRP 65 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: Supine AXR shows dilated bowel loops with intramural curvilinear lucencies; left lateral decubitus film shows no free intraperitoneal gas; no portal venous gas seen

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue current feeds, add oral probiotic, and repeat AXR in 24 hours
Increase enteral feed volume to advance gut maturation and start oral gentamicin for bowel decontamination
Urgent laparotomy with bowel resection for suspected NEC-related intestinal perforation today
Cease feeds, large-bore OG free drainage, IV benzylpenicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole, fluid resuscitation, surgical review
Cease feeds, give a single dose of IV cefotaxime and continue monitoring without surgical review

stem:
A male infant born at 39+0 weeks by elective caesarean section without labour is admitted to the special care nursery at 1 hour of life for ongoing respiratory distress. Birthweight 3520 g, APGARs 8 and 9. He developed tachypnoea, mild grunting and intercostal recession from 15 minutes of age. He is now 4 hours old on nasal high-flow at 6 L/min with FiO2 0.30, maintaining SpO2 96 percent preductal and 96 percent postductal.

Mother had a negative group B Strep screen, no fever, no prolonged rupture of membranesplications; no meconium-stained liquor. T 36.9 deg C, HR 152, RR 78, BP 62/40 with capillary refill 2 seconds and warm peripheries. Chest is clear with no asymmetry. Chest radiograph at 30 minutes showed hyperinflation, prominent perihilar streaking, fluid in the right horizontal fissure, and no air bronchograms or focal consolidation.

He has not yet fed. Blood gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 48 mmHg, BE -2. Sepsis bloods are pending. You are confident this is transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN).

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 152 bpm, RR 78 /min, SpO2 97 percent on high-flow FiO2 0.25
data_table.Examination: Mild grunting, intercostal recession, equal air entry bilaterally, no asymmetry, no scaphoid abdomen, normal peripheral pulses
data_table.Imaging: CXR: hyperinflation, prominent perihilar vascular streaking, fluid in the right horizontal fissure, no air bronchograms, no focal consolidation, no pneumothorax

lead_in: Which next management step is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue nasal high-flow titrated to SpO2 91-95 percent, nil by mouth on IV maintenance, reassess at 72 hours
Administer endotracheal surfactant via the INSURE technique now, given the persisting FiO2 requirement at 4 hours of postnatal life
Commence empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending blood culture results and continue the current respiratory support level
Wean nasal high-flow off now and commence demand breastfeeding to encourage fetal lung-fluid clearance and feeding tolerance
Urgently transfer to a tertiary neonatal intensive care unit for elective intubation and mechanical ventilation now

stem:
A term female infant born at 39+5 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth is reviewed at 12 hours of age on the postnatal ward. Mother is a 28-year-old G2P1 who had a positive GBS rectovaginal swab at 36 weeks of gestation and was penicillin allergic with a remote history of a non-anaphylactic rash documented in her records; she received two doses of IV cefazolin intrapartum, the second dose 6 hours before delivery.

Membranes were ruptured for 20 hours. Maternal temperature peaked at 38.2 deg C during labour and white cell count was 16 x10^9/L. The baby is now lethargic with poor feeding for the last 3 hours, has had one episode of grunting respiration with transient desaturation, and looks pale and mottled. She was previously well from birth, with APGARs 9 and 9, no resuscitation required, and birthweight 3300 g.

The receiving registrar reviews her promptly and recognises the combination of maternal fever, prolonged ROM and clinical deterioration as warranting urgent septic workup and empirical antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.2 deg C axillary, HR 178 bpm, RR 70 /min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, BP 58/32 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, pale, mild grunting, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: FBC, blood culture and CRP taken; lumbar puncture deferred pending stabilisation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV cefotaxime twelve-hourly as initial empirical monotherapy
IV benzylpenicillin 12-hourly plus gentamicin every 24 hours
IV flucloxacillin 6-hourly plus gentamicin every 24 hours
IV vancomycin 12-hourly plus cefotaxime 12-hourly
Withhold antibiotics and observe 4-hourly for 12 hours given intrapartum cefazolin

stem:
A term female infant is born at 38+4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth with a birthweight of 2360 g (below the 3rd centile), a head circumference of 31.5 cm (below the 3rd centile), and scattered petechiae on the trunk and limbs noted on first examination. APGARs were 8 and 9 and no resuscitation was required. The mother is a 24-year-old preschool teacher who had a flu-like illness with malaise, sore throat and mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy at around 14 weeks gestation; the GP attributed it to a viral URTI and routine maternal serology was not repeated and TORCH screening was not done.

On day 2 of life, the baby has a moderately enlarged liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, a spleen tip palpable, mild conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and thrombocytopenia on FBC. A cranial ultrasound performed by the neonatologist shows scattered periventricular calcifications and mild ventricular dilatation, prompting paediatric infectious diseases review. Initial automated otoacoustic emission screen on day 2 is REFER bilaterally and is repeated next day with the same result.

Audiology brainstem testing is pending. The treating team obtains urine and saliva PCR samples within the first week of life to confirm the suspected diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 150 bpm, RR 48 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: SGA, microcephaly, petechiae on trunk, hepatomegaly 3 cm, mild jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 62 x10^9/L, total bilirubin 110 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 35 micromol/L, ALT 90 U/L, AST 120 U/L
data_table.Imaging: Cranial ultrasound: periventricular calcifications, mild ventricular dilatation
data_table.Microbiology: Saliva and urine CMV PCR collected on day 3 of life

lead_in: Once congenital CMV is confirmed by PCR within 21 days of life, what is the single most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Oral valganciclovir twice daily for 6 months with weekly FBC/LFT and audiology
Observe with serial audiology, no antiviral, treat only confirmed progressive hearing loss after 12 months
Commence IV ganciclovir twice daily for 6 weeks followed by no further therapy
CMV hyperimmune globulin infusion and arrange paediatric infectious diseases service review today
Treat only audiological component with hearing aid fitting after ABR; provide no antiviral therapy

stem:
A male infant is born at 38+1 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a 21-year-old G1P0 woman from a remote community who had limited antenatal care, with her first antenatal visit at 34 weeks of gestation. Routine antenatal screening at that visit returned a reactive treponemal EIA, a non-treponemal RPR titre of 1 in 64, and confirmatory TPPA positive. The mother received a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 million units) at 35 weeks of gestation and a planned second dose was missed because she returned to her community without follow-up.

There is no documented prior syphilis treatment and contact tracing of her partner is incomplete. Repeat RPR at 38 weeks remained 1 in 64 with no fourfold drop. HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C serology were negative. At birth the baby weighs 2680 g (10th centile), has a maculopapular rash on the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly with the liver palpable 3 cm and spleen 2 cm below the costal margins, and clear persistent rhinorrhoea (snuffles). He is alert with normal vital signs and no respiratory distress. APGARs were 8 and 9.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 144 bpm, RR 46 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: SGA, maculopapular rash palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, clear nasal discharge (snuffles), no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Infant RPR titre 1 in 128 (fourfold higher than maternal), FBC platelets 120 x10^9/L, ALT 70 U/L, long bone radiographs show metaphyseal lucencies; LP CSF VDRL pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate treatment regimen for this infant?

options.text: Single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin with outpatient RPR follow-up at 3, 6, 12 months
Oral azithromycin daily for 14 days as macrolide cover for spirochaete infection
Defer treatment until FTA-ABS IgM positive and CSF VDRL reported, then treat only if both confirm
IV benzylpenicillin q12h first 7 days then q8h, total 10 days, monitor reaction
IV ceftriaxone once daily for 10 days as a penicillin-sparing regimen today

stem:
A male infant is born at 38+5 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a 32-year-old G3P2 woman on methadone 80 mg daily through pregnancy as part of an established opioid treatment program at a metropolitan tertiary centre. She has been engaged with antenatal care and the perinatal addictions team throughout pregnancy, attending all scheduled appointments and counselling sessions. There is no other substance use on serial urine drug screens, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology are negative, and she has tested negative for syphilis.

She smokes 5 cigarettes daily and uses no alcohol. Birthweight is 3120 g (50th centile) and APGARs were 8 and 9 with no resuscitation required. He is breastfeeding well with audible swallows. From 36 hours of age the midwives note increasing irritability, a high-pitched cry, frequent yawning, mild tremor with handling, loose stools that have caused excoriation around the buttocks, and a sleep period of less than one hour after a feed.

Modified Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring System scores done 4-hourly have been 9, 11 and 10 over the last 12 hours despite optimised non-pharmacological care including swaddling, low stimulation environment, demand breastfeeding, and skin-to-skin contact.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1 deg C, HR 168 bpm, RR 60 /min, SpO2 99 percent on room air
