data_table.Examination: Tremulous with handling, mottled, hyperreflexic, no seizures, loose yellow stools, excoriation over the chin, breastfeeding established
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 3.4 mmol/L, FBC and CRP normal, maternal toxicology positive for methadone only

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to formula feeding and continue non-pharmacological care alone without any pharmacotherapy
Commence oral phenobarbital as monotherapy for opioid withdrawal syndrome
Administer naloxone IM to reverse residual maternal opioid effects in the neonate
Discharge home now with community midwife follow-up and a parent-completed NAS scoring sheet
Optimise non-pharmacological care and commence oral morphine q4h titrated to Finnegan below 8

stem:
A male infant is born at 40+1 weeks by emergency caesarean for placental abruption after a sentinel maternal collapse 25 minutes before delivery; the mother presented to a regional birthing unit with sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding and was transferred urgently to theatre when the CTG showed prolonged bradycardia at 60 bpm. Estimated time of insult to delivery is 22 minutes.

APGARs were 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes and 5 at 10 minutes. Cord arterial gas shows pH 6.92, base deficit 18 mmol/L, and lactate 11 mmol/L. He required positive pressure ventilation from birth, intubation at 4 minutes for ongoing bradycardia, and three doses of intratracheal then intravenous adrenaline 10 microg/kg via emergency umbilical venous catheter before return of spontaneous circulation at 8 minutes.

He is now 45 minutes old, intubated on conventional ventilation in the NICU at a tertiary centre with active servo-controlled cooling preparations underway, including a cooling mattress and oesophageal probe. He has reduced spontaneous activity with intermittent generalised tonic posturing of the limbs lasting around 20 seconds, sluggish pupils that are 3 mm and equally reactive, a weak suck and absent gag, and an exaggerated Moro reflex with prolonged opening.

His axillary temperature on arrival was 36.4 deg C and the team has held active warming, allowing passive cooling, while preparing servo-controlled cooling. There is no congenital anomaly, no major birth trauma, and no clinical evidence of bleeding. The treating consultant must decide on definitive neuroprotective therapy in the next 15 minutes, well within the 6 hour therapeutic window from birth.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4 deg C axillary on arrival, HR 130 bpm post-resuscitation, mean BP 38 mmHg on dobutamine 5 microg/kg/min, SpO2 95 percent on FiO2 0.4
data_table.Examination: Reduced activity, intermittent tonic posturing, weak suck, absent gag, exaggerated Moro, hypotonia in limbs, sluggish pupils, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Cord gas: Arterial pH 6.92, base deficit 18 mmol/L, lactate 11 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Permit passive cooling to 35.5 deg C until 24 hours of age then rewarm over 12 hours
Maintain strict normothermia 36.5-37.5 deg C and commence prophylactic phenobarbital loading dose
Whole-body therapeutic hypothermia 33-34 deg C for 72 hours with aEEG, rewarm 12 hours, phenobarbital for seizures
Initiate selective head cooling with cap to scalp temperature 28 deg C for 48 hours and rapid rewarming
Delay cooling for 12 hours pending MRI brain, commence hypothermia only if injury confirmed

stem:
A male infant is born at 40+3 weeks after a labour complicated by thick meconium-stained liquor and a non-reassuring CTG with late decelerations in the second stage. Birthweight is 3680 g. APGARs were 4 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. He required brief positive pressure ventilation in the delivery room and is now 6 hours old in the level 3 NICU at a tertiary perinatal centre, on conventional ventilation with FiO2 0.85, peak inspiratory pressure 24 cm H2O, PEEP 6 cm H2O, mean airway pressure 14 cm H2O, and an oxygenation index of 22 calculated from an arterial blood gas with PaO2 50 mmHg.

Preductal SpO2 measured on the right hand is 92 percent and postductal SpO2 on the right foot is 78 percent, a sustained difference of 14 percent. Chest radiograph shows patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation consistent with meconium aspiration. Urgent echocardiography by the neonatal cardiologist shows right-to-left shunting across the patent ductus arteriosus, tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 70 mmHg, septal flattening at end-systole, and structurally normal cardiac anatomy with normal pulmonary venous return on detailed views.

Surfactant 100 mg/kg has already been given via the endotracheal tube. He has a normal capillary refill of 2 seconds on milrinone 0.5 microg/kg/min and dobutamine 5 microg/kg/min, with a mean arterial pressure of 42 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, mean BP 42 mmHg on inotropes, preductal SpO2 92 percent, postductal SpO2 78 percent, T 36.9 deg C
data_table.Ventilation: Conventional ventilation, FiO2 0.85, mean airway pressure 14 cm H2O, oxygenation index 22
data_table.Echocardiography: Right-to-left ductal shunt, RVSP 70 mmHg, septal flattening, structurally normal heart, normal pulmonary veins

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
Inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm via ventilator and reassess oxygenation index after 30-60 min
Switch to high-frequency oscillatory ventilation immediately and avoid pulmonary vasodilators today
Refer immediately for emergency ECMO without commencing iNO or HFOV trial
Commence oral sildenafil every 6 hours as primary pulmonary vasodilator therapy

stem:
A female infant born at 39+3 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth in a rural hospital is now 18 hours old. She had APGARs of 9 and 9 and was initially well, but the midwives have noted increasing central cyanosis over the last 2 hours, particularly with feeds. She remains alert with mild tachypnoea but no respiratory distress and no grunting.

Preductal SpO2 is 78 percent and postductal SpO2 is 76 percent, both on room air. She does not improve on 8 L/min of facemask oxygen, with preductal SpO2 rising only to 84 percent after 10 minutes. Examination reveals a soft 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, palpable femoral pulses, no hepatomegaly, and a normal newborn examination otherwise.

A chest radiograph shows clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette. ECG shows sinus rhythm. The on-call neonatal retrieval consultant accepts the case for transfer.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C, HR 150 bpm, RR 60 /min, BP 64/40 mmHg, preductal SpO2 78 percent room air, 84 percent on 8 L/min O2
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed, alert, mild tachypnoea, 2/6 ESM at LUSE, femoral pulses palpable equally, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hyperoxia test: preductal SpO2 84 percent and PaO2 78 mmHg after 10 minutes of 100 percent oxygen; CXR clear; ECG sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management while awaiting retrieval and echocardiography?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion and prepare for intubation given the risk of apnoea
Continue facemask oxygen at 100 percent and observe for a further 4 hours before any intervention
Commence inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm for presumed persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and arrange transthoracic echo in working hours next morning
Administer indometacin IV to close any patent ductus and reduce shunting

stem:
A term male infant born at 39+6 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth to a 27-year-old G1P0 woman is now 36 hours old on the postnatal ward of a tertiary maternity hospital. APGARs were 9 and 9 and the perinatal course was uncomplicated with no maternal infection, no chorioamnionitis gas (arterial pH 7.32, base deficit 4 mmol/L). Birthweight was 3380 g.

He has been breastfeeding well with audible swallows, with normal heelprick BSLs of 3.0 to 4.5 mmol/L throughout, and has had three wet nappies and meconium passed at 8 hours. At 36 hours he develops sudden onset rhythmic jerking of the right arm and right leg lasting around 90 seconds, with lip smacking and a brief apnoea with desaturation to 88 percent, followed by a similar focal motor seizure 20 minutes later.

He is now post-ictal with reduced tone in the right limbs but rouseable to handling. He has not been cooled and has no risk factors for HIE. Sodium is 138 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.25 mmol/L, magnesium 0.8 mmol/L, BSL 4.2 mmol/L, ammonia 60 micromol/L, blood gas pH 7.36 with normal lactate, and a sepsis screen including blood culture, FBC, CRP and lumbar puncture is in progress. EEG and cranial ultrasound are being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 deg C, HR 158 bpm, RR 50 /min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, BP 70/42 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal, reduced tone right side, rouseable, no dysmorphism, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L, ionised Ca 1.25 mmol/L, Mg 0.8 mmol/L, BSL 4.2 mmol/L, ammonia 60 micromol/L, pH 7.36, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, FBC and CRP normal pending culture

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer rectal diazepam and observe for cessation of seizure activity
Give intravenous calcium gluconate 10% empirically for presumed hypocalcaemic seizure
Commence pyridoxine 100 mg IV and withhold antiepileptic therapy until response is assessed
IV phenobarbital load, blood/urine for metabolic and infection screen, LP, urgent MRI
Initiate therapeutic hypothermia at 33.5 deg C for 72 hours as initial seizure therapy

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 woman is reviewed in the antenatal clinic at 36 weeks gestation by the midwifery and obstetric team. She and her partner have a written birth plan declining intramuscular vitamin K for their baby because of concerns about historical claims linking IM vitamin K with childhood leukaemia. They are willing to consider oral vitamin K as a compromise but want to know the specific regimen and the residual risk.

The pregnancy has been uncomplicated with reassuring serial growth and screening, the mother is on no medications (no anticonvulsants, antibiotics, rifampicin, or anticoagulants), and there are no risk factors for fetal coagulopathy or maternal liver disease. Their first child received IM vitamin K and had no problems. They intend to exclusively breastfeed and the booking is for a planned vaginal birth at 39 weeks. They specifically ask you to compare the oral and IM regimens by Australian guidance and have read that the leukaemia link has been refuted.

data_table.Maternal history: G2P1, no anticoagulants, no antiepileptics, no rifampicin, no significant medical history
data_table.Plan: Booked for vaginal birth at 39 weeks if uncomplicated

lead_in: Which counselling and recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: IM vitamin K 1 mg single dose at birth first-line; if declined, oral 1 mg at birth, day 3-5, and 4 weeks with residual-risk counselling
Recommend a single oral 1 mg vitamin K dose given at birth as an equivalent alternative to IM with comparable late-VKDB protection
Recommend no vitamin K prophylaxis at all, since the historical leukaemia link is refuted and modern Australian background bleeding risk is negligible
Recommend maternal oral vitamin K 20 mg daily from 36 weeks until delivery as a substitute for any neonatal prophylaxis given at birth
Defer the decision until after delivery so the family can meet the baby and decide with the postnatal midwife in the hours after birth

stem:
A male infant is born at 32+0 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth to a 28-year-old G1P0 woman with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 5 days before delivery. She was admitted for monitoring, received prophylactic erythromycin and a course of antenatal corticosteroids; specifically, two doses of antenatal betamethasone with the second dose 48 hours before delivery, and a single dose of magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection commenced 4 hours before delivery.

There was no maternal fever, the CRP remained normal, and the white cell count was 11 x10^9/L pre-delivery. APGARs were 7 and 8 with brief CPAP via T-piece in the delivery room. Birthweight is 1640 g (50th centile for gestation). He is transferred to the level 3 NICU at 10 minutes of age. From birth he has had moderate work of breathing with intercostal recession, mild grunting, and SpO2 of 89 percent in room air.

He is now on nasal CPAP 7 cm H2O with FiO2 0.35 delivered via short binasal prongs, has mild grunting that is gradually improving, and is haemodynamically stable with a mean BP of 38 mmHg. The team prepares to administer surfactant in the next 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 160 bpm, RR 65 /min on CPAP, SpO2 92 percent on FiO2 0.35, BP mean 38 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild grunting and intercostal recession, equal air entry, capillary refill 2 seconds, no peripheral cyanosis
data_table.Antenatal: Single course antenatal betamethasone 48 hours pre-delivery, MgSO4 for neuroprotection, no maternal fever, no chorioamnionitis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate surfactant administration strategy in this infant?

options.text: Continue CPAP without surfactant unless FiO2 rises above 0.6 or work of breathing worsens
Intubate, give surfactant, and continue mechanical ventilation for at least the first 24 hours
Repeat a second course of antenatal corticosteroid postnatally as IM betamethasone to the infant to enhance lung maturation
Give nebulised surfactant via the CPAP circuit over 30 minutes
Continue CPAP and give surfactant via thin catheter using LISA technique with spontaneous breathing

subtopic_detail: Roseola - recognition of post-defervescence rash pattern
stem:
A 14-month-old fully immunised boy is reviewed in suburban general practice after three days of high fever to 39.7 deg C that resolved overnight. He is now afebrile and playful with a blanching, maculopapular, trunk-predominant rash that appeared this morning, sparing face, palms and soles. He has had no cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, oral lesions, or diarrhoea. There is no lymphadenopathy and no meningism, capillary refill is under two seconds, and mucous membranes are moist.

He attends family daycare, where a 4-year-old sibling of another child has confirmed measles diagnosed yesterday by the public health unit and other children with similar fever-then-rash presentations have been seen at this practice in the past fortnight. The MMR vaccine is due at 18 months and has not yet been given. There is no household member who is immunocompromised or pregnant. The mother asks about diagnosis, time off daycare, and whether her son needs anything more.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 deg C (previously 39.7), HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Blanching pink maculopapular rash on trunk/neck, sparing face/palms/soles; no Koplik spots, no conjunctivitis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Immunisations: Up to date for age (MMR not yet due)

lead_in: Which combination of diagnosis and exclusion advice is most appropriate?

options.text: Roseola infantum; he may return to family daycare once afebrile and well, with no formal childcare exclusion period required under Australian guidance
Measles given the daycare contact; exclude from family daycare for 4 days from rash onset and notify the public health unit
Rubella; exclude from family daycare for 7 days from rash onset and arrange confirmatory serology before any return
Scarlet fever; commence oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days and exclude from daycare for 24 hours after starting antibiotics
Roseola infantum; commence oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days and exclude from daycare for the duration of treatment

subtopic_detail: Measles - prodrome and Koplik spots before rash onset
stem:
A 3-year-old unimmunised boy is brought to a regional Victorian emergency department with four days of fever to 39.8 deg C, barking moist cough, profuse coryza, and red watery photophobic eyes. He returned 10 days ago from a 3-week family trip to a rural province in Vietnam. He has no skin rash yet. On examination he is miserable with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, clear nasal discharge, and several 1 to 2 mm bluish-white papules on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa opposite the second molars.

Temperature 39.6 deg C, HR 138, RR 32, SpO2 97 percent room air. He has no rash, no lymphadenopathy, chest is clear, and he is haemodynamically stable. He is currently in an open paediatric ED bay alongside other waiting children, including a 6-month-old infant and a pregnant accompanying parent. You strongly suspect measles based on Koplik spots and the three Cs.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 deg C, HR 138, RR 32, SpO2 97% RA, BP 95/55
data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctivitis, coryza, productive cough, Koplik spots on buccal mucosa; no skin rash yet
data_table.History: Unimmunised; recent travel from Vietnam 10 days ago
data_table.Investigations: Pending

lead_in: Which next step is most appropriate before laboratory confirmation?

options.text: Move him to a negative-pressure single room with airborne and contact precautions, and phone the public health unit to begin notification now
Send measles IgM and PCR (throat swab and urine) and await laboratory confirmation before notifying public health or isolating
Place him in a standard single room with droplet precautions only and await senior review before any notification action
Administer stat MMR vaccine and oral vitamin A 200 000 IU now, then discharge with isolation advice and review tomorrow
Commence empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and admit for full sepsis workup including lumbar puncture before any isolation measures

subtopic_detail: Measles - public health management and contact prophylaxis
stem:
A 4-year-old unimmunised child has measles confirmed on PCR after a maculopapular rash spread from the face caudally over 24 hours. He had three days of fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis before the rash, and Koplik spots were identified at the GP visit the day before rash onset. He attended a community playgroup on the day before his rash appeared and the morning of rash onset, while infectious.

The public health unit has been notified and is contacting the playgroup register. Among the playgroup contacts identified within the 4 hours before to 4 days after his rash, several need urgent post-exposure management decisions. They include: a 5-month-old infant whose mother is rubella-immune but has no documented measles history or serology; a 13-month-old child who received a single dose of MMR five days ago; a 35-year-old pregnant playgroup helper at 22 weeks gestation with no documented measles immunity and a negative measles IgG on urgent serology done this morning; a 7-year-old child with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in week 2 of induction chemotherapy and currently neutropenic; and a 30-year-old playgroup leader born in 1992 with two documented MMR doses on her workplace immunisation record.

data_table.Exposure window: 4 hours before prodrome to 4 days after rash onset (still infectious)
data_table.Contacts requiring decision: 5-month infant; 13-month with one MMR five days ago; pregnant 22-week non-immune helper; 7-year-old on induction chemo for ALL; 30-year-old with 2x MMR documented
data_table.Time since exposure: Within 72 hours for all listed contacts

lead_in: Which post-exposure action for one of the listed playgroup contacts is the single most appropriate?

options.text: Give the 5-month-old infant intramuscular MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure
Give the 13-month-old who had one MMR five days ago an additional MMR dose now as post-exposure prophylaxis
Give the pregnant 22-week non-immune playgroup helper NHIG intramuscularly within 6 days of exposure
Give the 7-year-old with ALL on induction chemotherapy intramuscular MMR within 72 hours of exposure
Give the 30-year-old playgroup leader with two documented MMR doses a third MMR dose as a precautionary booster

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is in week 3 of induction chemotherapy for high-risk B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia at a tertiary paediatric oncology centre. He shared a 1-hour indoor classroom session in the day hospital school room with another child who has since been confirmed by PCR to have early varicella, with a vesicular rash that had been present for less than 24 hours during the session.

The exposure was 36 hours ago. The boy has had no past episode of clinical varicella, no varicella vaccination on his record (his older sibling refused MMRV at 18 months for the family on philosophical grounds and the patient was diagnosed before catch-up), and his pre-treatment baseline varicella IgG was negative on serology drawn before induction. He is currently profoundly neutropenic with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.4 x 10^9/L, has no rash, no fever, and feels well.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 96, RR 20, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Well; no rash, no vesicles, no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.4 x 10^9/L, pre-chemo varicella IgG negative
data_table.History: ALL induction week 3; significant face-to-face exposure 36 hours ago to a child with early varicella

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine within 72 hours of exposure as post-exposure prophylaxis
Administer zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG/VZIG) intramuscularly within 96 hours of exposure as post-exposure prophylaxis
Commence prophylactic oral valaciclovir from day 7 to day 21 post-exposure
Reassurance and observation, treating with intravenous aciclovir only if a rash develops
Send urgent varicella IgG and IgM and decide on prophylaxis based on the result

subtopic_detail: Meningococcal disease - non-blanching rash recognition vs HSP
stem:
A 2-year-old fully immunised girl is brought to a regional emergency department by ambulance after her parents noticed a rapidly spreading rash. Six hours ago she became unwell with fever and irritability; she has now had two episodes of non-bilious vomiting and is increasingly drowsy and floppy. On examination she is grey, mottled, and lethargic with poor central tone. Temperature 38.9 deg C, heart rate 168, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 96% on room air, blood pressure 78/40, capillary refill 5 seconds peripherally and 4 seconds centrally.

There are scattered non-blanching petechiae and several larger irregular purpuric lesions on the trunk, abdomen and proximal limbs that have spread visibly while in the resuscitation cubicle over the last 10 minutes. Her neck is supple but she cries when picked up and her anterior fontanelle is no longer palpable. No focal neurology. She has had no recent URTI, no arthritisay. Her routine immunisations including MenB and MenACWY are up to date as confirmed on the Australian Immunisation Register printout her parents have brought.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 deg C, HR 168, RR 44, SpO2 96% RA, BP 78/40, CRT 5 sec
data_table.Examination: Grey, mottled, drowsy; spreading non-blanching purpuric rash on trunk and proximal limbs
data_table.History: 6h illness; fully immunised including MenB and MenACWY
data_table.Investigations: Pending

lead_in: Which is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Obtain IV or IO access and give IV ceftriaxone without delay
Arrange urgent CT head and then lumbar puncture given the drowsiness and rash
Defer antibiotics until blood cultures are processed to maximise diagnostic yield from cultures
Commence IV hydrocortisone before antibiotics to pre-treat Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal failure
Reassess in 30 minutes after antipyretics as her current immunisations make invasive bacterial illness unlikely

subtopic_detail: Scarlet fever - recognition and antibiotic selection
stem:
A 7-year-old previously well Aboriginal girl from a remote community in the Northern Territory is reviewed during a paediatric outreach clinic in her community with a 2-day history of fever, sore throat and a rash that began today on the neck and chest before spreading to the trunk. She has no cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis. Temperature 38.6 deg C, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent room air, capillary refill under two seconds.

On examination she has a fine, blanching, erythematous papular eruption with a sandpaper texture accentuated in the antecubital and inguinal flexures, prominent fungiform papillae against a coated tongue, exudative tonsillitis, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and circumoral pallor. She has no known drug allergies, is fully immunised, has no history of acute rheumatic fever, and the family confirms she will be staying in community for at least the next two weeks. Throat swab for group A streptococcus has been collected. There is no current penicillin shortage in the community pharmacy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 deg C, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Sandpaper rash with flexural accentuation, strawberry tongue, exudative tonsillitis, tender cervical nodes, circumoral pallor
data_table.History: No allergies; non-remote setting; fully immunised

lead_in: Which first-line antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg (up to 500 mg) twice daily for 10 days, with community follow-up at completion
Single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (900 mg if 20 kg or more, 450 mg if under 20 kg) administered now
Oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg once daily for 10 days as a more palatable equivalent to first-line oral penicillin
Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg (up to 1 g) twice daily for 10 days as initial therapy
Symptomatic care with paracetamol and reassurance, with antibiotics only if the throat swab returns positive in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease - recognition and discrimination from HSV
stem:
A 22-month-old fully immunised girl is reviewed in general practice with three days of low-grade fever to 38.4 deg C, drooling, and reduced oral intake. Her mother noticed today that she has spots on her hands, feet, and inside her mouth. On examination she is alert and well-perfused. Temperature 37.6 deg C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent room air.

There are shallow ulcers on the tongue, buccal mucosa, and posterior pharynx, and several small grey-roofed oval vesicles on an erythematous base on the palms, soles, and dorsa of the hands and feet. There is no lip clustering, no gingival inflammation, and no lymphadenopathy. The nappy area shows a few similar vesicles. Mucous membranes are slightly dry but she has just taken 50 mL of cold water in clinic.

There is a known outbreak of vesicular illness at her childcare centre that includes one recent admission to the local children's hospital. You diagnose hand-foot-and-mouth disease. Her mother asks what to do about childcare attendance and what warning signs would warrant urgent return.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 deg C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Oval grey-roofed vesicles on palms/soles/dorsa of hands and feet, shallow oral ulcers including posterior pharynx, sparse nappy-area lesions
data_table.History: Childcare outbreak; fully immunised; no prior cold sores

lead_in: Which combination of childcare exclusion advice and red-flag escalation criteria is most appropriate?

options.text: Exclude from childcare until all blisters have dried; return urgently for vomiting, ataxia, myoclonus, or reduced wet nappies
Exclude from childcare only until afebrile for 24 hours, then return regardless of any remaining skin lesions
No childcare exclusion required as HFMD is self-limiting; return whenever the child is willing and able
Commence oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days and exclude from childcare for the duration of treatment
Admit now for IV fluids and serial neurological observations, given the childcare outbreak link to EV71

subtopic_detail: Pregnant contact of parvovirus B19 - obstetric implications
stem:
A 32-year-old early childhood teacher at 18 weeks of her second pregnancy attends her GP after multiple confirmed cases of erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek) in the kindergarten class she teaches over the past fortnight. She had close prolonged indoor contact with two affected children one week ago, before they were excluded with their characteristic facial erythema and lacy peripheral rash.

She is asymptomatic with no rash, arthralgia or fever. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated and her 4-year-old is in her class. Her 18-week morphology scan last week showed structurally normal anatomy with appropriate growth and amniotic fluid volume, and her first-trimester combined screen was low risk. She has no documented past clinical history of slapped cheek and no parvovirus B19 serology on file.

Vital signs are normal, fundal height is consistent with dates, and her physical examination is unremarkable. She specifically asks whether she needs immediate fetal medicine referral or whether further blood tests come first.

data_table.Examination: Normal, no rash, gravid uterus at fundal height consistent with dates
data_table.History: 18 weeks pregnant; significant occupational exposure to confirmed parvovirus B19 1 week ago; no documented prior serology

lead_in: Which next investigation or referral is most appropriate?

options.text: Maternal parvovirus B19 IgG and IgM serology now, with further action determined by the IgG and IgM pattern
Immediate referral to maternal fetal medicine for weekly MCA Doppler velocimetry from now for 12 weeks regardless of serology
Urgent amniocentesis with parvovirus B19 PCR on amniotic fluid now to confirm or exclude vertical fetal transmission
Intramuscular normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG) administered within 7 days of exposure as parvovirus post-exposure prophylaxis
Reassure and discharge as parvovirus B19 has no documented effect on a pregnancy past 12 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Tinea corporis vs pityriasis rosea - discrimination and management
stem:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to general practice with a 10-day history of an enlarging itchy rash on the right side of his trunk. It began as a single oval pink scaly patch about 4 cm across, with a slightly raised edge and clearing centre. Over the last week several smaller similar pink scaly patches have appeared on his back, both flanks, and proximal arms.

He plays competitive judo and shares mats and rashguards weekly with several teammates. One teammate has had a similar-looking rash on the arm for several weeks. He is otherwise well, afebrile, and has no preceding URTI symptoms. There is no mucosal involvement. Examination shows scaly annular lesions with active erythematous scaly borders and central clearing; the original 'herald' lesion is the largest.

There is no Christmas-tree distribution along the lines of Langer, no oral ulceration. Direct mycological microscopy of skin scrapings from a border lesion is positive for septate hyphae.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 86, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Multiple annular scaly lesions with raised active scaly border and central clearing on trunk and proximal arms; largest 'herald' lesion 4 cm
data_table.Investigations: Skin scraping microscopy: septate hyphae present
data_table.History: Shared judo mats; teammate with similar rash

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Reassurance, emollient, and observation for 6 to 8 weeks for self-resolution
Topical terbinafine 1% cream twice daily for 2 weeks beyond the visible border
Oral griseofulvin for 6 weeks given the multiple lesions and contact sport
Topical hydrocortisone 1% twice daily for the inflammatory component plus oral antihistamines
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and exclusion from sport for presumed superficial bacterial infection

subtopic_detail: Erythema multiforme vs Stevens-Johnson syndrome - recognition and triage
stem:
An 11-year-old boy presents to a paediatric emergency department with a rash and oral pain. He started oral lamotrigine 3 weeks ago after a recent diagnosis of focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation, and the dose was rapidly titrated by his treating neurologist alongside ongoing sodium valproate, which he had been taking for 6 months. He has had no other new medications, no recent herpes simplex outbreak, and no recent Mycoplasma-like respiratory illness.

Over the last 36 hours he has developed a flu-like prodrome with fever to 38.7 deg C, malaise, photophobia, and a sore mouth and eyes. Today the rash has spread rapidly. On examination he is unwell, mildly tachycardic, with temperature 38.6 deg C, heart rate 124, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% room air, and BP 105/65. There are confluent dusky erythematous macules with central duskiness and bullae forming on the trunk and proximal limbs covering an estimated 8% body surface area, with sloughing on light lateral pressure on intact-appearing skin.

He has haemorrhagic crusting of the lips, painful ulcers on the buccal mucosa and palate, bilateral red painful eyes with conjunctival injection and mucopurulent discharge, and dysuria with genital erosions visible on inspection. There are some flat lesions on the palms but no classic three-zone targets. He is alert, distressed, and able to drink only sips.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 deg C, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 98% RA, BP 105/65
data_table.Examination: Dusky macules with central blistering on 8% BSA, positive lateral skin shear (Nikolsky), mucous membrane involvement of mouth, eyes, and genitals
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine started 3 weeks ago, rapidly titrated

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch lamotrigine to oral carbamazepine and start IV ceftriaxone for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Continue lamotrigine at half dose and start oral prednisolone for presumed erythema multiforme major
Commence empirical IV aciclovir and admit to a general paediatric ward for HSV-associated erythema multiforme major
Cease lamotrigine immediately, admit to a paediatric burns/HDU service, and consult ophthalmology and dermatology urgently
Reassure, advise paracetamol, and arrange neurology review in 2 weeks for lamotrigine dose review

subtopic_detail: Atypical exanthem with shock - differentiating toxin-mediated rashes
stem:
A 6-year-old previously well fully immunised girl is brought to a tertiary paediatric emergency department by her parents. Five days ago she had varicella that was treated supportively at home, with the rash now beginning to crust over and no new lesions for 48 hours. Three days ago she developed pain in her left thigh which has been progressively worsening - she now refuses to bear weight on that leg and her parents describe the pain as seeming out of proportion to the modest external skin changes they can see.

Over the last 12 hours she has become febrile to 39.8 deg C, vomited twice without diarrhoea, and developed a diffuse blanching macular erythematous rash particularly on the trunk and the affected thigh. On arrival she is grey, mottled, and confused, with temperature 39.6 deg C, heart rate 178, respiratory rate 48, SpO2 95% on room air, BP 70/35, and capillary refill 6 seconds in the limbs and 5 seconds centrally.

Her left thigh has a 6 x 8 cm area of dusky erythema overlying a healing varicella lesion, with marked tenderness extending well beyond the visible erythema and a small area of skin anaesthesia centrally. There is no obvious crepitus on the limb. Bloods show WCC 24 x 10^9/L with marked left shift, CRP 285 mg/L, lactate 5.6 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L (baseline normal), ALT 240 U/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, and platelets 92 x 10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 deg C, HR 178, RR 48, SpO2 95% RA, BP 70/35, CRT 6 sec
data_table.Examination: Diffuse blanching erythroderma, dusky tender 6 x 8 cm patch on thigh overlying healing varicella, pain extending beyond erythema, focal skin anaesthesia
data_table.Investigations: WCC 24, CRP 285 mg/L, lactate 5.6, creatinine 110, ALT 240
data_table.History: Varicella 5 days ago, now crusting

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: MRI of the left thigh before intervention to delineate the extent of soft tissue involvement
Admit, commence IVIG 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus high-dose aspirin for atypical Kawasaki disease
Empirical IV aciclovir monotherapy for disseminated varicella with secondary haemodynamic compromise and septic shock
Commence oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and admit to a general paediatric ward for scarlet fever observation
Resuscitate, give IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin and clindamycin, and call surgery for urgent debridement

stem:
A 4-month-old, ex-39-week, fully vaccinated, formula-fed girl is brought to a regional ED by her mother after 24 hours of fever to 38.7 degC and increased irritability with poor feeding. There is no cough, coryza, rash, vomiting or diarrhoea. She was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth and discharged on day 2. Antenatal ultrasounds were reported as normal. She has had no previous febrile illnesses and is thriving on the 50th centile for weight.

On arrival she is alert, well perfused, has a flat fontanelle, clear chest and a soft non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses. Vitals: T 38.5 degC, HR 158, RR 38, SpO2 99% RA, cap refill 2 s. The triage nurse asks how to collect a urine sample. The local pathway specifies that any positive urine result must be confirmed on a sample suitable for accurate culture and quantitative colony count (Kass criteria) before committing to a treatment course. The mother is happy to wait. She has no urinary catheter contraindications and no coagulopathy. A bedside ultrasound machine is available.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.5 degC, HR 158, RR 38, SpO2 99% RA, cap refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, fontanelle flat, chest clear, abdomen soft, no flank mass
data_table.Investigations: Nil sent; awaiting urine collection

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate urine collection method?

options.text: Adhesive perineal bag urine sample for microscopy and culture
In-out urethral catheter specimen for microscopy and culture
Clean catch midstream urine after gentle suprapubic stimulation
Suprapubic bladder aspiration performed under bedside ultrasound guidance
Cotton wool ball squeezed from nappy onto dipstick

stem:
An 8-week-old, ex-38-week, breastfed boy is brought to a metropolitan ED by his parents with 18 hours of fever to 38.6 degC, increased fussiness and reduced feeding. There is no cough, rash, vomiting or diarrhoea. His birth was uncomplicated; maternal GBS was negative; he received vitamin K and hepatitis B at birth. Routine antenatal ultrasounds showed no renal tract abnormality.

He is on the 25th centile for weight and is thriving. On arrival he is alert, settles to feed but tires quickly. Examination: T 38.4 degC, HR 162, RR 48, SpO2 99 percent RA, cap refill 2 s, fontanelle flat, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft, circumcision recent and clean. A catheter urine specimen shows leucocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, microscopy 200 WBC per high power field with Gram-negative rods.

Bloods: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 8.4, CRP 42 mg/L, venous lactate 1.2 mmol/L, glucose 4.6 mmol/L, sodium 137. The ED registrar has commenced IV access and given a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degC, HR 162, RR 48, SpO2 99% RA, cap refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Alert, tires with feeds, fontanelle flat, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine: LE+, nitrites+, 200 WBC/HPF, GNR. WCC 14.2, CRP 42, lactate 1.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home on oral trimethoprim with GP review in 24 hours
Admit for nasogastric fluids and observation without antibiotics pending culture
Short-stay observation on oral cefalexin and discharge if afebrile at 6 hours
Admit for IV ceftriaxone monotherapy without performing a lumbar puncture today
Admit for IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and perform a lumbar puncture

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents to her GP for review after a third culture-confirmed E. coli UTI in 12 months. The first episode at 18 months was treated with oral trimethoprim with rapid recovery; the second at 2 years required a 48-hour admission with IV gentamicin for fever, vomiting and a CRP of 110 mg/L. The current episode resolved after 5 days of oral cefalexin.

She is now well, afebrile, growing along the 50th centile and is fully toilet trained without daytime wetting. She has no constipation, no abnormal voiding patternc reflux and no antenatal renal abnormality on the 20-week scan. A renal tract ultrasound performed two days ago showed normal kidney size with no hydronephrosis, normal corticomedullary differentiation and complete bladder emptying.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 mmHg, afebrile
data_table.Examination: Normal genitalia, no flank tenderness, no palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Urea 4.2, creatinine 32, eGFR normal. Renal USS normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound and paediatric nephrology referral for recurrent UTI per the RCH Melbourne pathway
DMSA renal scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for cortical scarring after the most recent infection in this child
Micturating cystourethrogram with fluoroscopy now to grade vesicoureteric reflux severity in this recurrent UTI child
MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess differential renal function and exclude obstructive drainage in this 3-year-old patient
Non-contrast CT urogram to evaluate the renal cortex and collecting system for any anatomical abnormality or scarring

stem:
A 9-month-old fully vaccinated boy is brought to his GP with 36 hours of low-grade fever (38.1 deg C) and mild irritability. He has had no rash, vomiting, diarrhoea or cough. He has 5-6 wet nappies a day and is feeding only slightly less than usual. He is otherwise well, on the 50th centile and developmentally normal. There were no antenatal renal concerns.

He is uncircumcised. Examination: alert, well perfused, flat fontanelle, clear chest, soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable bladder, no flank tenderness. T 37.9, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent. The practice nurse applied an adhesive perineal bag for screening urinalysis. Bag urine: LE trace, nitrites negative, blood negative, protein negative, microscopy 8 WBC per high power field with no organisms seen. The lab offers same-day clean-catch processing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.9 degC, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, abdomen soft, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Bag urine: LE trace, nitrites neg, blood neg, protein neg, 8 WBC/HPF

lead_in: How should the bag urine result be interpreted and what is the next step?

options.text: Bag urine has poor specificity but the negative result reliably excludes UTI in this clinical context; discharge with safety-net advice for parents
Commence empirical oral trimethoprim while awaiting a repeat bag specimen for culture confirmation over the next 48 hours of observation
Negative nitrites reliably rule out E. coli UTI in this child given the typical urinary dwell time before bag collection in nappies
Send the bag specimen for culture; a negative culture result will definitively exclude UTI without further sterile sampling required
Bag urine is unreliable for diagnosing or excluding UTI; if suspicion remains, obtain clean catch (catheter if unwell); do not start antibiotics on bag urine

stem:
A 4-year-old boy presents to ED with 72 hours of profuse non-bloody diarrhoea and vomiting after a childcare gastro outbreak. He has had reduced oral intake for 24 hours and only one wet nappy in the last 12 hours. He is normally well, fully immunised, on no medications and has no known renal disease. On arrival he is lethargic with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, cap refill 4 s peripherally, HR 152, BP 86/50, RR 28, T 37.6 degC.

He receives a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus with modest improvement. Bloods: sodium 138, potassium 4.4, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L (baseline 38), bicarbonate 16, lactate 2.8 mmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L. A catheter urine returns sodium 12 mmol/L, creatinine 9.2 mmol/L, osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, no blood, no protein. The calculated fractional excretion of sodium is 0.4 percent. The bedside ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys with no hydronephrosis and a well-filling bladder. He is now passing urine after fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, BP 86/50, cap refill 4 s, T 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Cr 110 (baseline 38), urea 14, FENa 0.4%, urine osm 620, urine Na 12, no casts; USS normal

lead_in: Which AKI pattern best fits these findings?

options.text: Postrenal AKI from functional bladder outlet obstruction
Intrinsic AKI from established acute tubular necrosis with isosthenuria
Prerenal AKI from hypovolaemia with preserved tubular sodium reabsorption
Acute interstitial nephritis from a recent medication exposure
Acute glomerulonephritis with active nephritic urinary sediment

stem:
A 3-week-old boy is brought to a tertiary ED by his parents with poor feeding, lethargy and a weak urinary stream that his father has noticed only dribbles rather than arcs. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth. The 20-week morphology scan was reported as showing mild bilateral pelvicalyceal dilatation with a thickened bladder wall, but follow-up was delayed due to a family interstate move.

He has not had a postnatal renal tract ultrasound. He is exclusively breastfed and has lost 12 percent of his birth weight since birth. On examination he is lethargic with mottled peripheries, cap refill 4 s, HR 168, RR 60, BP 64/40, T 36.4 degC, weight 2.8 kg (10th centile). The abdomen is distended with a palpable suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion and a palpable left kidney.

Genitalia are normal male. Bloods: sodium 128, potassium 7.4, urea 28 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L, bicarbonate 12, pH 7.18, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. He has had 5 mL urine output in the last 6 hours and the bedside scanner shows a grossly distended bladder with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and trabeculated bladder wall.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 60, BP 64/40, cap refill 4 s, T 36.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, distended bladder, palpable kidney, normal male genitalia
data_table.Investigations: K 7.4, urea 28, Cr 220, HCO3 12, pH 7.18, lactate 4.6; bladder distended, bilateral hydronephrosis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for primary cystoscopic posterior urethral valve ablation now
Commence furosemide infusion to drive urine output
Insert an 8 Fr feeding tube urethrally to decompress the bladder
Arrange urgent percutaneous bilateral nephrostomy drainage under fluoroscopic guidance for upper-tract decompression
Give IV calcium gluconate plus salbutamol then arrange urgent haemodialysis transfer

stem:
A 6-year-old girl with biopsy-naive nephrotic syndrome diagnosed 5 weeks ago has been on oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily since presentation. Her initial presentation was typical: oedema, UPCR 520 mg/mmol, albumin 16 g/L, normal C3 and C4, no haematuria, normal blood pressure and normal renal function. She has remained compliant per home dosing diary and parental observation. At 4 weeks she remained heavily proteinuric (UPCR 460 mg/mmol) and albumin 19 g/L; methylprednisolone pulses 600 mg/m2 IV daily for 3 days were given according to local protocol with no remission.

She is now Cushingoid, has BP 124/78 mmHg (over the 95th centile), urea 7.2 mmol/L, creatinine 64 micromol/L (baseline 30), albumin 18 g/L, UPCR 480 mg/mmol. Repeat C3 and C4 are normal. Hepatitis B and C serology, HIV, ANA and dsDNA are all negative. She has had no recent infections. Family history is negative for renal disease and there is no consanguinity.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg (>95th centile), afebrile
data_table.Examination: Cushingoid, persistent oedema
data_table.Investigations: UPCR 480, albumin 18, Cr 64 (baseline 30), C3/C4 normal, serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current prednisolone dose for a further 4 weeks and reassess
Commence empirical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus) without further investigation
Arrange percutaneous renal biopsy with genetic testing for podocyte gene panel
Switch to rituximab induction and taper prednisolone over 12 weeks
Add ACE inhibitor and cease steroids given Cushingoid features

stem:
A 7-year-old boy presents to ED with 2 days of dark cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and headache. Three weeks ago he had a sore throat treated symptomatically with paracetamol; throat swab at the time was not performed. He has had no abdominal pain, joint swelling, rash, recent travel or family history of renal disease. He was previously well and is fully immunised.

On examination he is alert, has periorbital and pretibial oedema, BP 138/88 mmHg (above the 99th centile for age and height), HR 88, RR 20, T 36.9 degC. There is no purpuric rash, no joint swelling, abdomen is soft and non-tender. Urinalysis: blood 4+, protein 2+, leucocytes negative, nitrites negative; microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts. Bloods: urea 9.4 mmol/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, C3 0.42 g/L (low), C4 0.20 g/L (normal), ASO titre elevated at 800 IU/mL, anti-DNase B elevated. ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM are negative. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/88 mmHg (>99th centile), HR 88, T 36.9
data_table.Examination: Periorbital + pretibial oedema, no purpura, no arthritis
data_table.Investigations: Blood 4+, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts. Cr 76, low C3, normal C4, ASO 800, anti-DNase B raised

lead_in: Which finding most strongly supports post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis over IgA nephropathy or HSP nephritis?

options.text: Low C3 with normal C4 after recent pharyngitis
Macroscopic haematuria with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
Haematuria within 1-2 days of a sore throat (synpharyngitic haematuria)
Palpable purpuric rash over extensor surfaces with associated arthralgia
Elevated serum IgA level documented on protein electrophoresis

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is admitted from a regional ED after 6 days of bloody diarrhoea attributed to a daycare gastro outbreak. Stool PCR has confirmed Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157. On day 7 of illness she becomes pale and oliguric with worsening lethargy and one episode of seizure-like jerks lasting 30 seconds. She had been managed with oral rehydration; she received no antibiotics or antimotility agents.

On examination she is pale, has periorbital puffiness, scattered petechiae, T 36.8 degC, HR 132, BP 138/86 mmHg (above the 99th centile for age and height), cap refill 3 s. Bloods: Hb 72 g/L, platelets 38 x10^9/L, blood film shows schistocytes and burr cells, LDH 1620 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, direct Coombs negative, reticulocytes raised. Urea 24 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 35), sodium 132, potassium 5.4, bicarbonate 17, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L. Coagulation profile is normal. Urinalysis: blood 3+, protein 2+, granular casts present.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg (>99th centile), HR 132, cap refill 3 s
data_table.Examination: Pale, periorbital puffiness, scattered petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Hb 72, plt 38, schistocytes, LDH 1620, haptoglobin nil, Coombs neg, Cr 198 (baseline 35), normal coags

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management decision?

options.text: Transfuse one adult-dose platelet pool prophylactically to reduce bleeding risk from petechiae
Initiate urgent plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma replacement therapy daily
Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone to cover ongoing Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
Cautious isotonic fluids, transfuse red cells for symptomatic anaemia, avoid platelets
Give an antimotility agent such as loperamide to reduce diarrhoeal losses

stem:
A 4-year-old boy with day 9 of confirmed Shiga toxin-producing E. coli HUS is on the paediatric ward with worsening biochemistry over 24 hours despite cautious fluid restriction and one red cell transfusion. He has been anuric for 18 hours. He is alert but listless and complaining of nausea. On examination he has scattered petechiae, periorbital and pretibial oedema, mild bibasal crackles, T 36.8 degC, HR 124, RR 38, BP 142/92 mmHg, SpO2 96 percent on room air, weight 18.4 kg (up from admission weight of 17.8 kg).

Bloods now: Hb 78 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, urea 38 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L, sodium 128, potassium 6.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12, pH 7.20, calcium 1.85 mmol/L corrected, phosphate 2.6, lactate 1.8. ECG shows peaked T waves in V2-V5 with QRS still 90 ms. He has been given IV calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol with only partial response (repeat K 6.4). Chest X-ray shows interstitial oedema.

data_table.Examination: Oedema, bibasal crackles, weight up 600 g
data_table.Investigations: K 6.8 -> 6.4 after stabilisation, HCO3 12 pH 7.20, Cr 320, anuric 18 h, CXR pulmonary oedema

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat IV calcium gluconate and continue medical therapy for hyperkalaemia
Commence furosemide infusion to drive a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hr
Give 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus 10 mL/kg to improve renal perfusion
Initiate acute renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis and fluid overload
Add oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate and review potassium in 6 hours

stem:
A 5-year-old girl presents with 4 days of progressive pallor and lethargy. She has had no diarrhoea, no recent travelf bloody stools. There is a family history of a maternal aunt who required dialysis in childhood for an unspecified kidney disease. She had a mild URTI 10 days ago. On examination she is pale, has scattered petechiae, BP 134/84 mmHg (above the 95th centile), HR 122, RR 28, T 37.0 degC, oedema absent.

Bloods: Hb 68 g/L, platelets 32 x10^9/L, blood film with schistocytes and burr cells, LDH 2200 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, direct Coombs negative, reticulocytes high. Urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 184 micromol/L (no baseline available), sodium 134, potassium 4.4, bicarbonate 19. Coags normal, fibrinogen 3.0 g/L. ADAMTS13 activity 65 percent (normal). Stool PCR for Shiga toxin and stool culture for STEC are negative on two specimens. C3 0.48 g/L (low), C4 0.18 g/L (normal). Urinalysis: blood 2+, protein 2+. ANA, ANCA negative.

data_table.Examination: Pale, petechiae, no oedema, no diarrhoea
data_table.Investigations: MAHA, plt 32, Cr 184, ADAMTS13 65%, STEC negative x2, low C3 normal C4, family hx

lead_in: Which feature most strongly suggests atypical (complement-mediated) HUS over STEC-HUS?

options.text: Absent diarrhoeal prodrome with negative STEC PCR plus a relevant family history
The combined finding of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
Sustained hypertension above the 95th centile for age and patient height
Measured ADAMTS13 activity within the normal range above 10 percent
A recent upper respiratory tract infection within the preceding 2 weeks period

stem:
A 6-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote NT community is reviewed in clinic with 3 days of dark urine, periorbital puffiness and reduced urine output. Two weeks earlier he was treated with topical mupirocin for impetigo on his legs. He has no rash now, no joint swelling and no abdominal pain. On examination he has periorbital and ankle oedema, BP 142/92 mmHg (above the 99th centile for age and height), HR 96, RR 24, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 99 percent RA.

Chest is clear with no crackles, abdomen soft, no organomegaly. Urinalysis: blood 4+, protein 2+, leucocytes negative; dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts on microscopy. Bloods: urea 11.2 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, sodium 134, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 22, albumin 34 g/L, C3 0.38 g/L (low), C4 0.22 g/L (normal), anti-DNase B elevated, ASO elevated. ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM negative. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys with no hydronephrosis. He has had no headache and no seizures and is currently asymptomatic from his hypertension. He is mid-feed.

data_table.Examination: Periorbital and ankle oedema, chest clear, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Cr 92, low C3, normal C4, anti-DNase B raised, blood 4+ protein 2+ RBC casts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: High-dose oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 with low-salt diet and review in 1 week
Urgent renal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis before commencing treatment
Commence ACE inhibitor and plasma exchange for proteinuria with hypertension
Discharge home with strict salt restriction and outpatient nephrology review in 2 weeks
Admit for fluid and salt restriction, antihypertensive treatment, and oral phenoxymethylpenicillin

stem:
A first-time mother attends with her 2-week-old ex-39-week breastfed son. The family has booked a religious circumcision next week. The infant is thriving, alert and well, with no jaundice, normal scrotum with bilateral palpable descended testes, and no inguinal hernia. The penis shows a glanular meatus opening on the ventral surface of the glans rather than the tip, a hooded incomplete dorsal foreskin, and mild ventral chordee on tractioned examination.

There is no scrotal involvement, no bifid scrotum and no perineal abnormality. He passes urine in a normal forward stream. Antenatal scans showed no renal tract abnormality. Newborn examination at birth was documented as normal but appears to have missed these features. Paediatric urology offers outpatient review within 8 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Glanular ventral meatus, hooded incomplete foreskin, mild ventral chordee, normal scrotum and testes
data_table.History: Voiding normally, antenatal scans normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice, and is karyotyping required?

options.text: Proceed with the planned circumcision because voiding is normal and the cosmetic ventral curvature is not clinically significant in this otherwise well infant
Defer circumcision and refer to paediatric urology for distal hypospadias with mild chordee; prepuce will be used for reconstruction at 6-18 months; karyotype not required
Proceed with partial circumcision preserving the dorsal hood for future repair, accepting some risk to future reconstructive options for the hypospadias
Reassure as a normal anatomical variant and arrange no follow-up
Arrange karyotype and pelvic ultrasound to exclude a disorder of sex development as part of the workup for the ventral meatal opening

stem:
A term infant phenotypically appearing male is reviewed at the bedside on day 1 of life. Pregnancy was uneventful with no maternal androgen exposure. The 20-week morphology scan reported male genitalia and normal renal tract. The midwife asks for an opinion. On examination the infant has a penoscrotal meatus, marked ventral chordee, a bifid scrotum with rugation but only one palpable gonad in the right hemiscrotum, and the left side is empty with no palpable gonad in the inguinal canal.

There is no hyperpigmentation of the genitalia. The infant is well perfused, vitals normal for age, feeding established, has passed meconium and urine. Birth weight is on the 50th centile and anthropometry is otherwise normal. There is no family history of disorders of sex development, infertility or salt-wasting illness. Bedside electrolytes are pending; urea, sodium and potassium are reported normal on a sample taken at delivery.

The family asks about birth registration and naming. The newborn screen has not yet been collected. The neonatal unit has access to paediatric endocrinology and urology on call.

data_table.Examination: Penoscrotal meatus, marked chordee, bifid scrotum, right palpable gonad, left non-palpable
data_table.Investigations: Bedside Na/K normal; newborn screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer sex assignment, arrange urgent karyotype, pelvic ultrasound and 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Plan single-stage hypospadias repair at 6 months and routine paediatric follow up
Reassure the family this is isolated distal hypospadias not requiring further workup
Commence empirical oral hydrocortisone replacement therapy pending karyotype and biochemistry results
Discharge with outpatient urology review in 6 weeks for hypospadias assessment

stem:
An 11-month-old, ex-39-week, fully vaccinated boy is reviewed by his GP after a community child and family health nurse documented a non-palpable left testis at the 9-month well-child check. Newborn examination at birth noted bilateral palpable testes, but the 6-week and 4-month checks documented a left testis that retracted into the inguinal canal and was difficult to bring into the scrotum.

The right testis has been consistently scrotal. He is on the 75th centile, developing normally, and there are no other genitourinary concerns. On examination today he is well, and the right testis is in the dependent scrotum. The left testis is palpable in the superficial inguinal pouch and can be manipulated into the upper scrotum but immediately retracts on release with no traction tolerance and no stable scrotal position.

There is no inguinal hernia, no hydrocele, the penis is normal and his abdomen is unremarkable. The mother asks whether her son needs an operation and when. The local paediatric surgical service has a 6-month waiting list for elective orchidopexy.

data_table.Examination: Left testis palpable in superficial inguinal pouch, will not stay in scrotum; right testis scrotal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure as retractile testis and review at the 4-year preschool check
Refer to paediatric surgery for orchidopexy planned between 12 and 18 months
Refer for orchidopexy at age 4 years to minimise anaesthetic risk in infancy
Commence hormonal therapy with human chorionic gonadotropin for 6 weeks
Arrange inguinal ultrasound to locate the testis before any referral decision

stem:
A term, phenotypically male newborn is reviewed in the postnatal ward at 18 hours of age. Pregnancy was uneventful with no maternal androgen exposure. The 20-week scan reported male genitalia. The neonatal examination raises concern. The infant is alert, has stable vitals for age (HR 138, RR 46, SpO2 98 percent RA), capillary refill 2 s, normal cardiac auscultation, soft non-tender abdomen with no masses and no inguinal swellings.

Genital examination shows a normal-sized phallus with a glanular meatus, no chordee, but the scrotum is small, mildly rugated and EMPTY bilaterally with NO palpable gonads in either scrotum or along the inguinal canals. There is no hyperpigmentation. Family history is unremarkable; there is no consanguinity and no relatives with infertility, salt-wasting illness or ambiguous genitalia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 46, SpO2 98%, cap refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Normal phallus, empty bilaterally rugated scrotum, NO gonads palpable on either side
data_table.History: No family DSD or salt-wasting history; feeding established

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, electrolytes and paediatric endocrine review
Discharge with outpatient paediatric surgical review at 6 weeks for bilateral cryptorchidism
Arrange laparoscopic exploration in the first week to locate intra-abdominal gonads
Commence empirical IM hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone for presumed salt-wasting CAH
Reassure parents this is constitutional and recheck at the 6-week well-child examination

stem:
A primigravida attends a postnatal ward review at 8 hours after an uncomplicated term vaginal birth. The 32-week growth scan reported isolated SFU grade 2 left hydronephrosis with renal pelvis anteroposterior diameter 8 mm, normal contralateral kidney, normal ureters, normal bladder, normal amniotic fluid index and no other anomalies. The male infant (ex-40-week) is breastfeeding well, alert, well perfused with normal vitals.

Examination: normal cardiorespiratory examination, no flank masses, bilateral descended testes, normal penis with glanular meatus, no spinal abnormality, normal hip examination, and a documented strong urinary stream. No family history of renal disease, VUR or consanguinity. The hospital offers outpatient renal ultrasound from day of life 4 onwards. Discharge home is planned for tomorrow.

data_table.Examination: Normal newborn, no flank masses, normal genitalia, strong urinary stream observed
data_table.Antenatal: SFU grade 2 left hydronephrosis, AP diameter 8 mm at 32 weeks, normal ureters/bladder/AFI

lead_in: When should the postnatal renal tract ultrasound be performed, and what additional imaging (if any) is needed at this stage?

options.text: Within the first 24 hours of life before discharge from the postnatal ward, plus a routine MCUG before discharge regardless of severity grade
Within the first 12 hours of life with a concurrent MCUG before any postnatal feeds or planned discharge from the postnatal ward
At 3 months of age routinely regardless of severity grade, without any earlier postnatal imaging or paediatric urology specialist input
Only if the infant develops a febrile illness or fails to thrive; with no routine postnatal imaging otherwise, regardless of grade
Renal tract ultrasound between day 4 and 6 weeks of life as an outpatient; MCUG NOT required for isolated SFU 1-2; reserve MCUG for SFU 3-4 or suspected PUV

stem:
A 9-year-old previously well prepubertal boy (Tanner 1) presents to a regional ED with 24 hours of gradually worsening pain at the upper pole of the right testis. The pain is localised and dull rather than severe and has not been associated with nausea, vomiting or systemic upset. He has had no trauma, no urinary symptoms and no urethral discharge.

His parents have noticed a small dark spot through the scrotal skin. He is alert and afebrile with normal vitals. The right hemiscrotum has mild diffuse swelling. The testis lies in normal vertical orientation with a normal cremasteric reflex. There is a discrete 5 mm point of tenderness at the UPPER POLE of the testis with a visible bluish discolouration through the thinned scrotal skin. The remainder of the testis is non-tender and palpable in normal position. The epididymis is non-tender. Urinalysis is negative.

data_table.Examination: Tenderness localised to upper pole; visible blue dot; testis in vertical lie, cremasteric reflex present
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and most appropriate management is correct?

options.text: Acute testicular torsion; immediate scrotal exploration without imaging given the absolute time-sensitivity of testicular salvage in suspected torsion
Torsion of the appendix testis (torted hydatid); analgesia and rest with safety-net advice that the appendage infarcts spontaneously over 7-14 days
Bacterial epididymo-orchitis from urinary pathogens; commence oral cefalexin and arrange urology outpatient follow-up within one week of presentation
Idiopathic scrotal oedema; observation alone with reassurance that the painless erythema resolves over 2-3 days without specific intervention
Incarcerated indirect inguinal hernia; immediate surgical reduction in theatre with paediatric general surgery to prevent bowel ischaemia or strangulation

stem:
A 14-year-old boy attends a metropolitan ED at 02:00 with the third episode in 6 months of acute left testicular pain. Previous episodes lasted 30-90 minutes and resolved spontaneously before he could be assessed. Tonight the pain started 4 hours ago, was severe, associated with vomiting and lower abdominal radiation, and has now partially settled to a moderate ache. He has had no trauma, no urinary symptomsexually active.

He is Tanner 4. He has no significant past medical history, takes no regular medications and has no allergies. On arrival he is afebrile with HR 92, BP 118/68, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent. The left hemiscrotum is mildly swollen. The left testis is now in a normal vertical lie, mildly tender diffusely, the cremasteric reflex is present but sluggish on the left and brisk on the right, and there is no erythema.

The right testis lies high in the scrotum on a horizontal axis (transverse lie) with a bell-clapper appearance. Urinalysis is negative. A formal scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler within 30 minutes reports normal symmetric arterial flow bilaterally with a heterogeneous left testis and a small reactive hydrocele. The on-call paediatric surgical fellow is reviewing the case.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/68, SpO2 99%, afebrile
data_table.Examination: Left testis vertical, sluggish cremasteric reflex; right testis high/transverse - bell-clapper
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative. USS Doppler: symmetric flow, heterogeneous left testis, reactive hydrocele

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient urology review given normal Doppler flow
Admit for observation with serial scrotal examinations and repeat Doppler later
Arrange same-day MRI scrotum to characterise testicular perfusion and architecture
Proceed to urgent scrotal exploration with bilateral orchidopexy regardless of Doppler
Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline for presumed epididymo-orchitis
